Chapter 1
Introduction

In this thesis, we have studied certain geometric structures over Lie groupoids and differentiable stacks.

A Lie groupoid is a groupoid
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
, where
\mathcal{G}_{0},\mathcal{G}_{1}
are smooth manifolds, the maps
s,t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
are submersions, and all other structure maps are smooth maps. The notion of a Lie groupoid covers many interesting geometric structures over a manifold. For example,

•

a Lie group action on a manifold
M
assigns a Lie groupoid whose base is
M
,

•

a principal
G
-bundle over a manifold
M
assigns a Lie groupoid whose base is
M
,

•

a vector bundle over a manifold
M
assigns a Lie groupoid whose base is
M
,

•

a foliation on a manifold
M
assigns a Lie groupoid whose base is
M
.

Some standard “textbook references” for the notion of Lie groupoids are
[
49
,
43
,
44
]
.

The geometric structures over Lie groupoids that we study in this thesis are Lie groupoid extensions and principal bundles over Lie groupoids (
Chapters

3
and
4
).

A Lie groupoid extension is a morphism of Lie groupoids
(F,1_{M}):[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
, such that,
F:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}
is (at least) a surjective submersion. Various author require different conditions on the map
F
. We ask
F
to be a surjective submersion. The notion of (and other geometric structures on) Lie groupoid extensions is discussed, for example, in
[
47
,
39
,
31
]
.

Let
G
be a Lie group. The principal
G
-bundles over a manifold have a rich geometric structure, and many interesting questions arise out of it. Motivated by the notion of principal bundle over a manifold, we introduce the notion of a principal
G
-bundle over a Lie groupoid. Let
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
be a Lie groupoid. A principal
G
-bundle over
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
is given by a principal
G
-bundle
E_{G}\rightarrow X_{0}
, over the manifold
X_{0}
, with an action of the Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
on
E_{G}
, such that the action of
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
and
G
on
E_{G}
are compatible. The notion of principal
G
-bundles over a Lie groupoid cover the following classical cases of principal bundles:

•

a principal
G
-bundle over a Lie groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows M]
is a principal
G
-bundle over the manifold
M
,

•

a principal
G
-bundle over a Lie groupoid
[H\times M\rightrightarrows M]
is an
H
-equivariant principal
G
-bundle over the manifold
M
.

Some of the papers that discuss (geometric structures on) principal bundle over Lie groupoids are
[
11
,
40
,
48
,
66
]
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category, and
\mathcal{J}
be a Grothendieck topology on
\mathcal{C}
. We call the pair
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
to be a site. A stack over the site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
can be thought of as a “generalized object” of the category
\mathcal{C}
. To explain the terminology of “generalized object” of the category
\mathcal{C}
, we need to recall the Yoneda lemma (Yoneda embedding) of category theory.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a (locally-small) category. Let
A
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
. Consider the functor of points
h_{A}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
. This assigns a functor
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow[\mathcal{C}^{\op},\text{Set}]
. The Yoneda embedding says that this functor
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow[\mathcal{C}^{\op},\text{Set}]
is an embedding of categories. So, we see the objects of
[\mathcal{C}^{\op},\text{Set}]
as “generalized objects of
\mathcal{C}
”.

Once we fix a Grothendieck topology on
\mathcal{C}
, we can talk about the notion of covering of an object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
. Using this notion of a covering, we can restrict our attention to functors
\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
that are “locally determined”. A functor
\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
that is locally determined is called a sheaf on the site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
. So, sheaves on
\mathcal{C}
should be seen as a generalized object of
\mathcal{C}
. We want to ensure that this Grothendieck topology is such that the functors
h_{A}
, for each object
A
, are “locally determined”. A Grothendieck topology on
\mathcal{C}
for which
h_{A}
is locally determined for each object
A
of
\mathcal{C}
is called a subcanonical site.

Let us further generalize the notion of sheaf by considering “maps” from
\mathcal{C}
that takes values in categories instead of sets. By “maps”, we actually mean pseudo-functors on
\mathcal{C}
. A pseudo-functor on a category consists of the following data:

•

a category for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a functor for each morphism
U\rightarrow V
of
\mathcal{C}
,

satisfying certain compatibility conditions. Fixing a Grothendieck topology
\mathcal{J}
on
\mathcal{C}
, we can also declare the notion for a pseudo-functor to be “locally determined”. We call a locally determined pseudo-functor to be a stack on the site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
. Some standard references for the notion of stacks are
[
67
,
63
,
38
,
32
]
.

In this thesis, we are interested in stacks on the category
\mathcal{C}=\text{Man}
, equipped with the Grothendieck topology
\mathcal{J}
defined by the open cover topology. One can define “many” stacks over the site
(\text{Man},\mathcal{J})
. We have mentioned that, for each object of the category
Man
, we have a stack over the site
(\text{Man},\mathcal{J})
. To work with stacks coming from manifolds would be uninteresting, and to work with arbitrary stacks over
(\text{Man},\mathcal{J})
would be too general. So, in this thesis, we settle with stacks that come from Lie groupoids. The stacks that come from Lie groupoids are called differentiable stacks.

In particular, the geometric structures over differentiable stacks that we study in this thesis are gerbes over differentiable stacks and principal bundles over differentiable stacks (
Chapters

3
and
5
).

A gerbe over a topological space
X
is a sheaf of groupoids on
X
that is “locally connected” and “locally non-empty” (
[
47
, Definition
3.1
]
). The notion of a gerbe over a stack is a generalization of the notion of a gerbe over a topological space. A gerbe over a differentiable stack is a morphism of differentiable stacks satisfying some conditions similar to “locally non-emptiness” and “locally connectedness” (
[
6
, Definition

4.7
]
). Some papers that discuss (geometric structures on) gerbes over differentiable stacks are
[
6
,
5
,
31
]
. In
[
6
]
the authors discuss connections and curvature for groupoid central
S^{1}
-extensions. They also describe a prequantization result for principal
S^{1}
-bundles and
S^{1}
-gerbes. In
[
31
]
the authors give a one-one correspondence between principal
[\text{Aut}(G)\rtimes G\rightrightarrows G]
-bundles over differentiable stacks and
G
-gerbes over differentiable stacks. There is a different notion of gerbe, introduced by M.K. Murray, which are called
bundle gerbes
(
[
50
, Section
3
]
). In
[
51
]
the author gives an exposition of the notion of bundle gerbe and relates them to the Hitchin-Chatterjee gerbes (
[
35
,
20
]
). In
[
2
]
the authors discuss a higher version of principal bundles, which they call the nonabelian bundle gerbes. They also study the connection, curvature, gauge transformations of such higher principal bundles.

As mentioned earlier, a differentiable stack is the same as a Morita equivalence class of a Lie groupoid. The notion of principal bundle over Lie groupoid is “Morita invariant”, thus giving the notion of principal bundles over differentiable stacks. In (the lecture notes)
[
33
]
, the author gives a detailed exposition to differentiable stacks and their cohomology. In
[
10
]
the authors determine a criterion for a principal bundle (over a root stack) to have an algebraic connection. The notion of parallel transport on principal bundles over differentiable stacks is studied in
[
24
]
. A slight generalization of the notion of principal
G
-bundle over a differentiable stack, namely principal
[H/G]
-bundle over a differentiable stack, for a Lie crossed module
(G,H,\tau,\alpha)
is studied in
[
30
]
. The principal
S^{1}
-bundles over differentiable stacks are the main content of the study in
[
5
]
.

In
Chapter

6
, we study some topological structures over topological stacks. A topological stack is a stack over the category
\mathcal{C}=\text{Top}
, with the Grothendieck topology being the open cover topology.
In
[
54
,
53
]
the author give an exposition to the notion of topological stacks. In his thesis
[
18
]
, David Carchedi gives a detailed primer on topological and differentiable stacks. In
[
46
]
, the author offers a detailed comparison between topological and differentiable stacks. In
[
19
]
, the author discusses topological stacks arising out of Cartesian closed categories. Algebraic topological properties of topological stacks, for example, singular chains, fibrations, Homotopy types, mapping stacks, and fundamental groups, are discussed in
[
25
,
58
,
57
,
56
,
55
,
28
]
. In this thesis, we introduce the notion of topological groupoid extension and study some topological properties of such extensions.

Contents of the thesis

Preliminaries

In
Chapter

2
, we have recalled some standard material from different backgrounds of category theory and differential geometry.

In

2.1
, we have recalled some background from category theory and

-category theory. Some references on which this section is based are

,

,

]

In
Section

, we have recalled the notions of fibered categories, pseudo-functors, and stacks. This section is mainly based on Angelo Vistoli’s “Grothendieck topologies, fibered categories, and descent
theory”
[
67
]
.

In
Section

, we have recalled the necessary background of Lie groupoids, Morita equivalence, and differentiable stacks. We have used

,

,

]
as references for this section.

In

, we have recalled the notion of Atiyah sequence and Chern-Weil theory for principal bundles over the smooth manifold. This section is mainly based on

.

1.1.2
On two notions of a gerbe over a stack

In
Chapter

3
, based on our paper
[
21
]
, we have given a correspondence between two notions of a gerbe over a stack.

The notion of gerbes was introduced by Giraud in
[
32
]
to study nonabelian cohomology. An algebraic geometry point of view of gerbes are studied by Breen in
[
13
,
14
]
, and by Breen and Messing in
[
15
]
. Nonabelian gerbes over manifolds are studied in
[
45
,
60
,
61
]
. The abelian bundle gerbe is introduced by Murray (
[
50
,
51
]
). The notion of a nonabelian bundle gerbe is introduced by Aschieri, Jurco, Cantini in
[
2
]
. The paper
[
52
]
discusses four equivalent versions of nonabelian gerbes.

The outline of this chapter is as follows:

In
Section

3.1
, we have recalled the two existing notions of a gerbe over a stack (one is a morphism of stacks
Definition

3.1.6
, the other is a morphism of Lie groupoids
Definition

3.1.5
). We give some examples of a gerbe over a differentiable stack.

In
Section

3.2
, we start with the definition of a gerbe over a stack. Assuming an extra condition on a gerbe over a stack, we associate a Lie groupoid extension. This is done in multiple steps. Given a gerbe over a stack
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, we first, prove that, there exists a special kind of atlas
q:\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
for
\mathcal{C}
, and a morphism of stacks
p:\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
with some compatibility conditions. Using the property that the diagonal morphism associated to the morphism
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism, we prove that
p:\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism of stacks. We then use our assumption that the diagonal morphism is a representable surjective submersion to prove that
p:\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas. These atlases give Lie groupoids for
\mathcal{D},\mathcal{C}
. We prove that this morphism of stacks
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
thus associates a morphism of Lie groupoids (that is, a Lie groupoid extension).

In
Section

3.3
we have proved that the morphism of stacks associated to a Lie groupoid extension is a gerbe over a stack.
Firstly, we have associated a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle for a morphism of Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
(
Section

3.3.1
). We have then assigned a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
for a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle (
Section

3.3.2
). Combining these two constructions, we have a description of assigning a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
for a morphism of Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
. Finally, in
Section

3.3.4
, we proved that the morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
, associated to a Lie groupoid extension
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
, is a gerbe over the stack
B\mathcal{H}
.

1.1.3
Chern-Weil theory for principal bundles over Lie groupoids

In
Chapter

4
, we have assigned a Chern-Weil map for a principal bundle over Lie groupoid using the Atiyah sequence approach.

Let
G
be a Lie group,
M
a smooth manifold, and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle. The standard way to introduce the notion of connection on
P(M,G)
is in terms of differential forms (and distributions). The notion of connection can also be seen as splitting of the Atiyah sequence of the
G
-bundle
P(M,G)
. The Atiyah sequence is a short exact sequence

0\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow(TP)/G\rightarrow TM\rightarrow 0,

of vector bundles over the manifold
M
.

In this chapter, we introduce the notion of a connection on a principal bundle over a Lie groupoid using the notion of the Atiyah sequence.

Let
G
be a Lie group,
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
a Lie groupoid. A principal
G
-bundle over
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
is a principal
G
-bundle
E_{G}\rightarrow X_{0}
over the manifold
X_{0}
, with an action of
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
on
E_{G}
, that is compatible with the action of
G
on
E_{G}
. This notion of principal bundles
(E_{G}\rightarrow X_{0},[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}])
include the example of principal bundle over a manifold, equivariant principal bundles.

In
[
40
]
the authors introduced the Chern-Weil map from a different point of view. In our paper, we use the Atiyah sequence approach. It turns out that an extra structure of a connection on
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
is necessary to get a short exact sequence of vector bundles over
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
, which we call the Atiyah sequence associated to the principal bundle
(E_{G}\rightarrow X_{0},[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}])
. A vector bundle over a Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
is a vector bundle
E\rightarrow X_{0}
over the manifold
X_{0}
with an action of
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
on
E
such that the induced maps on fibers of
E\rightarrow X_{0}
are linear maps.

The outline of this chapter is as follows:

In
Section

4.1
, we introduce the notion of principal bundles over Lie groupoids. Some standard references for this notion are
[
11
,
40
,
48
,
66
]
. In
Definition

4.1.9
, we introduce the notion of a connection on a Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
. Using this notion of connection, we turn the tangent bundle
TX_{0}\rightarrow X_{0}
into a vector bundle over the Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
(
Section

4.1.2
).

In
Section

4.2
, we introduce the notion of Atiyah sequence associated to a principal bundle
(E_{G}\rightarrow X_{0},[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}])
, as a short exact sequence of vector bundles over the Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
.

In
Section

4.3
, we introduce the notion of differential form on a Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
, equipped with an integrable connection
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
. We also prove some results about differential forms on Lie groupoids (
Lemma

4.3.3
,
Proposition

4.3.5
,
Proposition

4.3.6
).

In
Section

4.4
, we assign differential
1
-form (on Lie groupoid
[s^{*}E_{G}\rightrightarrows E_{G}]
) associated to a connection
\mathcal{D}
on the principal bundle
(E_{G}\rightarrow X_{0},[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}])
. In
Section

4.5
, we associate a differential
2
-form (on the Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
) associated to a connection
\mathcal{D}
on
(E_{G}\rightarrow X_{0},[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}])
.

In
Section

4.6
, we first introduce the notion of de Rham cohomology of the pair
(\mathbb{X},\mathcal{H})
(
Section

4.6.1
). Imitating the construction of the Chern-Weil map for a principal bundle over a manifold, we introduce the notion of Chern-Weil map for a principal bundle over a Lie groupoid (
Section

4.6.2
).

1.1.4
Connections on principal bundles over differentiable stacks

In
Chapter

5
, we have introduced the notion of connection on principal bundles over differentiable stacks.

Let
G
be a Lie group, and
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
a Lie groupoid. There is a notion of pullback of a principal bundle along a morphism of Lie groupoids, and more generally, along a “generalized morphism of Lie groupoids”. It is a standard result that, under this notion of pullback of a principal bundle along generalized morphism of Lie groupoids, for two Morita equivalent Lie groupoids
\mathbb{X},\mathbb{Y}
, there is an equivalence of categories between category of principal bundles over
\mathbb{X}
and category of principal bundles over
\mathbb{Y}
(
[
40
, Corollary
2.12
]
). As a differentiable stack is a Morita equivalence class of a Lie groupoid, the notion of principal bundle over Lie groupoid induces the notion of principal bundle over a differentiable stack. The notion of parallel transport on principal bundles over differentiable stacks is studied in
[
24
]
.

The outline of this chapter is as follows:

In
Section

5.1
, we recall the notion of principal bundles over differentiable stacks. This notion of principal bundle over differentiable stacks can be found in
[
24
,
33
,
6
]
.

In
Definition

5.2.1
, we introduce the notion of connection on a principal bundle over differentiable stacks. In
Section

5.3
, we introduce the Atiyah sequence for a principal bundle over a Deligne-Mumford stack. We also mention some results about connection on principal bundle over differentiable stacks.

1.1.5
Extensions of topological groupoids

In
Chapter

6
, we introduce the notion of topological groupoid extensions and study their correspondence with gerbes over topological stacks.

In
Section

6.1
, we recall the notion of topological groupoids and topological stacks. These notions can be found in
[
18
,
46
,
54
]
.

In
Section

6.3
, we introduce the notion of topological groupoid extension. We prove that the morphism of stacks associated to a topological groupoid extension is a gerbe over a topological stack. In
Section

6.4
, we recall the notions of Serre/Hurewicz stacks and see some results about gerbes over Serre/Hurewicz stacks.

1.1.6
Future directions of research

There are several possible directions of enquiries may emerge out of this thesis. Here we mention some of them. One can think of extending the correspondence discussed in
Chapter

3
for a gerbe over stack with a connection. It would be interesting to relate our Chern-Weil theory developed in
Chapters

4
and
5
with simplicial homotopy theoritic ideas introduced in
[
29
]
. Another more ambitious project would be to apply our constructions to study the notion of gerbes over an algebraic stack.

Preliminaries

In this chapter, we recall some preliminaries needed for the thesis. This chapter is split into four sections:

Category theory and

)

Fibered categories, pseudo-functors, and stacks (

2.1
Category theory and
2
-category theory

In this section, we recall some of the standard terminology, examples, results from the category theory and the
2
-category theory. The content of this section is mostly standard, and can be found in books, such as
[
12
,
34
,
62
]
.

Definition 2.1.1

(Category)
.

A
category, denoted as
\mathcal{C}
, consists of the following data:

•

a class
\mathcal{C}_{0}
, whose elements are called
objects of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a class
\mathcal{C}_{1}
, whose elements are called
morphisms of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a map
s_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{0}
, called
the source map of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a map
t_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{0}
, called
the target map of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a map
m_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{t_{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{C}_{0},s_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{1}
, called
the composition map of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a map
e_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{1}
, called
the identity map of
\mathcal{C}
,

satisfying the following conditions:

•

s_{\mathcal{C}}\circ m_{\mathcal{C}}=s_{\mathcal{C}}\circ\pr_{1}
, and
t_{\mathcal{C}}\circ m_{\mathcal{C}}=t_{\mathcal{C}}\circ\pr_{2}
,

•

s_{\mathcal{C}}\circ e_{\mathcal{C}}=1_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}
, and
t_{\mathcal{C}}\circ e_{\mathcal{C}}=1_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}
,

•

m_{\mathcal{C}}\circ(m_{\mathcal{C}},1_{\mathcal{C}_{1}})=m_{\mathcal{C}}\circ(1_{\mathcal{C}_{1}},m_{\mathcal{C}})
,

•

m_{\mathcal{C}}(f,e_{\mathcal{C}}(a))=f
for all
a\in C_{0}
, and
f\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
with
t_{\mathcal{C}}(f)=a
,

•

m_{\mathcal{C}}(e_{\mathcal{C}}(a),f)=f
for all
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, and
f\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
with
s_{\mathcal{C}}(f)=a
.

A category, with all the associated maps, can be expressed by the following diagram,

\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}\mathcal{C}_{1}\xrightarrow{m_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}_{1}{\mathrel{\to}^{s_{\mathcal{C}}}_{t_{\mathcal{C}}}}\mathcal{C}_{0}\xrightarrow{e_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}_{1}.

However, often, we use a less elaborate notation and denote a category as
[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]
. We call the maps
s_{\mathcal{C}},t_{\mathcal{C}},m_{\mathcal{C}},e_{\mathcal{C}}
to be the structure maps of the category
\mathcal{C}
. When there is no confusion, we ignore the subscript
\mathcal{C}
in structure maps and write them as
s,t,m,e
. The classes
\mathcal{C}_{0}
, and
\mathcal{C}_{1}
will be denoted alternatively as
\text{Obj}(\mathcal{C})
, and
\text{Mor}(\mathcal{C})
respectively.

Remark 2.1.2

(Notation)
.

For
(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})\in\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{t_{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{C}_{0},s_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we denote the element
m_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})
as
\gamma_{2}\circ\gamma_{1}
.
For
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we denote the element
e_{\mathcal{C}}(a)
by
1_{a}
. With this notations, the conditions in the definition of a category can be seen as the following:

•

for all
(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})\in\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we have
s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma_{2}\circ\gamma_{1})=s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma_{1})
, and
t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma_{2}\circ\gamma_{1})=t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma_{2})
,

•

for all
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we have
s_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{a})=a
and
t_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{a})=a
,

•

for all
(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3})\in\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we have
\gamma_{3}\circ(\gamma_{2}\circ\gamma_{1})=(\gamma_{3}\circ\gamma_{2})\circ\gamma_{1}
,

•

for all
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0},\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
, with
s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma)=a
, we have
\gamma\circ 1_{a}=\gamma
,

•

for all
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0},\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
, with
t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma)=a
, we have
1_{a}\circ\gamma=\gamma
.

For
\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
with
s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma)=a
and
t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma)=b
, we say that,
\gamma
is a
morphism from
a
to
b
. For
a,b\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we denote the collection
\{\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}:s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma)=a,t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma)=b\}
, as
\mathcal{C}(a,b)
. An element
\gamma
of
\mathcal{C}(a,b)
is denoted as
\gamma:a\rightarrow b
.

Remark 2.1.3
.

Depending on the “size of the class
\mathcal{C}_{1}
”, we call a category
\mathcal{C}
to be a small, or, a locally-small, or, a large category. A category
\mathcal{C}
in which
\mathcal{C}_{1}
is a set, is called a
small category
. A category
\mathcal{C}
, in which
\mathcal{C}(a,b)
is a set for each
a,b\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, is called a
locally-small category
. A category
\mathcal{C}
, in which
\mathcal{C}(a,b)
is not a set for some
a,b\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, is called a
large category
. In this thesis we will not discuss such foundational issues in much detail.

In this thesis, our primary interest would be a special kind of small categories, namely, Lie groupoids.

Example 2.1.4
.

Let
M
be a set. Consider the category
[M\rightrightarrows M]
, whose object class is the set
M
, whose morphism class is the set
M
. All the structure maps are identity maps. We call
[M\rightrightarrows M]
to be the
discrete category associated to the set
M
. In particular, when
M
has the structure of a smooth manifold, we get a category
[M\rightrightarrows M]
, which we call
the category associated to the smooth manifold
M
.

Example 2.1.5
.

Let
G
be a group. Consider the category
[G\rightrightarrows*]
, whose object class is the singleton set
\{*\}
, whose morphism class is the set
G
. The source, target maps are given by the constant map that takes every element of
G
to the element
*
. The composition map
m:G\times G\rightarrow G
is the group operation. The identity map
*\rightarrow G
is the map that takes
*
to the identity element
e_{G}
. We call
[G\rightrightarrows*]
to be the
category associated to the group
G
. In particular, when
G
has the structure of a Lie group, we get a category
[G\rightrightarrows*]
, which we call
the category associated to the Lie group
G
.

Example 2.1.6
.

Let
G
be a group,
M
a set, and
\mu:M\times G\rightarrow M
an action of the group
G
on the set
M
. Consider the category
[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]
with the following description:

•

the source map is given by the first projection,

•

the target map is given by the action map,

•

the composition map is given by
((m_{1},g_{1}),(m_{2},g_{2}))\mapsto(m_{1},g_{1}g_{2})
,

•

the identity map is given by
m\mapsto(m,e_{G})
.

We call
[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]
to be the
category associated to the action of
G
on
M
. In particular, when
G
is a Lie group,
M
a smooth manifold, and
\mu
an action of Lie group on manifold, we call
[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]
to be the
category associated to the Lie group action of
G
on
M
.

Definition 2.1.7

(Groupoid)
.

A
groupoid
is a category
\mathcal{C}
(with structure maps
(s_{\mathcal{C}},t_{\mathcal{C}},m_{\mathcal{C}},e_{\mathcal{C}})
) along with a map
i_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{1}
such that, the following conditions are satisfied:

•

s_{\mathcal{C}}\circ i_{\mathcal{C}}=t_{\mathcal{C}}
, and
t_{\mathcal{C}}\circ i_{\mathcal{C}}=s_{\mathcal{C}}
,

•

m_{\mathcal{C}}\circ(1_{\mathcal{C}_{1}},i_{\mathcal{C}})=e_{\mathcal{C}}\circ s_{\mathcal{C}}
, and
m_{\mathcal{C}}\circ(i_{\mathcal{C}},1_{\mathcal{C}_{1}})=e_{\mathcal{C}}\circ t_{\mathcal{C}}
.

Remark 2.1.8

(Notation)
.

In a groupoid
\mathcal{C}
, for an element
\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we call
i(\gamma)
as,
the inverse of
\gamma
and denote by
\gamma^{-1}
. The first condition in the above definition says that
s(\gamma)=t(\gamma^{-1})
, and
t(\gamma)=s(\gamma^{-1})
. The second condition in the above definition says that, for
\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we have,

\gamma\circ\gamma^{-1}=1_{t(\gamma)}
, and
\gamma^{-1}\circ\gamma=1_{s(\gamma)}
.

Example 2.1.9
.

All the three examples
[M\rightrightarrows M],[G\rightrightarrows*]
, and
[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]
, mentioned as

Examples

2.1.4
,
2.1.5
and
2.1.6
are groupoids. The maps
i_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{1}
for these categories have the following description:

•

the map
M\rightarrow M
, defined as
m\mapsto m
for each
m\in M
,

•

the map
G\rightarrow G
, defined as
g\mapsto g^{-1}
for each
g\in G
,

•

the map
M\times G\rightarrow M\times G
, defined as
(m,g)\mapsto(mg,g^{-1})
for each
(m,g)\in M\times G
.

Definition 2.1.10

(Functor)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}=[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]
, and
\mathcal{D}=[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
be categories with structure maps given by
(s_{\mathcal{C}},t_{\mathcal{C}},m_{\mathcal{C}},e_{\mathcal{C}})
, and

(s_{\mathcal{D}},t_{\mathcal{D}},m_{\mathcal{D}},e_{\mathcal{D}})
respectively. A
functor from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{D}
, denoted as
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
, is given by a pair of maps

(F_{1}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1},F_{0}:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{0}),

such that, the following conditions are satisfied:

•

F_{0}\circ s_{\mathcal{C}}=s_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{1}
, and
F_{0}\circ t_{\mathcal{C}}=t_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{1}
,

•

F_{1}\circ m_{\mathcal{C}}=m_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(F_{1},F_{1})
,

•

F_{1}\circ e_{\mathcal{C}}=e_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{0}
.

One can express a functor
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
as the following diagram,

We simplify it by expressing a functor as the middle square in the above diagram. We denote a functor as
(F_{1},F_{0}):[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
.

Remark 2.1.11
.

In the definition of a functor, the condition
F_{0}\circ s_{\mathcal{C}}=s_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{1}
, and
F_{0}\circ t_{\mathcal{C}}=t_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{1}
, says that, for each
\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
, the element
F_{1}(\gamma)
is a morphism from
F_{0}(s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))
to
F_{0}(t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))
. In other words, for
\gamma:a\rightarrow b
in
\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we have
F_{1}(\gamma):F_{0}(a)\rightarrow F_{0}(b)
. The condition
F_{1}\circ m_{\mathcal{C}}=m_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(F_{1},F_{1})
says that, for each
(\gamma,\gamma^{\prime})\in\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we have
F_{1}(\gamma^{\prime}\circ\gamma)=F_{1}(\gamma^{\prime})\circ F_{1}(\gamma)
.
The condition
F_{1}\circ e_{\mathcal{C}}=e_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{0}
says that
F_{1}(1_{a})=1_{F_{0}(a)}
for all
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
. Thus, for each
a,b\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we have a map
\mathcal{C}(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(F_{0}(a),F_{0}(b))
.

Based on the properties satisfied by the map
\mathcal{C}(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(F_{0}(a),F_{0}(b))
, for each
a,b\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we name the functor
(F_{1},F_{0}):[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
.

Definition 2.1.12
.

A functor
(F_{1},F_{0}):[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
is said to be a
faithful (or full) functor
if, for each
a,b
in
\mathcal{C}_{0}
, the map

\mathcal{C}(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(F_{0}(a),F_{0}(b))
is an injective (or a surjective) map.

Example 2.1.13
.

Let
M,N
be smooth manifolds, and
f:M\rightarrow N
a smooth map. Then,
(f,f):[M\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[N\rightrightarrows N]
is a functor.

Example 2.1.14
.

Let
G,H
be Lie groups, and
f:G\rightarrow H
a Lie group homomorphism. Then,

(f,*):[G\rightrightarrows*]\rightarrow[H\rightrightarrows*]
is a functor.

Example 2.1.15
.

Let
G
be a Lie group, acting on smooth manifolds
M,N
. Let
f:M\rightarrow N
be a
G
-equivariant map, that is
f(mg)=f(m)g
for all
(m,g)\in M\times G
. Then,

(f\times 1,f):[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[N\times G\rightrightarrows N]

is a functor.

Definition 2.1.16

(composition of functors)
.

Let
\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}
, and
\mathcal{E}
be categories. Consider the functors
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
G:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
that are given by the maps
(F_{1}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1},F_{0}:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{0})
, and
(G_{1}:\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1},G_{0}:\mathcal{D}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{0})
respectively. Then, the maps

(G_{1}\circ F_{1}:\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1},G_{0}\circ F_{0}:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{0}),

gives a functor from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{E}
, which we call
the composition of
F,G
, and denote by
G\circ F
.

Definition 2.1.17

(Natural transformation)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}=[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]
and
\mathcal{D}=[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
be categories with structure maps given by
(s_{\mathcal{C}},t_{\mathcal{C}},m_{\mathcal{C}},e_{\mathcal{C}})
and

(s_{\mathcal{D}},t_{\mathcal{D}},m_{\mathcal{D}},e_{\mathcal{D}})
respectively. Let
(F_{1},F_{0})
, and
(G_{1},G_{0})
be functors from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{D}
. A
natural transformation
\eta
from
F
to
G
, denoted by
\eta:F\Rightarrow G
, is a map
\eta:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
, such that, the following conditions are satisfied:

•

s_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\eta=F_{0}
, and
t_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\eta=G_{0}
,

•

s_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\eta\circ t_{\mathcal{C}}=t_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{1}
, and
t_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\eta\circ s_{\mathcal{C}}=s_{\mathcal{D}}\circ G_{1}
,

•

m_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(F_{1},\eta\circ t_{\mathcal{C}})=m_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(\eta\circ s_{\mathcal{C}},G_{1})
as maps
\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
.

Remark 2.1.18
.

In the
Definition

2.1.17
, the condition
s_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\eta=F_{0}
, and
t_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\eta=G_{0}
says that, for each
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we have
\eta(a):F_{0}(a)\rightarrow G_{0}(a)
. The second condition says that, for each
\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
, the elements
\eta(t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma)),F_{1}(\gamma)
are composable, giving an element

\eta(t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))\circ F_{1}(\gamma)\in\mathcal{D}_{1}
. Similarly, the elements

G_{1}(\gamma),\eta(s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))
being composable, gives

G_{1}(\gamma)\circ\eta(s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))\in\mathcal{D}_{1}
. The third condition says that, for each
\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{1}
, we have

\eta(t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))\circ F_{1}(\gamma)=G_{1}(\gamma)\circ\eta(s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))
. If
\gamma\in\mathcal{C}(a,a^{\prime})
, then, the third condition says that the following diagram is commutative,

Definition 2.1.19

(Natural isomorphism)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}=[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}],\mathcal{D}=[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
be categories, and
(F_{1},F_{0}),(G_{1},G_{0}):[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
functors from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{D}
. A natural transformation
\eta:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
, from
F
to
G
, in which
\eta(a)
is an isomorphism for each
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, is called a
natural isomorphism from
(F_{1},F_{0})
to
(G_{1},G_{0})
.

Definition 2.1.20

(Equivalence of categories)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}=[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}],\mathcal{D}=[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
be categories. A functor
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is said to be
an equivalence of categories
, if, there exists a functor
G:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, such that, there are natural isomorphism of functors
F\circ G\Rightarrow 1_{\mathcal{D}}
, and
G\circ F\Rightarrow 1_{\mathcal{C}}
. An equivalence of categories is said to be an isomorphism of categories if the natural isomorphisms are given by identity maps. Two categories
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
are said to be
equivalent (or isomorphic) categories
if there is an equivalence (or an isomrophism) of categories
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
.

Theorem 2.1.21

(
[
42
, Theorem
4.4.1
]
)
.

The following properties of a functor
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
are logically equivalent:

1.

F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an equivalence of categories.

2.

F
is full and faithful, and each object
c\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
is isomorphic to
F(d)
for some object
d\in\mathcal{D}_{0}
.

To motivate the definition of a
2
-category,
using
Remark

2.1.2
, we rewrite the definition of a category (
Definition

2.1.1
).

(2.1.2)

The Diagram
2.1.1
is a fancy way of saying that
1_{y}\circ f=f
and
f\circ 1_{x}=f
for all
f\in\mathcal{C}(x,y)
.
The Diagram
2.1.2
says that
h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f
for all
(f,g,h)\in\mathcal{C}(x,y)\times\mathcal{C}(y,z)\times\mathcal{C}(z,w)
.

Example 2.1.23
.

Let
X
be a topological space. Consider a category
\mathcal{O}(X)
, with the following description:

•

objects are open subsets of
X
,

•

for open sets
U,V
of
X
, we declare

\mathcal{O}(X)(U,V)=\begin{cases}\emptyset&\text{ if }U\nsubseteq V\\
\{i_{U}:U\hookrightarrow V\}&\text{ if }U\subseteq V\\
\end{cases}

We call
\mathcal{O}(X)
to be the
category of open subsets of
X
.

Example 2.1.24
.

Let
\rm{Set}
be the category described as follows:

•

objects are sets,

•

for sets
A,B
, the morphism class
\text{Set}(A,B)
is the collection of functions from
A
to
B
,

•

the composition map is given by composition of functions.

We call
\rm{Set}
to be the category of sets.

Example 2.1.25
.

Let
Top
be the category with the following description:

•

objects are topological spaces,

•

for topological spaces
X,Y
, the morphism class
\text{Top}(X,Y)
is the set of all continuous maps from
X
to
Y
,

•

the composition map is given by composition of functions.

We call
Top
to be the category of topological spaces.

Example 2.1.26
.

Let
Man
be the category with the following description:

•

objects are smooth manifolds,

•

for smooth manifolds
M,N
, the morphism class
\text{Man}(M,N)
is the set of all smooth maps from
M
to
N
,

•

the composition map is given by composition of functions.

We call
Man
to be the category of smooth manifolds.

We have given some examples of functors
(
Examples

2.1.13
,
2.1.14
and
2.1.15
). Those examples are between small categories. Now we give some more examples of functors (between arbitrary categories).

Example 2.1.27
.

Consider the categories
\rm{Top}
and
\rm{Set}
. Consider the assignment
\text{Top}_{0}\rightarrow\text{Set}_{0}
, that maps a topological space
(A,\tau)
to the underlying set
A
, and the assignment
\text{Top}(A,B)\rightarrow\text{Set}(A,B)
that maps a continuous map to the underlying set map. This gives a functor
\text{Top}\rightarrow\text{Set}
, which we call the forgetful functor from
Top
to
Set
.

Example 2.1.28
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a (locally small) category. Fix an object
A
in
\mathcal{C}
. The assignment
B\mapsto\mathcal{C}(A,B)
for objects
B
of
\mathcal{C}
, and the assignment
(B\rightarrow C)\mapsto(\mathcal{C}(A,B)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(A,C))
for morphisms
B\rightarrow C
in
\mathcal{C}
, gives a functor
h^{A}:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\text{Set}
. We call
h^{A}
to be
the (covariant) functor of points associated to the object
A
.

Definition 2.1.29

(Opposite category of a category)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. The
opposite category of
\mathcal{C}
, denoted by
\mathcal{C}^{\op}
, is a category with the following description:

•

the class
\mathcal{C}^{\op}_{0}
is equal to the class
\mathcal{C}_{0}
,

•

for each
x,y\in\mathcal{C}^{\op}_{0}
, we have
\mathcal{C}^{\op}(x,y)=\mathcal{C}(y,x)
,

•

for each triple
(x,y,z)
in
\mathcal{C}^{\op}_{0}
, the map
\circ:\mathcal{C}^{\op}(x,y)\times\mathcal{C}^{\op}(y,z)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}^{\op}(x,z)
is the map

\circ:\mathcal{C}(z,y)\times\mathcal{C}(y,x)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(z,x)
,

•

the map
\{1\}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}^{\op}(x,x)
is the map
\{1\}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(x,x)
.

Remark 2.1.30
.

A functor on the category
\mathcal{C}^{\op}
is called a
contravariant functor on the category
\mathcal{C}
. Let
F:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
be a functor.
Consider a morphism
\gamma:a\rightarrow b
in
\mathcal{C}
. This can be seen as
\gamma:b\rightarrow a
in
\mathcal{C}^{\op}
.
The condition
s_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{1}=F_{0}\circ s_{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}
says that
s_{\mathcal{D}}(F_{1}(\gamma))=F_{0}(s_{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}(\gamma))=F_{0}(t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))
. Similarly, the condition
t_{\mathcal{D}}\circ F_{1}=F_{0}\circ t_{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}
says that
t_{\mathcal{D}}(F_{1}(\gamma))=F_{0}(t_{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}(\gamma))=F_{0}(s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))
. Thus, we have
F_{1}(\gamma):F_{0}(t_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))\rightarrow F_{0}(s_{\mathcal{C}}(\gamma))
. So, for
\gamma:a\rightarrow b
in
\mathcal{C}
, we have
F_{1}(\gamma):F_{0}(b)\rightarrow F_{0}(a)
. Similarly, the compatibility with composition map says that,
F_{1}(\gamma\circ\gamma^{\prime})=F_{1}(\gamma^{\prime})\circ F_{1}(\gamma)
for all
(\gamma^{\prime},\gamma)\in\mathcal{C}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}\mathcal{C}_{1}
.

In the
Example

2.1.28
, we have mentioned the (covariant) functor of points. Now, we give another example of a functor, the contravariant functor of points.

Example 2.1.31
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a (locally small) category. Fix an object
A
in
\mathcal{C}
. The assignment
B\mapsto\mathcal{C}(B,A)
for objects
B
of
\mathcal{C}
, and the assignment
(B\rightarrow C)\mapsto(\mathcal{C}(C,A)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(B,A))
for morphisms
B\rightarrow C
in
\mathcal{C}
, gives a functor
h_{A}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
. We call
h_{A}
to be
the (contravariant) functor of points associated to the object
A
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a (locally-small) category and
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
a functor.
Let
\text{Hom}(h_{U},\mathcal{F})
be the set of all natural transformations from the functor
h_{U}
to the functor
\mathcal{F}
, and
\eta:h_{U}\Rightarrow\mathcal{F}
a natural transformation. Consider the morphism
\eta(U):h_{U}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
. The identity element
1_{U}\in h_{U}(U)=\mathcal{C}(U,U)
gives an element
\eta(U)(1_{U})\in\mathcal{F}(U)
. Thus, we have a morphism of sets
\text{Hom}(h_{U},\mathcal{F})\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
.
The following result says that, this morphism of sets
\text{Hom}(h_{U},\mathcal{F})\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
is a bijection.

Lemma 2.1.32

(Yoneda Lemma
[
67
, Section
2.1.2
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a (locally-small) category and
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
a functor. For an object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
, the morphism of sets
\text{Hom}(h_{U},\mathcal{F})\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
is a bijection.

Given a category
\mathcal{C}
, we have the functor category
[\mathcal{C}^{\op},\text{Set}]
with the following description:

•

objects are functors
\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
,

•

morphisms are natural transformations.

For a locally small category
\mathcal{C}
, we have the functor
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow[\mathcal{C}^{\op},\text{Set}]
with the following description:

•

an object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
is mapped to the functor of points
h_{U}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
,

•

a morphism
f:U\rightarrow V
of
\mathcal{C}
is mapped to the natural transformation
f^{*}:h_{U}\Rightarrow h_{V}
, obtained by composition.

As a corollary of the Yoneda lemma, we have the following result, which says that the above functor is an embedding of categories.

Lemma 2.1.33

(Yoneda embedding
[
59
, Corolalrry
2.2.8
]
)
.

For a (locally small) category
\mathcal{C}
, the functor
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow[\mathcal{C}^{\op},\text{Set}]
is an embedding of categories.

Similar to the notion of the composition of functors, we can talk about the composition of two natural transformations. There are two ways we can compose; one is that of a horizontal composition, and the other is that of the vertical composition.

Vertical composition of natural transformations
:
Let
\mathcal{C}=[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]
and
\mathcal{D}=[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
be categories. Let

(F_{1},F_{0}),(G_{1},G_{0}),(H_{1},H_{0}):[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]

be functors,
\alpha:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
a natural transformation from
F
to
G
, and

\beta:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
a natural transformation from
G
to
H
, as in the following diagram,

The morphisms
\alpha:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1},\beta:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
combine to give a map
(\alpha,\beta):\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}\mathcal{D}_{1}
. Composing the map
(\alpha,\beta)
with the composition map
m_{\mathcal{D}}:\mathcal{D}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
gives the map
m_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(\alpha,\beta):\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
. It is easy to check that this map
m_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(\alpha,\beta):\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
gives a natural transformation from the functor
F
to the functor
H

(
Definition

2.1.17
). We call
m_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(\alpha,\beta)
to be the
vertical composition of the natural transformations
\alpha,\beta
, and denote by
\beta\circ_{\textit{ver}}\alpha
. So, for
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we have

\displaystyle(\beta\circ_{\textit{ver}}\alpha)(a)=\beta(a)\circ\alpha(a).

(2.1.3)

Horizontal composition of natural transformations
:
Let
\mathcal{C}=[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}],\mathcal{D}=[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]
, and
\mathcal{E}=[\mathcal{E}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{E}_{0}]
be categories. Let

(F_{1},F_{0}),(G_{1},G_{0}):[\mathcal{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{C}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}],

(F^{\prime}_{1},F^{\prime}_{0}),(G^{\prime}_{1},G^{\prime}_{0}):[\mathcal{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{D}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{E}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{E}_{0}],

be functors, and
\alpha:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
and
\beta:\mathcal{D}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
are natural transformations, as in the following diagram

Similar to the notion of vertical composition, we would like to define a natural transformation from the functor
(F_{1}^{\prime}\circ F_{1},F_{0}^{\prime}\circ F_{0})
to the functor
(G_{1}^{\prime}\circ G_{1},G_{0}^{\prime}\circ G_{0})
.

So, given
\alpha:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{1}
and
\beta:\mathcal{D}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
, we need to construct a map
\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
. Motivated by the vertical composition, we look for a map
\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{E}_{0}}\mathcal{E}_{1}
and then using the composition map
\mathcal{E}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{E}_{0}}\mathcal{E}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
, we get a map
\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{E}_{0}}\mathcal{E}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
.
Given an element
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, there are
4
ways to get an element in
\mathcal{E}_{1}
, namely
(F_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)(a),(G_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)(a),(\beta\circ F_{0})(a),(\beta\circ G_{0})(a)
. Looking at the source, target of these
4
morphisms, we see that

((G_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)(a),(\beta\circ F_{0})(a))\in\mathcal{E}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{E}_{0}}\mathcal{E}_{1},

((\beta\circ G_{0})(a),(F_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)(a))\in\mathcal{E}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{E}_{0}}\mathcal{E}_{1}.

Thus, there are two maps
\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{E}_{0}}\mathcal{E}_{1}
given by
(G_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha,\beta\circ F_{0})
and
(\beta\circ G_{0},F_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)
. But, as
\beta:\mathcal{D}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
is a natural transformation, we see that,
m_{\mathcal{E}}\circ(G_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha,\beta\circ F_{0})=m_{\mathcal{E}}\circ(\beta\circ G_{0},F_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)
. Thus, we have “unique” map
\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
, given by
m_{\mathcal{E}}\circ(G_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha,\beta\circ F_{0})
or
m_{\mathcal{E}}\circ(\beta\circ G_{0},F_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)
. It is easy to check that, this map
\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{1}
satisfies the condition for a map to be a natural transformation
(
Definition

2.1.17
). We call
m_{\mathcal{E}}\circ(G_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha,\beta\circ F_{0})
or
m_{\mathcal{E}}\circ(\beta\circ G_{0},F_{1}^{\prime}\circ\alpha)
to be
the horizontal composition of the natural transformations
\alpha,\beta
, and denote by
\beta\circ_{\textit{hor}}\alpha
. So, for
a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, we have

\displaystyle(\beta\circ_{\textit{hor}}\alpha)(a)=\beta(F_{0}(a))\circ G_{1}^{\prime}(\alpha(a))=F_{1}^{\prime}(\alpha(a))\circ\beta(G_{0}(a)).

(2.1.4)

2
-category theory notions

Definition 2.1.34

(
2
-category

12
, Definition
7.1.1
]
)
.

A

-category

\mathcal{C}

1.

a collection
\mathcal{C}_{0}
, whose elements are called
objects of
\mathcal{C}

2.

a small category
\mathcal{C}(x,y)
for each pair of objects
(x,y)
in
\mathcal{C}

3.

a functor
\{1\}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(x,x)
for each object
x
in
\mathcal{C}
,

4.

a functor
\mathcal{C}_{xyz}:\mathcal{C}(x,y)\times\mathcal{C}(y,z)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(x,z)
for each triple
(x,y,z)
of objects in
\mathcal{C}
,

for each

Before we proceed further, we fix some notation.

Remark 2.1.35

(Notation)
.

A
1
-morphism in a
2
-category
\mathcal{C}
is an object in the category
\mathcal{C}(x,y)
for some
x,y
in
\mathcal{C}_{0}
. A
2
-morphism in a
2
-category
\mathcal{C}
is a morphism in the category
\mathcal{C}(x,y)
for some
x,y
in
\mathcal{C}_{0}
.

The word “composition” occurs in
3
places in a
2
-category:

1.

Let
f,g
be
1
-morphisms in a
2
-category
\mathcal{C}
. If
(f,g)\in\mathcal{C}(x,y)_{0}\times\mathcal{C}(y,z)_{0}
for some
x,y,z\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, then, the functor
\mathcal{C}_{xyz}
gives an element
\mathcal{C}_{xyz}(f,g)\in\mathcal{C}(x,z)_{0}
. We denote this element
\mathcal{C}_{xyz}(f,g)
by
g\circ f
.

2.

Let
\alpha,\beta
be
2
-morphisms in a
2
-category
\mathcal{C}
. There are two possibilities here: either
\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{C}(x,y)_{1}
for some
x,y\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
, or
(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{C}(x,y)_{1}\times\mathcal{C}(y,z)_{1}
for some
x,y,z\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
.

•

Suppose that
\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{C}(x,y)_{1}
. Further, if
t(\alpha)=s(\beta)
, then, the composition map in the category
\mathcal{C}(x,y)
gives an element
m_{\mathcal{C}(x,y)}(\alpha,\beta)
. We denote this element by
\beta\odot\alpha
, and call it
the vertical composition of the
2
-morphisms
\alpha,\beta
. We see it as the following diagram,

Suppose that
(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{C}(x,y)_{1}\times\mathcal{C}(y,z)_{1}
for some
x,y,z\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
. The morphism level map of the functor

\mathcal{C}_{xyz}:\mathcal{C}(x,y)\times\mathcal{C}(y,z)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(x,z)
gives an element
\mathcal{C}_{xyz}(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{C}(x,z)_{1}
. We denote this element
\mathcal{C}_{xyz}(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{C}(x,z)_{1}
by
\beta\star\alpha
, and call it the horizontal composition of the
2
-morphisms
\alpha,\beta
. We see it as the following diagram,

We end this section with some miscellaneous concepts from category theory.

2.1.2
Pull-back in a category

One notion from category theory we come across in this thesis quite often is that of a pull-back in a category.

Definition 2.1.38

(pull-back in a category)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category, and
\gamma:a\rightarrow b,\delta:c\rightarrow b
morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
. A
pull-back of the pair
(\gamma,\delta)
is given by an object
d
of
\mathcal{C}
, along with morphisms
{\pr}_{2}:d\rightarrow c,{\pr}_{1}:d\rightarrow a
, such that,
\delta\circ{\pr}_{2}=\gamma\circ{\pr}_{1}
, and for any pair of morphisms
(\tau:e\rightarrow c,\sigma:e\rightarrow a)
with
\delta\circ\tau=\gamma\circ\sigma
, there exists a unique morphism
\Phi:e\rightarrow d
with
{\pr}_{2}\circ\Phi=\tau
, and
{\pr}_{1}\circ\Phi=\sigma
. We see a pull-back as the following diagram,

Alternatively, we use the terminology “fiber product" to mean the pull-back.

Remark 2.1.39
.

Not all categories have all pull-backs. If a pull-back of a pair
(\gamma,\delta)
exists in a category, then it is unique up to a unique isomorphism.

Example 2.1.40
.

Let
{\rm Set}
be the category of sets. Let
f:A\rightarrow B
and
g:C\rightarrow B
be set maps. Then, the pull-back of the pair
(f,g)
is given by the set
\{(a,c)\in A\times C:f(a)=g(c)\}
. We denote this set as
A\times_{B}C
.

Example 2.1.41
.

Let
{\rm Top}
be the category of topological space. Let
f:A\rightarrow B
and
g:C\rightarrow B
be continuous maps. Then, the pull-back of the pair
(f,g)
is given by the set
\{(a,c):f(a)=g(c)\}
, with subspace topology induced from the product topology on
A\times C
. We denote this space as
A\times_{B}C
.

Example 2.1.42
.

Let
Man
be the category of smooth manifolds. Let
f:M\rightarrow N
and
g:M^{\prime}\rightarrow N
be smooth maps. Then, the set-theoretic pull-back
M\times_{N}M^{\prime}
does not always have a nice smooth structure to become a pull-back in the category of smooth manifolds. When either
f:M\rightarrow N
or
g:M^{\prime}\rightarrow N
is a submersion, then
M\times_{N}M^{\prime}
becomes the pull-back of the pair
(f,g)
, in the category of smooth manifolds.

2.1.3
Epimophisms in a category

We come across a special kind of morphism in a category, namely an epimorphism. One of the good references to read more about epimorphisms is
[
12
,
1.8
Epimorphisms]
.

Definition 2.1.43

(epimorphism in a category)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. A morphism
\theta:X\rightarrow Y
in
\mathcal{C}
is said to be
an epimorphism
, if for any
g_{1},g_{2}:Y\rightarrow Z
with
g_{1}\circ\theta=g_{2}\circ\theta
implies
g_{1}=g_{2}
.

Consider the category
Set
, whose objects are sets and whose morphisms are functions. Then, epimorphisms in this category are precisely the surjective functions in it
[
12
, Example
1.8.5(a)
]
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category whose objects are sets with extra structure, whose morphisms are functions with extra conditions (such categories, up to some technicality, are called concrete categories).

Let
\theta:X\rightarrow Y
be a morphism in
\mathcal{C}
. Ignoring the extra conditions on
\theta
, this map
\theta
can be seen as a morphism in
Set
.
If
\theta
is an epimorphism in
Set
, then
g_{1}\circ\theta=g_{2}\circ\theta
implies
g_{1}=g_{2}
for all appropriate
g_{1},g_{2}
in
Set
. In particular,
g_{1}\circ\theta=g_{2}\circ\theta
implies
g_{1}=g_{2}
for all appropriate
g_{1},g_{2}
in
\mathcal{C}
. Thus, every morphism in
\mathcal{C}
, whose underlying set map is an epimorphism in
Set
, will be an epimorphism in
\mathcal{C}
. In other words, every morphism in
\mathcal{C}
, whose underlying set map is surjective, is an epimorphism in
\mathcal{C}
.

Suppose
\theta
is an epimorphism in
\mathcal{C}
, then, it only means that
g_{1}\circ\theta=g_{2}\circ\theta
implies
g_{1}=g_{2}
for all appropriate
g_{1},g_{2}
in
\mathcal{C}
. This does not say that
g_{1}\circ\theta=g_{2}\circ\theta
implies
g_{1}=g_{2}
for all appropriate
g_{1},g_{2}
in
Set
, as the collection of appropriate morphism in
Set
may be bigger than the collection in
\mathcal{C}
. Thus, not every epimorphism in
\mathcal{C}
needs to be a surjective map on the underlying sets.

2.2
Fibered categories, pseudo-functors, and stacks

In this section, we recall the notions of fibered categories, pseudo-functors and stacks. Most of this section is based on Angelo Vistoli’s “Notes on Grothendieck topologies, fibered categories and descent theory”
[
67
]
.

2.2.1
Sheaf on a topological space

Let
X
be a topological space and
\mathcal{O}(X)
the category of open subsets of
X
(
Example

2.1.23
). A functor
\mathcal{F}\colon\mathcal{O}(X)^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
is called a
presheaf (of sets) on the topological space
X
. For an object
U
of
\mathcal{O}(X)
, we call the elements of
\mathcal{F}(U)
as the sections of
U
.
For a morphism
f:U\rightarrow V
in
\mathcal{O}(X)
, we denote the map
\mathcal{F}(f):\mathcal{F}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
as
f^{*}:\mathcal{F}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
.

Let
U
be an open subset of
X
and
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
an open cover of
U
. For indices
i,j\in\Lambda
, let
U_{ij}
denote the pull-back of the inclusion maps
\sigma_{i}:U_{i}\rightarrow U
and
\sigma_{j}:U_{j}\rightarrow U
; that is,
U_{ij}=U_{i}\cap U_{j}
. We denote the corresponding (inclusion) maps
U_{ij}\rightarrow U_{i}
and
U_{ij}\rightarrow U_{j}
as
{\pr}_{1}
and
{\pr}_{2}
respectively, as in the following (commutative) diagram,

Consider the set
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
with the following description:

•

an element of
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is a collection
\{s_{i}\}
, where
s_{i}\in\mathcal{F}(U_{i})
for each index
i\in\Lambda
and
{\pr}_{1}^{*}(s_{i})={\pr}_{2}^{*}(s_{j})
in
\mathcal{F}(U_{ij})
for each pair of indices
i,j\in\Lambda
.

Given an open set
U
of
X
and an open cover
\{\sigma_{i}:U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
, we have the function
\mathcal{F}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
given by
s\mapsto\{\sigma_{i}^{*}(s)\}_{i\in\Lambda}
.

Definition 2.2.1

(Sheaf on a topological space)
.

Let
X
be a topological space. Let
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{O}(X)^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
be a functor. We say that
\mathcal{F}
is a
locally determined functor
, if, for each open set
U
of
X
and an open cover
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
, the function
\mathcal{F}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is a bijection. A locally determined functor
\mathcal{F}\colon\mathcal{O}(X)^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
is said to be
a sheaf (of sets) on the topological space
X
.

Example 2.2.2
.

Consider the functor
\mathcal{F}\colon\mathcal{O}(X)^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
with the following description:

•

for an object
U
of
\mathcal{O}(X)
, we have
\mathcal{F}(U)=\{\text{continuous maps }U\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\}
,

•

for a morphism
f:U\rightarrow V
of
\mathcal{O}(X)
, the morphism

\mathcal{F}(f):\mathcal{F}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
is given by restriction.

This functor
\mathcal{F}
is locally determined, thus gives a sheaf on
X
.

2.2.2
Sheaf on a site

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. A functor
\mathcal{F}\colon\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
is called a
presheaf (of sets) on the category
\mathcal{C}
.

The notion of “a functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{O}(X)^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
being locally determined” can be extended to a functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
, for a general category
\mathcal{C}
, when
\mathcal{C}
is equipped with the so called Grothendieck topology, which we recall below.

Definition 2.2.3

(Grothendieck topology

[
67
, Definition
2.24
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. For an object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
, a
covering of
U
is a collection of morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
whose target is
U
. Consider a collection
\mathcal{J}=\{\mathcal{J}_{U}:U\in\text{Obj}(\mathcal{C})\}
, where
\mathcal{J}_{U}
be a collection of coverings of
U
. We say that
\mathcal{J}
is a
Grothendieck topology on
\mathcal{C}
if
the following conditions are satisfied:

1.

for every object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
and an isomorphism
V\rightarrow U
of
\mathcal{C}
, the covering
\{V\rightarrow U\}
is in
\mathcal{J}_{U}
,

2.

for every object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
, a covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
in
\mathcal{J}_{U}
, and a covering
\{U_{ij}\rightarrow U_{i}\}_{j\in\Lambda_{i}}
in
\mathcal{J}_{U_{i}}
, for each
i\in\Lambda
, the composition covering
\{U_{ij}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda,j\in\Lambda_{i}}
is in
\mathcal{J}_{U}
,

3.

for every object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
, a covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
in
\mathcal{J}_{U}
and a morphism
V\rightarrow U
in
\mathcal{C}
, the fiber product
U_{i}\times_{U}V
exists for each
i\in\Lambda
, and the covering
\{{\pr}_{2}\colon U_{i}\times_{U}V\rightarrow V\}_{i\in\Lambda}
is in
\mathcal{J}_{V}
.

A category
\mathcal{C}
equipped with a Grothendieck topology
\mathcal{J}
is called a
site
. We denote a site as a pair
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
, or simply as
\mathcal{C}
when it is clear what
\mathcal{J}
is.

Remark 2.2.4
.

Only for the convenience of defining the notion of a Grothendieck topology, we used the phrase “covering of
U
” for an arbitrary collection of morphisms
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
. Once we fix a Grothendieck topology
\mathcal{J}
on
\mathcal{C}
, by a covering of
U
, we always mean a collection
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
with
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}\in\mathcal{J}_{U}
.

Example 2.2.5

(big étale topology on
Man
)
.

Consider the category
Man
of smooth manifolds. For an object
M
of the category
Man
, define a covering of
M
to be a collection of étale morphisms
\{\sigma_{i}:U_{i}\rightarrow M\}_{i\in\Lambda}
such that
\bigcup_{i\in\Lambda}\sigma_{i}(U_{i})=M
. This gives a Grothendieck topology on
Man
, which we call the big étale topology on
Man
. We denote this site by
(\text{Man},\mathcal{J}_{{e}tale})
.

Before we proceed further, we fix some notations. Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site. Let
U
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
and
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
a covering of
U
.
For indices
i,j\in\Lambda
, let
U_{ij}
denote the fiber product of morphisms
\sigma_{i}:U_{i}\rightarrow U
and
\sigma_{j}:U_{j}\rightarrow U
, as in the following diagram,

(2.2.2)

Let
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
be a functor. Let
U
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
and
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
a covering of
U
. Consider the set
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
with the following description:

•

an element of
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is of the form
\{s_{i}\}_{i\in\Lambda}
, where
s_{i}\in\mathcal{F}(U_{i})
for each
i\in\Lambda
and
{\pr}_{2}^{*}(s_{j})={\pr}_{1}^{*}(s_{i})
in
\mathcal{F}(U_{ij})
for each pair of indices
i,j\in\Lambda
.

Let
U
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
and
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
a covering of
U
. Then, we have the function
\mathcal{F}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
defined by
s\mapsto\{\sigma_{i}^{*}(s)\}_{i\in\Lambda}
.

Definition 2.2.6

(Sheaf on a site)
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site. A functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
is said to be a
locally determined functor
, if, for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
and a covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
, the function
\mathcal{F}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is a bijection. A locally determined functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
is said to be a
sheaf on the site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
.

Remark 2.2.7
.

A site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
is called a
subcanonical site
if for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
, the functor of points
h_{U}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
is a sheaf on the site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
. In this thesis, all our sites are assumed to be subcanonical.

2.2.3
Stack on a site

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site.
The notion of “a functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
being locally determined” can be extended to a pseudo-functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
.
Firstly, we recall the notion of a pseudo-functor on a category
\mathcal{C}
.

Definition 2.2.8

(
[
67
, Definition
3.10
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category.
A
pseudo-functor on
\mathcal{C}
, denoted by
\mathcal{F}\colon\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
, consists of the following data:

1.

a category
\mathcal{F}(U)
for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
,

2.

a functor
f^{*}\colon\mathcal{F}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
for each morphism
f\colon U\rightarrow V
of
\mathcal{C}
,

3.

a natural isomorphism of functors
\epsilon_{U}\colon(1_{U})^{*}\Rightarrow 1_{\mathcal{F}(U)}\colon\mathcal{F}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
,

4.

a natural isomorphism of functors
\alpha_{f,g}\colon f^{*}g^{*}\Rightarrow(g\circ f)^{*}\colon\mathcal{F}(W)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
for each pair of morphisms
U\xrightarrow{f}V\xrightarrow{g}W
of
\mathcal{C}
,

satisfying the following conditions:

1.

for every morphism
f\colon U\rightarrow V
in
\mathcal{C}
, and an object
\eta
of
\mathcal{F}(V)
, we have

\alpha_{f,1_{V}}(\eta)=f^{*}(\epsilon_{V}\eta),\text{~and~}\alpha_{1_{U},f}(\eta)=\epsilon_{U}(f^{*}\eta),

2.

for every triple of composable morphisms
U\xrightarrow{f}V\xrightarrow{g}W\xrightarrow{h}T
in
\mathcal{C}
, and an object
\eta
of
\mathcal{F}(T)
, we have

\alpha_{gf,h}(\eta)\circ\alpha_{f,g}(h^{*}\eta)=\alpha_{f,hg}(\eta)\circ f^{*}\alpha_{g,h}(\eta).

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site. Consider a pseudo-functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
. Let
U
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
and
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
a covering of
U
. Consider
the category
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
, with the following description:

•

an object in
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is a collection
\big\{\{s_{i}\}_{i\in\Lambda},\{\phi_{ij}\}_{i,j\in\Lambda}\big\}
, where

1.

s_{i}
is an object of
\mathcal{F}(U_{i})
for each
i\in\Lambda
,

2.

\phi_{ij}\colon{\pr}_{2}^{*}s_{j}\rightarrow{\pr}_{1}^{*}s_{i}
is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{F}(U_{ij})
for each
i,j\in\Lambda
,

satisfying the condition
{\pr}_{13}^{*}(\phi_{ik})={\pr}_{12}^{*}(\phi_{ij})\circ{\pr}_{23}^{*}(\phi_{jk})
in the category
\mathcal{F}(U_{ijk})
for each
i,j,k\in\Lambda
,

•

a morphism from an object
\big\{\{s_{i}\},\{\phi_{ij}\}\big\}
to an object
\big\{\{t_{i}\},\{\psi_{ij}\}\big\}
is given by a collection
\{\theta_{i}\colon s_{i}\rightarrow t_{i}\}_{i\in\Lambda}
, here,
\theta_{i}
is a morphism in
\mathcal{F}(U_{i})
for each
i\in\Lambda
, satisfying the condition
{\pr}_{1}^{*}(\theta_{i})\circ\phi_{ij}=\psi_{ij}\circ{\pr}_{2}^{*}(\theta_{j})
in
\mathcal{F}(U_{ij})
for each
i,j\in\Lambda
.

We call the category
\mathcal{F}(U_{i}\rightarrow U)
to be
the descent category of the covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
.

Let
U
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
and
\{\sigma_{i}:U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
a covering of
U
. Consider the functor
\mathcal{F}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
with the following description:

•

an object
s
of
\mathcal{F}(U)
is mapped to the object
\{\{\sigma_{i}^{*}(s)\},\{\phi_{ij}\}\}
of
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
, where
\phi_{ij}:{\pr}_{2}^{*}(\sigma_{j}^{*}(s))\rightarrow{\pr}_{1}^{*}(\sigma_{i}^{*}(s))
is the isomorphism given by composing the morphisms
\alpha_{{\pr}_{1},\sigma_{i}}(s):{\pr}_{1}^{*}(\sigma_{i}^{*}(s))\rightarrow(\sigma_{i}\circ{\pr}_{1})^{*}(s)
and
\alpha_{{\pr}_{2},\sigma_{j}}(s):{\pr}_{2}^{*}(\sigma_{j}^{*}(s))\rightarrow(\sigma_{j}\circ{\pr}_{2})^{*}(s)
,

•

a morphism
\theta:s\rightarrow t
in
\mathcal{F}(U)
is mapped to the morphism
\{\sigma_{i}^{*}(\theta):\sigma_{i}^{*}(s)\rightarrow\sigma_{i}^{*}(t)\}_{i\in\Lambda}
in
\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
.

Definition 2.2.9

(stack on a site)
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site. A pseudo-functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
is said to be a
locally determined pseudo-functor
, if, for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
and a covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
the functor
\mathcal{F}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is an equivalence of categories. A locally determined pseudo-functor on a site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
is said to be a
stack on the site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
.

2.2.4
Fibered categories

It is sometimes useful to think of a pseudo-functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
as a fibered category
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
. In this subsection, we recall the notion of a fibered category, give an outline of correspondence between pseudo-functors and fibered categories, and introduce the notion of a stack as a fibered category.

Definition 2.2.10

(
[
67
, Definition
3.1
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category and
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
a functor. A morphism
\theta\colon\xi\rightarrow\eta
in
\mathcal{D}
is said to be a
Cartesian arrow in
\mathcal{D}
if, for every morphism
\theta^{\prime}\colon\xi^{\prime}\rightarrow\eta
in
\mathcal{D}
and a morphism
h\colon\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\xi^{\prime})\rightarrow\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\xi)
in
\mathcal{C}
with
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\theta)\circ h=\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\theta^{\prime})
, there exists a unique morphism
\Phi\colon\xi^{\prime}\rightarrow\xi
in
\mathcal{D}
such that,
\theta\circ\Phi=\theta^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{D}
and
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\Phi)=h
in
\mathcal{C}
. We visualize a Cartesian arrow as the morphism
\theta
in the following diagram,
