(2.2.3)

Definition 2.2.11

(
[
67
, Definition
3.5
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category and
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
a functor. We say that
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
is a
fibered category over
\mathcal{C}
, if, for every

(\eta,f)\in\mathcal{D}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0},t}\mathcal{C}_{1}
, there exists a Cartesian arrow
\theta\colon\xi\rightarrow\eta
with
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\theta)=f
. We call such
\xi
to be
a pull-back of
\eta
along
f
.

A pull-back of an object of
\mathcal{D}
along a morphism of
\mathcal{C}
, if it exists, is unique up to a unique isomorphism.

Following are some examples of fibered categories that we come across in this thesis often.

Example 2.2.12
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category, and
U
an object of
\mathcal{C}
. Let
\mathcal{C}/U
be the category with the following description:

•

an object of
\mathcal{C}/U
is a morphism in
\mathcal{C}
whose target is
U
; that is of the form
f:V\rightarrow U
for some object
V
of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a morphism in
\mathcal{C}/U
from an object
(f:V\rightarrow U)
to an other object
(f^{\prime}:V^{\prime}\rightarrow U)
is a morphism
g:V\rightarrow V^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{C}
with
f^{\prime}\circ g=f
.

Consider the functor
\pi_{U}:\mathcal{C}/U\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
with the following description:

•

an object
(f:V\rightarrow U)
of
\mathcal{C}/U
is mapped to the object
V
of
\mathcal{C}
,

•

a morphism
g:(f:V\rightarrow U)\rightarrow(f^{\prime}:V^{\prime}\rightarrow U)
of
\mathcal{C}/U
is mapped to the morphism
g:V\rightarrow V^{\prime}
of
\mathcal{C}
.

The functor
\pi_{U}:\mathcal{C}/U\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is a fibered category over
\mathcal{C}
. We denote this fibered category by
\underline{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
or just by
\underline{U}
.

Example 2.2.13
.

Let
G
be a Lie group. Consider the category
BG
, whose objects are principal
G
-bundles and morphisms are morphisms of principal
G
-bundles. Consider the functor
\pi_{G}:BG\rightarrow\text{Man}
with the following description:

•

an object
P(M,G)
of
BG
is mapped to the object
M
of
Man
,

•

a morphism
(F,f):P(M,G)\rightarrow P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G)
of
BG
is mapped to the morphism
f:M\rightarrow M^{\prime}
of
Man
.

The functor
\pi_{G}:BG\rightarrow\text{Man}
is a fibered category.

Definition 2.2.14

(
[
67
, Definition
3.6
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. Let
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
and
(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{C})
be fibered categories. A
morphism of fibered categories
from

(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
to
(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{C})
is given by a functor
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
such that,

1.

the functor
F
is compatible with the functors
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}
and
\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}
; that is,
\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\circ F=\pi_{\mathcal{D}}
,

2.

the functor
F
maps Cartesian arrows in
\mathcal{D}
to Cartesian arrows in
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
.

Definition 2.2.15
.

A morphism of fibered categories
F:(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})\rightarrow(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{C})
is called an
isomorphism of fibered categories
, if, the underlying functor
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
is an equivalence of categories.

Remark 2.2.16
.

As mentioned in
[
53
, Section
1.1
]
, “It is not uncommon in the literature to call two equivalent fibered categories isomorphic”.

Let
A,B
be sets and
f:A\rightarrow B
a set map. For
b\in B
, the fiber of
b
is defined to be the set
\{a\in A:f(a)=b\}
. Similar to this notion of the fiber of an element in a set map, we define the notion of fiber of an object of
\mathcal{C}
in a fibered category
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
. For obvious reasons, fiber of an object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
will be a category.

Definition 2.2.17

(
[
67
, Definition
3.8
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category and
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
a fibered category. For an object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
,
the fiber of
U
, denoted by
\mathcal{D}(U)
, is a category with the following description:

\displaystyle\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}(U))

\displaystyle=\{\eta\in\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D})|\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\eta)=U\},

\displaystyle\text{Mor}_{\mathcal{D}(U)}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\{f\in\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D})|\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(f)=1_{U}\}.

Definition 2.2.18
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category and
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
a fibered category. A
cleavage of the fibered category

(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
is, a collection
\mathcal{A}
, of Cartesian arrows in
\mathcal{D}
, such that, for each
(\eta,f)\in\mathcal{D}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{C}_{0},t}\mathcal{C}_{1}
, there exists exactly one element
\theta\in\mathcal{A}
, with
t(\theta)=\eta
and
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\theta)=f
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category and
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
a fibered category. Fix a cleavage
\mathcal{A}
of
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
.
Let
f\colon U\rightarrow V
be a morphism in
\mathcal{C}
, and
\eta
an object of
\mathcal{D}(V)
. Then, there exists unique element
\theta_{\eta}\in\mathcal{A}
such that
t(\theta_{\eta})=\eta

and
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(\theta_{\eta})=f
. Denote
s(\theta_{\eta})
by
f^{*}\eta
. This gives a map
\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}(V))\rightarrow\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}(U))
defined as
\eta\mapsto f^{*}\eta
. Let
\tau\colon\eta\rightarrow\eta^{\prime}
be a morphism in
\mathcal{D}(V)
. Then, by the definition of a fibered category, there exists a unique morphism
\Psi\colon f^{*}\eta\rightarrow f^{*}\eta^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{D}(U)
such that
\tau\circ\theta_{\eta}=\theta_{\eta^{\prime}}\circ\Psi
. We denote the morphism
\Psi
by
f^{*}\tau\colon f^{*}\eta\rightarrow f^{*}\eta^{\prime}
. This gives a map
\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D}(V))\rightarrow\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D}(U))
, defined by
\tau\mapsto f^{*}\tau
. The maps
\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}(V))\rightarrow\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}(U))
and

\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D}(V))\rightarrow\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D}(U))
combine to give a functor
\mathcal{D}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(U)
, which we denote by
f^{*}\colon\mathcal{D}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(U)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category and
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
a fibered category. Fixing a cleavage
\mathcal{A}
on the fibered category
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
we get the collection of functors
\{f^{*}\colon\mathcal{D}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(U)\}_{f\in\text{Mor}(\mathcal{C})}
. This collection
\{f^{*}\colon\mathcal{D}(V)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(U)\}_{f\in\text{Mor}(\mathcal{C})}
gives a pseudo-functor on the category
\mathcal{C}
(
Definition

2.2.8
).
Similarly, given a pseudo-functor on a category
\mathcal{C}
, we can associate a fibered category over
\mathcal{C}
(along with a cleavage of the fibered category). We refer to Chapter
3
of
[
67
]
for a detailed correspondence between pseudo-functors and fibered categories.

Example 2.2.19
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. Let
U
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
. Consider the functor (of points)
h_{U}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
. Treating a set as a discrete category, we see
h_{U}
as a pseudo-functor
h_{U}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
. Then, the associated fibered category for this pseudo-functor is the fibered category
\mathcal{C}/U\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
mentioned in
Example

2.2.12
.

The correspondence between pseudo-functors and fibered categories allows us to see a stack over a site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
as a fibered category over
\mathcal{C}
. The notion of descent category of a covering
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of an object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
, for a pseudo-functor is transferred to the set up of fibered categories to give the notion of descent category of the covering
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
for a fibered category over
\mathcal{C}
.

2.2.4.1
Descent Category associated to a covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site, and
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
a fibered category.
Fix a cleavage
\mathcal{A}
of the fibered category
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
. Let
U
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
and
\{\sigma_{i}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
a covering of
U
.
For this covering
\{\sigma_{i}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
, we associate a category
\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
. For indices
i,j
, let
U_{ij}
denote the pull-back in the Diagram
2.2.1
, and for indices
i,j,k
, let
U_{ijk}
denote the pull-back in the Diagram
2.2.2
.

An object in the category
\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is of the form
(\{\xi_{i}\},\{\phi_{ij}\})
, where,

1.

\xi_{i}
is an object of
\mathcal{D}(U_{i})
for each index
i\in\Lambda
,

2.

\phi_{ij}\colon{\pr}_{2}^{*}(\xi_{j})\rightarrow{\pr}_{1}^{*}(\xi_{i})
is an isomorphism in
\mathcal{D}(U_{ij})
for each pair of indices
i,j\in\Lambda
such that
{\pr}_{13}^{*}(\phi_{ik})={\pr}_{12}^{*}(\phi_{ij})\circ{\pr}_{23}^{*}(\phi_{jk})
in
\mathcal{D}(U_{ijk})
for three indices
i,j,k\in\Lambda
.

A morphism from
(\{\xi_{i}\},\{\phi_{ij}\})
to
(\{\eta_{i}\},\{\psi_{ij}\})
is given by a collection
\{\alpha_{i}\colon\xi_{i}\rightarrow\eta_{i}\}_{i\in\Lambda}
. Here,
\alpha_{i}:\xi_{i}\rightarrow\eta_{i}
is a morphism in
\mathcal{D}(U_{i})
for each
i\in\Lambda
satisfying the condition
\psi_{ij}\circ({\pr}_{2}^{*}\alpha_{j})=({\pr}_{1}^{*}\alpha_{i})\circ\phi_{ij}
in the category
\mathcal{D}(U_{ij})
for each pair of indices
i,j\in\Lambda
.
We call
\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
to be the
descent category associated to the covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
.

Let
\xi
be an object of
\mathcal{D}(U)
. For each index
i\in\Lambda
, the functor
\sigma_{i}^{*}\colon\mathcal{D}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(U_{i})
(associated to the morphism
\sigma_{i}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U
) gives an object
\sigma_{i}^{*}(\xi)
in
\mathcal{D}(U_{i})
. For indices
i,j
, the uniqueness of pull-back gives an isomorphism
\phi_{ij}\colon{\pr}_{2}^{*}(\sigma_{j}^{*}(\xi))\rightarrow{\pr}_{1}^{*}(\sigma_{i}^{*}(\xi))
in
\mathcal{D}(U_{ij})
. It is easy to see that, for indices
i,j,k
the morphisms
\phi_{ij},\phi_{jk},\phi_{ik}
satisfies the co-cycle condition mentioned above. Thus, we get an object
\{\{\sigma_{i}^{*}(\xi)\},\{\phi_{ij}\}\}
in
\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
. This gives a map
\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}(U))\rightarrow\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}))
. Similarly, the pull-back defines a map
\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D}(U))\rightarrow\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}))
. Thus, we have a functor
\mathcal{D}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
.

Definition 2.2.20

(Stack over a site)
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site.
A fibered category
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
is said to be
a stack over the site
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
if, for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
and a covering
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
, the functor
\mathcal{D}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}(\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\})
is an equivalence of categories.

In this thesis, we are interested in fibered categories
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
that are fibered in groupoids, that is, the fiber
\mathcal{D}(U)
is a groupoid for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
. We call them
categories fibered in groupoids over
\mathcal{C}
. By a stack, we always mean a stack fibered in groupoids.

Definition 2.2.21

(morphism of stacks)
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{J})
be a site,
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
and
(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{C})
are stacks. A
morphism of stacks from
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
to
(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{C})
is a morphism of fibered categories from
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})
to
(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{C})
. A morphism of stacks
F:(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{C})\rightarrow(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{C})
is called an
isomorphism of stacks
if it is an isomorphism of fibered categories over
\mathcal{C}
(
Definition

2.2.15
).

Example 2.2.22
.

Let
\mathcal{S}
be a category, and
\mathcal{J}
a subcanonical topology on
\mathcal{S}
. For an object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
, the fibered category
\pi_{U}:\mathcal{S}/U\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
is a stack over the site
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
.

Definition 2.2.23

(representable stack)
.

Let
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
be a subcanonical site. A stack
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{S})
over the site
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
, is said to be a
representable stack
, if, there exists an object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
such that

(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{S})
is isomorphic to
(\underline{U},\pi_{U},\mathcal{S})
as stacks over
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
.

We are interested in morphisms of stacks that are representable by objects of the site. To define the notion of representable morphisms we need to introduce the notion of
2
-fiber product of fibered categories (in particular,
2
-fiber product of stacks).

Definition 2.2.24

(
2
-fiber product of fibered categories)
.

Let
\mathcal{S}
be a category,
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
,
\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\colon\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
and
\pi_{\mathcal{C}}\colon\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}

are fibered categories.
Let

F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C},F^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}

be a pair of morphisms of fibered categories.
Consider the category
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
with
the following description:

•

an object of
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
is a triple
(d,d^{\prime},\alpha)
, where
d\in\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}),d^{\prime}\in\text{Obj}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})
with
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(d)=\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}(d^{\prime})
and
\alpha\in\text{Mor}(\mathcal{C})
with
s(\alpha)=F(d),t(\alpha)=F^{\prime}(d^{\prime})
,

•

a morphism of
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
from
(d_{1},d_{1}^{\prime},\alpha_{1})
to
(d_{2},d_{2}^{\prime},\alpha_{2})
is given by a pair
(u,v)
where
u\colon d_{1}\rightarrow d_{2}
is in
\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D})

and
v\colon d_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow d_{2}^{\prime}
is in
\text{Mor}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})
such that

\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(u)=\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}(v)
and
F^{\prime}(v)\circ\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}\circ F(u)
.

Consider the functor
\Phi\colon\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
with the following description

•

an object
(d,d^{\prime},\alpha)
of
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
is mapped to the object
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(d)=\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}(d^{\prime})
of
\mathcal{S}
,

•

a morphism
(u,v)
of
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
is mapped to the morphism
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}(u)=\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}(v)
of
\mathcal{S}
.

Then,
\Phi\colon\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
is a fibered category over
\mathcal{S}
, which we call
the
2
-fiber product of
\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
with respect to the morphisms

F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
and
F^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
. We see the
2
-fiber product as the following diagram,

Remark 2.2.25
.

If
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{S}),(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{S})
and
(\mathcal{C},\pi_{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{S})
are categories fibered in groupoids over
\mathcal{S}
, then
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
is a category fibered in groupoids over
\mathcal{S}
. If
\mathcal{J}
is a Grothendieck topology on
\mathcal{S}
such that
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{S}),(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\mathcal{S})
and
(\mathcal{C},\pi_{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{S})
are stacks over the site
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
, then
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
is a stack over the site
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
.

Definition 2.2.26

(representable morphism of stacks)
.

Let
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
be a subcanonical site. Let
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{S})
and
(\mathcal{C},\pi_{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{S})
be stacks. A morphism of stacks
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is said to be a
representable morphism of stacks
if for every object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
and a morphism of stacks
\underline{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, the
2
-fiber product
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{U}
is a representable stack (
Definition

2.2.23
).

We are also interested in another special type of morphism of stacks, namely an epimorphism of stacks.

Definition 2.2.27

(epimorphism of stacks
[
16
]
)
.

Let
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
be a subcanonical site, and
(\mathcal{D},\pi_{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{S}),(\mathcal{C},\pi_{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{S})
are stacks. A morphism of stacks
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is said to be an
epimorphism of stacks
if, for every object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
and a morphism of stacks
q:\underline{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, there exists a covering
\{\sigma_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}_{\alpha\in\Lambda}
of
U
and a morphism of stacks
p_{\alpha}:\underline{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
with a
2
-commutative diagram,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{U_{\alpha}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{U}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{\alpha}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{\alpha}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}

for each
\alpha\in\Lambda
.

2.2.5
2
-Yoneda lemma

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category. For a functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
, the Yoneda lemma gives a bijection
\text{Hom}(h_{U},\mathcal{F})\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
for objects
U
of
\mathcal{C}
.

Let
\pi_{\mathcal{F}}:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be the fibered category associated to the functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
. As mentioned before,
\pi_{U}:\mathcal{C}/U\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is the fibered category associated to the functor
h_{U}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
. Then, the Yoneda lemma says that the map
\text{Hom}(\pi_{U},\pi_{\mathcal{F}})\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
is a bijection, where
\mathcal{F}(U)
is fiber of the object
U
in the fibered category
(\mathcal{F},\pi_{\mathcal{F}},\mathcal{C})
. The
2
-Yoneda lemma is a higher version of the Yoneda lemma where the pseudo-functors do not necessarily takes values in Sets.

Let
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
be a pseudo-functor, and
\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
the associated fibered category. Let
\text{Hom}(\mathcal{C}/U,\mathcal{F})
be the category whose objects are morphisms of fibered categories over
\mathcal{C}
from
\mathcal{C}/U
to
\mathcal{F}
and morphisms are natural transformations. Consider the functor
\text{Hom}(\mathcal{C}/U,\mathcal{F})\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
with the following description

•

an object
\Phi
of
\text{Hom}(\mathcal{C}/U,\mathcal{F})
is mapped to the object
\Phi(U)(1_{U})
,

•

a morphism
\alpha
of
\text{Hom}(\mathcal{C}/U,\mathcal{F})
is mapped to the morphism
\alpha(1_{U})
.

Lemma 2.2.28

(
2
-Yoneda lemma
[
41
, Lemma
4.19
]
)
.

The functor
\text{Hom}(\mathcal{C}/U,\mathcal{F})\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(U)
, mentioned above, is an equivalence of categories.

The following result is an application of the
2
-Yoneda lemma, giving a characterization for epimorphisms of stacks. We will see the proof of this result in
Chapter

3
, as part of the
Lemma

3.1.7
.

Lemma 2.2.29
.

Let
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
and
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\text{Man}
be stacks.
A morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism of stacks if and only if the following conditions holds:
for each smooth manifold
U
, and an object
a
of
\mathcal{C}(U)
, there exists an open cover
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}_{i\in\Lambda}
of
U
and objects
x_{i}
of
\mathcal{D}(U_{i})
with an isomorphism
F(x_{i})\rightarrow a|_{U_{i}}
in
\mathcal{C}(U_{i})
for each
i\in\Lambda
.

2.3
Lie groupoids, Morita equivalence, and differentiable stacks

In this thesis, we are interested in stacks of a special kind, namely differentiable stacks. A characterization of differentiable stacks is that, it is “representable by a Lie groupoid”. In this section, we recall the notion of a Lie groupoid, Morita equivalence of Lie groupoids, and differentiable stacks. A major part of this section is based on
[
26
,
41
,
49
]
.

Definition 2.3.1
.

A
Lie groupoid
is a groupoid
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
, where
\mathcal{G}_{0},\mathcal{G}_{1}
are smooth manifolds, the structure maps
s,t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
are submersions, the other structure maps
m:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1},e:\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1},u:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1}
are smooth maps.

Example 2.3.2
.

Let
M
be a smooth manifold. The groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows M]
, associated to the smooth manifold
M
, mentioned in
Example

2.1.4
, is a Lie groupoid.

Example 2.3.3
.

Let
G
be a Lie group. The groupoid
[G\rightrightarrows*]
, associated to the Lie group
G
, mentioned in
Example

2.1.5
is a Lie groupoid.

Example 2.3.4
.

Let
G
be a Lie group,
M
be a smooth manifold.
Let
\mu:M\times G\rightarrow M
be an action of the Lie group
G
on the smooth manifold
M
. The groupoid
[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]
, associated to a Lie group action, mentioned in
Example

2.1.6
is a Lie groupoid.

Example 2.3.5
.

Let
G
be a Lie group,
M
a smooth manifold, and
P\rightarrow M
a principal
G
-bundle over
M
. Consider the category
[(P\times P)/G\rightrightarrows M]
with the following description:

•

objects are the points of the smooth manifold
M
,

•

morphisms are the points of the quotient space
(P\times P)/G
,

•

the source map is given by
[(x_{1},x_{2})]\mapsto\pi(x_{1})
, for all
[(x_{1},x_{2})]\in(P\times P)/G

•

the target map is given by

[(x_{1},x_{2})]\mapsto\pi(x_{2})
, for all
(x_{1},x_{2})\in(P\times P)/G
,

•

the composition map is given by
([(x_{1},x_{2})],[(x_{3},x_{4})])\mapsto[(x_{1},x_{4})]
, for all

[(x_{1},x_{2})]
, and
[(x_{3},x_{4})]
in
(P\times P)/G
with
\pi(x_{2})=\pi(x_{3})
.

We call
[(P\times P)/G\rightrightarrows M]
to be the
Gauge groupoid of the principal bundle
\pi:P\rightarrow M
.

Example 2.3.6
.

Let
M
be a smooth manifold, and
E\rightarrow M
a vector bundle over the smooth manifold
M
. Consider the category
[{\rm GL}(E)\rightrightarrows M]
, with the following description:

•

objects are the points of the smooth manifold
M
,

•

a morphism from an element
x
to an element
y
of
M
is given by a linear isomorphism
E_{x}\rightarrow E_{y}
,

•

the source map is given by
(\gamma:E_{x}\rightarrow E_{y})\mapsto x
,

•

the target map is given by
(\gamma:E_{x}\rightarrow E_{y})\mapsto y
,

•

the composition map is given by the usual composition of functions.

We call
[{\rm GL}(E)\rightrightarrows M]
to be the
general linear groupoid of the vector bundle
E\rightarrow M
.

Definition 2.3.7

(morphism of Lie groupoids
[
49
, Section
5.1
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
and
\mathcal{H}=[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
be Lie groupoids. A
morphism of Lie groupoids from
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
to
\mathcal{H}=[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
is a functor
(F_{1},F_{0}):[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
such that
F_{0}:\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
and
F_{1}:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}
are smooth maps.

(2.3.1)

Example 2.3.8
.

Let
G
and
H
be Lie groups acting on smooth manifolds
M
and
N
respectively. Let
\psi:G\rightarrow H
be a morphism of Lie groups, and
f:M\rightarrow N
a smooth map preserving the action of Lie groups; that is,
f(mg)=f(m)\psi(g)
for all
m\in M,g\in G
. Then,
((f\times\psi),f):[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[N\times H\rightrightarrows N]
is a morphism of Lie groupoids.

Example 2.3.9
.

Let
G
be a Lie group,
P\rightarrow M,P^{\prime}\rightarrow M^{\prime}
are principal
G
-bundles. A morphism of principal bundles
(F,f):P(M,G)\rightarrow P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G)
induce a morphism of Lie groupoids
((F,F)^{/G},f):[(P\times P)/G\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[(P^{\prime}\times P^{\prime})/G\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}]
.

Example 2.3.10
.

Let
M
be a smooth manifold. Consider vector bundles
E\rightarrow M
, and
E^{\prime}\rightarrow M
. A morphism of vector bundles
(F,f):(E\rightarrow M)\rightarrow(E^{\prime}\rightarrow M^{\prime})
induce a morphism of Lie groupoids
[{\rm GL}(E)\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[{\rm GL}(E^{\prime})\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}]
.

For each smooth manifold
M
, using
Example

2.2.19
we can associate a stack
\underline{M}:\text{Man}\rightarrow{\rm Gpd}
. Also for a Lie group
G
, we have associated a stack
BG:{\rm Man}\rightarrow\text{Gpd}
. As smooth manifolds, Lie groups are special cases of Lie groupoids; we expect a similar construction of stack for Lie groupoids.

For a Lie group
G
, the stack
BG
assigns for each manifold
M
, a category
BG(M)
, of principal
G
-bundles over
M
. Inspired by the notion of a principal
G
-bundle over a smooth manifold, we introduce the notion of a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over a smooth manifold for a Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
. For that, firstly, we introduce the notion of action of a Lie groupoid on a smooth manifold.

Definition 2.3.11

(action of a Lie groupoid on a Manifold)
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
be a Lie groupoid and
P
a smooth manifold.

A
right action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
consists of a pair of smooth maps

(a:P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},\mu:P\times_{a,\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow P)
satisfying the following conditions:

1.

\mu(p,1_{a(p)})=p
for all
p\in P
,

2.

a(\mu(p,\gamma))=s(\gamma)
for all
(p,\gamma)\in P\times_{a,\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}
,
and

3.

\mu(\mu(p,\gamma),\gamma^{\prime})=\mu(p,\gamma\circ\gamma^{\prime})
for all
(p,\gamma,\gamma^{\prime})\in P\times_{a,\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}
.

A
left action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
consists of a pair of smooth maps
(a\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},\mu\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},a}P\rightarrow P)
satisfying the following conditions:

1.

\mu(1_{a(p)},p)=p
for all
p\in P
,

2.

a(\mu(\gamma,p))=t(\gamma)
for all
(\gamma,p)\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},a}P
, and

3.

\mu(\gamma,\mu(\gamma^{\prime},p))=\mu(\gamma\circ\gamma^{\prime},p)
for all
(\gamma,\gamma^{\prime},p)\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},a}P
.

Example 2.3.12
.

The action of a Lie groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows M]
on a smooth manifold
N
consists of a smooth map
f:N\rightarrow M
.

Example 2.3.13
.

An action of a Lie groupoid
[G\rightrightarrows*]
on a smooth manifold
M
is given by an action
\mu:M\times G\rightarrow M
of the Lie group
G
on the manifold
M
.

Example 2.3.14
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
be a Lie groupoid. Consider the composition map

m:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t,\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1}.

The pair
(t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},m:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t,\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1})
gives a left action of
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
on
\mathcal{G}_{1}
. The pair
(s:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},m:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t,\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1})
gives a right action of
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
on
\mathcal{G}_{1}
.

Definition 2.3.15

(
[
41
, Definition
3.17
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{G}
be a Lie groupoid and
M
a smooth manifold. A
(right) principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over
M
consists of

1.

a smooth manifold
P
,

2.

a surjective submersion
\pi:P\rightarrow M
,

3.

an action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
given by a pair of maps
(a_{\mathcal{G}}:P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},\mu:P\times_{a_{\mathcal{G}},\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow P)
,

satisfying the following conditions:

1.

the map
\pi:P\rightarrow M
is such that,
\pi(p\cdot\gamma)=\pi(p)
for all
(p,\gamma)\in P\times_{a_{\mathcal{G}},\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}
,

2.

the map
P\times_{a_{\mathcal{G}},\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow P\times_{M}P
given by
(p,\gamma)\mapsto(p\cdot\gamma,p)
is a diffeomorphism.

A
left principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over
M
is defined similarly using the left action of
\mathcal{G}
.

\mathcal{G}

(2.3.4)

Definition 2.3.18
.

Let
\mathcal{G}
be a Lie groupoid,
P(M,\mathcal{G})
and
P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},\mathcal{G})
are principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles. A
morphism of principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles
from
P(M,\mathcal{G})
to
P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},\mathcal{G})
consists of a pair of smooth maps
(F:P\rightarrow P^{\prime},f:M\rightarrow M^{\prime})
such that,
\pi^{\prime}\circ F=f\circ\pi
,
a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}\circ F=a_{\mathcal{G}}
, and
\mu^{\prime}\circ(F,1)=F\circ\mu
.

We see a morphism of principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles as the following commutative diagram,

\hbox to286.65pt{\vbox to148.83pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 143.32277pt\lower-95.24808pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}

Similar to the notion of pull-back of a geometric structure on a manifold
M
along a smooth map
f:N\rightarrow M
, we have the notion of pull-back of a
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over a manifold
M
along a smooth map
f:N\rightarrow M
.

2.3.1
Pullback of a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle

Let
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
be a Lie groupoid and
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle. Let
f\colon N\rightarrow M
be a smooth map. As
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
is a submersion, the
pull-back
f^{*}P=N\times_{M}P=\{(n,p)\colon f(n)=\pi(p)\}
is a manifold (an embedded submanifold of
N\times P
).

We will express the pull-back by the following diagram,

(2.3.6)

Consider the map
\mu\colon(N\times_{M}P)\times\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow N\times_{M}P
, defined as
\big((n,p),g\big)\mapsto(n,pg)
.
The pair of maps

(a\circ{\pr}_{2}\colon N\times_{B}P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},\mu\colon(N\times_{M}P)\times\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow N\times_{M}P),

gives a (right) action of the Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
on the manifold
N\times_{M}P
. The projection map
{\pr}_{1}:N\times_{M}P\rightarrow N
will then be a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over the manifold
N
. We call
(N\times_{B}P,{\pr}_{1},N)
to be
the pull-back of the principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
along
f\colon N\rightarrow M
.

Similar to the example of a fibered category coming from a Lie group, we have a fibered category
(
Definition

2.2.11
) coming from a Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
.

2.3.2
A stack associated to a Lie groupoid

Let
\mathcal{G}
be a Lie groupoid. Let
B\mathcal{G}
be the category, whose objects are principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles and morphisms are morphisms of principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles. Consider the functor
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\text{Man}
with the following description:

•

an object
P(M,\mathcal{G})
of the category
B\mathcal{G}
is mapped to the object
M
of the category
Man
,

•

a morphism
(F,f):P(M,\mathcal{G})\rightarrow P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},\mathcal{G})
of the category
B\mathcal{G}
is mapped to the morphism
f:M\rightarrow M^{\prime}
of the category
Man
.

The functor
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\text{Man}
is a fibered category. Consider the big étale topology on the category
Man

(
Example

2.2.5
). Then, the functor
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\text{Man}
becomes a stack (
Definition

2.2.20
). We call the stack
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\text{Man}
to be the
classifying stack of the Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
.

The stack
B\mathcal{G}
comes with an extra property. We have a morphism of stacks
\underline{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}
defined by the pull-back of the trivial
\mathcal{G}
-bundle
t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
along a smooth map
M\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
for a smooth manifold
M
. This morphism is a representable morphism of stacks (
[
41
, Example
4.24
]
). This map is actually a “surjective submersion”.
To make sense of a (representable) morphism of stacks being surjective submersion, we need to recall an outcome of the Yoneda lemma.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category.
Let
A
be an object of
\mathcal{C}
.
Then, we have the functor (of points)
h_{A}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
.
This gives a functor
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow[C^{\op},\text{Set}]
.
The Yoneda lemma says that this functor is an embedding of categories.
Consider a functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
.
Seeing a set as a discrete category, we can see the functor
\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
as a pseudo-functor.
As mentioned before, for every pseudo-functor on
\mathcal{C}
, we can associate a fibered category over
\mathcal{C}
.
The same would be true for the category
Man
.
Thus, we have an embedding of categories
\text{Man}\rightarrow\text{Fib}_{\text{Man}}
.
For an object
M
of
Man
, the fibered category associated to the functor
h_{M}:\text{Man}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
is given by
\underline{M}\rightarrow\text{Man}
. As mentioned before, these fibered categories
\underline{M}\rightarrow\text{Man}
are stacks. So, we have an embedding of categories
\text{Man}\rightarrow\text{Stacks}_{\text{Man}}
. In particular, for smooth manifolds
M,N
, we have a bijection
\text{Hom}_{\text{Man}}(M,N)\rightarrow\text{Hom}_{\text{Stacks}}(\underline{M},\underline{N})
. We have the following lemma.

Lemma 2.3.19

(
[
41
, Corollary
4.16
]
)
.

The functor
\text{Man}\rightarrow\text{Stacks}_{\text{Man}}
defined above is an embedding of categories.

Thus, for smooth manifolds
M,N
, any morphism of stacks
\underline{M}\rightarrow\underline{N}
comes from a unique smooth map
M\rightarrow N
. Further, if a stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
is representable by a smooth manifold, then there exists, up to a diffeomorphism, exactly one smooth manifold representing the stack
\mathcal{D}
.

Definition 2.3.20
.

Let
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
and
\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\text{Man}
be stacks.
A representable morphism of stacks
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is said to be a
surjective submersion
if for each smooth manifold
M
and a morphism of stacks
\underline{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, the projection morphism
{\pr}_{2}:\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{M}\rightarrow\underline{M}
induce a surjective submersion of the smooth manifolds
X\rightarrow M
, where
\underline{X}=\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{M}
.

With this definition of a representable morphism being a surjective submersion, the morphism of stacks
\underline{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}
is a representable surjective submersion (
[
41
, Example
4.24
]
).
The existence of a representable surjective submersion
M\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
for a given stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
is a very special property, and there is a specific name to that.

Definition 2.3.21

(an atlas for the stack
[
41
, Definition
4.27
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
be a stack. An
atlas for the stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow{\rm Man}
consists of a smooth manifold
X
and a representable morphism of stacks
\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
which is a surjective submersion.

Definition 2.3.22

(differentiable stack
[
41
, Definition
4.27
]
)
.

A stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
is said to be a
differentiable stack
if there exists an atlas for the stack
\mathcal{D}
.

Remark 2.3.23
.

Given an atlas,
X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and a surjective submersion
Y\rightarrow X
, the composition
Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
would also be an atlas for the stack
\mathcal{D}
.

2.3.3
A Lie groupoid associated to a differentiable stack

In the last section, we have introduced the notion of a differentiable stack as a stack, which shares a common property with the
B\mathcal{G}
, namely both admits an atlas. In this section, we associate a Lie groupoid for a differentiable stack. More details can be found at
[
41
, Proposition
4.31
]
.

Let
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
be a differentiable stack, and
r\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
an atlas
for the stack
\mathcal{D}
.
Let

(2.3.7)

As
r\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for the stack
\mathcal{D}
, the
2
-fiber product
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}
is representable by a smooth manifold, which we denote by
X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X
.
Since, stacks are fibered in groupoids, we can define the Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}_{r}=[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X]
, with the following structure maps:

1.

the source map
s:X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightarrow X
is given by the morphism of smooth manifolds associated to the morphism of stacks
{\pr}_{1}\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}
,

2.

the target map
t:X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightarrow X
is given by the morphism of smooth manifolds associated to the morphism of stacks
{\pr}_{2}\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}
,

3.

the composition is given by the morphism of stacks

m\colon(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X})\times_{\underline{X}}(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X})\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X},

defined as

m\big((a,b,\alpha\colon r(a)\rightarrow r(b)),(b,c,\beta\colon r(b)\rightarrow r(c))\big)=\big(a,c,\beta\circ\alpha\colon r(a)\rightarrow r(c)\big),

4.

the unit map is given by the morphism of stacks

u\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X},

defined as

u(a)=\big(a,a,\text{Id}\colon r(a)\rightarrow r(a)\big),

5.

the inverse map is given by the morphism of stacks

i\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X},

defined as

i\big((a,b,\alpha\colon r(a)\rightarrow r(b))\big)=\big(b,a,\alpha^{-1}\colon r(b)\rightarrow r(a)\big).

It turns out that there is an isomorphism of stacks
\mathcal{D}\cong B\mathcal{G}_{r}
.

Lemma 2.3.24

(
[
41
, Proposition
4.31
]
)
.

Let
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
be a differentiable stack and
r\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
.
Then,
there exists a Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
with an isomorphism of stacks
\mathcal{D}\cong B\mathcal{G}
. Moreover, we may take
\mathcal{G}_{0}=X
and
\mathcal{G}_{1}=X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X
, where
X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X
is the smooth manifold representing the
2
-fiber product
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}
.

2.3.4
Morita equivalence of Lie groupoids

Y\rightarrow X
, and an atlas
X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
, the composition
Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
(
Remark

2.3.23
).

We expect some relation between the Lie groupoids
[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X]
and
[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y]
, given by the surjective submersion
f:X\rightarrow Y
. It turns out that the “pull-back of
[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y]
along
f:X\rightarrow Y
” is isomorphic to the Lie groupoid
[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows X]
.

2.3.4.1
pull-back of a Lie groupoid along a surjective submersion

Let
\Gamma=(\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0})
be a Lie groupoid and

J\colon P_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
a surjective submersion.

Consider the pull-back of the source map
s\colon\Gamma_{1}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
along
J\colon P_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
to obtain
P_{0}\times_{\Gamma_{0}}\Gamma_{1}
. We then pull-back the map
J\colon P_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
along
t\circ{\pr}_{2}\colon P_{0}\times_{\Gamma_{0}}\Gamma_{1}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
to obtain
(P_{0}\times_{\Gamma_{0}}\Gamma_{1})\times_{\Gamma_{0}}P_{0}
. Above pull-backs can be expressed by the following diagram,

(2.3.8)

Denote the smooth manifold
(P_{0}\times_{\Gamma_{0}}\Gamma_{1})\times_{\Gamma_{0}}P_{0}
by
P_{1}
. The smooth manifold
P_{1}
along with
P_{0}
gives a Lie groupoid
[P_{1}\rightrightarrows P_{0}]
, with the following description

1.

the source map
s\colon P_{1}\rightarrow P_{0}
is given by
(p,x,q)\mapsto p
,

2.

the target map
t\colon P_{1}\rightarrow P_{0}
is given by
(p,x,q)\mapsto q
,

3.

the composition map
m\colon P_{1}\times_{P_{0}}P_{1}\rightarrow P_{1}
is given by
\big((p,x,q),(q,y,r)\big)\mapsto(p,x\circ y,r)
,

4.

the identity map
u\colon P_{0}\rightarrow P_{1}
is given by
a\mapsto(a,1_{J(a)},a)
,

5.

the inverse map
i\colon P_{1}\rightarrow P_{1}
is given by
(a,\gamma,b)\mapsto(b,\gamma^{-1},a)
.

Definition 2.3.25
.

Let
\Gamma=[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
be a Lie groupoid and

J\colon P_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
a surjective submersion. The Lie groupoid
[P_{1}\rightrightarrows P_{0}]
mentioned above (in the Diagram
2.3.8
) is called the
pull-back groupoid of the Lie groupoid
[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
along the map
J\colon P_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
.

Under this notion of a pull-back of a Lie groupoid along a surjective submersion, the Lie groupoids
[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X]
and
[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y]
associated to atlases
X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
(related by a surjective submersion
f:X\rightarrow Y
) are related. More precisely, we have the following result.

Proposition 2.3.26
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be a differentiable stack, and
r_{X}:X\rightarrow\mathcal{D},r_{Y}:Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
are atlases for the stack
\mathcal{D}
. Suppose that, there exists a surjective submersion
f:X\rightarrow Y
, such that,
r_{Y}\circ f=r_{X}
. Then, the induced morphism of Lie groupoids
[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X]\rightarrow[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y]
is with the property that
[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X]
is isomorphic to the pull-back groupoid of
[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y]
along the surjective submersion.

The above property has a name associated to it, a
Morita morphism of Lie groupoids
.

Definition 2.3.27

(Morita morphism of Lie groupoids
[
39
, Section
2.2
]
)
.

Let
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}],[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
be Lie groupoids. We say that a morphism of Lie groupoids
(\phi_{1},\phi_{0}):[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]\rightarrow[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
is a
Morita morphism of Lie groupoids
, if,
\phi_{0}:X_{0}\rightarrow Y_{0}
is a surjective submersion, and
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
is isomorphic to the pull-back of the Lie groupoid
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
along the surjective submersion
\phi_{0}:X_{0}\rightarrow Y_{0}
.

Suppose that
r_{X}:X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
r_{Y}:Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
are atlases. Consider the following

As
r_{X}
is an atlas, the map
{\pr}_{2}:X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow Y
is a surjective submersion.
As
r_{Y}
is an atlas, the map
{\pr}_{1}:X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow X
is a surjective submersion. As
r_{Y}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
, and
{\pr}_{2}
is a surjective submersion, the composition
X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
. This gives a morphism of Lie groupoids
[(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\times_{\mathcal{D}}(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\rightrightarrows(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)]\rightrightarrows[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y]
. Similarly, treating
r_{X}
as an atlas, for the surjective submersion
{\pr}_{1}
as surjective submersion, we have morphism of Lie groupoids

[(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\times_{\mathcal{D}}(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\rightrightarrows(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)]\rightrightarrows[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X]
.

As a consequence of
Proposition

2.3.26
, we have the following result.

Proposition 2.3.28
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be a differentiable stack, and
r_{X}:X\rightarrow\mathcal{D},r_{Y}:Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
atlases for the stack
\mathcal{D}
. Then, there exists a Lie groupoid
[(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\times_{\mathcal{D}}(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\rightrightarrows(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)]
and a pair of morphism of Lie groupoids

\displaystyle[(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\times_{\mathcal{D}}(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\rightrightarrows(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)]

\displaystyle\rightarrow[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X],

\displaystyle[(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\times_{\mathcal{D}}(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\rightrightarrows(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)]

\displaystyle\rightarrow[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y],

such that, both these morphisms are Morita morphisms of Lie groupoids.

Two Lie groupoids sharing the property mentioned above are called
Morita equivalent Lie groupoids
, which we define below.

Definition 2.3.29

(Morita equivalent Lie groupoids
[
39
, Section
2.2
]
)
.

Let
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
and
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
be Lie groupoids. We say that
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
and
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
are
Morita equivalent Lie groupoids
, if, there exists a Lie groupoid
[Z_{1}\rightrightarrows Z_{0}]
and Morita morphisms of Lie groupoids
[Z_{1}\rightrightarrows Z_{0}]\rightarrow[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
, and

[Z_{1}\rightrightarrows Z_{0}]\rightarrow[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
.

Thus, we have the following result.

Lemma 2.3.30
.

Let
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
be a differentiable stack. If
X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
, and
Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
are atlases for the stack
\mathcal{D}
, then, the Lie groupoids
[X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X]
and
[Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y]
are Morita equivalent.

2.3.5
Bibundles

Let
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
and
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
be Morita equivalent Lie groupoids. Thus, there exists a Lie groupoid
[Z_{1}\rightrightarrows Z_{0}]
and Morita morphisms
[Z_{1}\rightrightarrows Z_{0}]\rightarrow[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
, and
[Z_{1}\rightrightarrows Z_{0}]\rightarrow[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
. In particular, we have surjective submersions
Z_{0}\rightarrow X_{0},Z_{0}\rightarrow Y_{0}
. As
[Z_{1}\rightrightarrows Z_{0}]
is actually determined by the maps
Z_{0}\rightarrow X_{0},Z_{0}\rightarrow Y_{0}
, we can see the notion of Morita equivalent Lie groupoids as the following.

Lemma 2.3.31
.

Suppose that
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
and
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
be Morita equivalent Lie groupoids. Then, there exists a smooth manifold
P
and surjective submersions
P\rightarrow X_{0},P\rightarrow Y_{0}
, along with an action of
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}],[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
on
P
, such that
P\rightarrow X_{0}
is a principal
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
-bundle and
P\rightarrow Y_{0}
is a principal
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
-bundle.

Relaxing the condition of
P\rightarrow Y_{0}
being a principal
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
-bundle in the
Lemma

2.3.31
, gives an interesting notion of a “generalized morphism from
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
to
[Y_{1}\rightrightarrows Y_{0}]
”. This structure goes by the name of an
\mathbb{X}-\mathbb{Y}
-bibundle.

Definition 2.3.32

(
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle)
.

Let
\mathcal{G},\mathcal{H}
be Lie groupoids. A
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
consists of,

1.

a smooth manifold
P
,

2.

a left action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
, with anchor map

a_{\mathcal{G}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
,

3.

a right action of
\mathcal{H}
on
P
, with anchor map
a_{\mathcal{H}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
,

such that,

1.

the anchor map
a_{\mathcal{G}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
is a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle,

2.

the anchor map
a_{\mathcal{H}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
is a
\mathcal{G}
-invariant map; that is,
a_{\mathcal{H}}(gp)=a_{\mathcal{H}}(p)
for
p\in P
and
g\in\mathcal{G}_{1}
with
s(g)=a_{\mathcal{G}}(p)
,

3.

the action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
is compatible with the action of
\mathcal{H}
on
P
; that is,
(gp)h=g(ph)
for
g\in\mathcal{G}_{1},p\in P
and
h\in\mathcal{H}_{1}
with
s(g)=a_{\mathcal{G}}(p)
and
t(h)=a_{\mathcal{H}}(p)
.

(2.3.9)

We denote a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle by
P\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
.

Remark 2.3.33
.

If the anchor map
a_{\mathcal{H}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
, in a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
P\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
, is a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle, then, we call
P\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
to be
a
\mathcal{G}
-principal bibundle
.

Example 2.3.34
.

Let
G
be a Lie group,
M
a smooth manifold, and
\pi:P\rightarrow M
a principal
G
bundle. As mentioned before, we see the Lie group
G
as the Lie groupoid
[G\rightrightarrows*]
, and the smooth manifold
M
as the Lie groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows M]
. The action of
G
on
P
gives an action of the Lie groupoid
[G\rightrightarrows*]
on the manifold
P
. The smooth map
\pi:P\rightarrow M
gives an action of the Lie groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows M]
on the manifold
P
. These actions are seen to be compatible, giving a
[M\rightrightarrows M]-[G\rightrightarrows*]
-bibundle, as in the following diagram,

Let
G,H
be Lie groups and
\phi:G\rightarrow H
be a Lie group morphism. Then, we have an action of
G
on
H
given by
(g,h)\mapsto\phi(g)h
. Thus, as a special case, we have a
[G\rightrightarrows*]-[H\rightrightarrows*]
-bibundle.

Remark 2.3.36
.

The
Example

2.3.35
says that, for a morphism of Lie groups
\phi:G\rightarrow H
, we can associate a
[G\rightrightarrows*]-[H\rightrightarrows*]
-bibundle.
This would give a hope to associate a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle for a morphism of Lie groupoids
\phi:\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
. We postpone this construction of associating a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle to a morphism of Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
to
Section

3.3.1
. This justifies the alternate terminology of a
generalized morphism from
\mathcal{G}
to
\mathcal{H}
to a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle.

Example 2.3.37
.

Let
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
be a Lie groupoid. We have seen
in
Example

2.3.16
that the target map
t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
is considered as a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle (see Diagram
2.3.3
). The map
t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
gives an action of the Lie groupoid
[\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
on the manifold
\mathcal{G}_{1}
. These actions of
[\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
from left side,
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
from right side, on the manifold
\mathcal{G}_{1}
are compatible. This gives the following
[\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]-[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
-bibundle,

\hbox to140.83pt{\vbox to82.96pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 70.41661pt\lower-41.4792pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{

Remark 2.3.38
.

In
Lemma

2.3.30
, we have seen that, for a differentiable stack
\mathcal{D}
, the associated Lie groupoids coming from any two atlases are Morita equivalent. In other words, if two differentiable stacks are isomorphic, then they can be represented by Morita equivalent Lie groupoids. It is also true that if two Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}
, and
\mathcal{H}
are Morita equivalent, then the associated differentiable stacks
B\mathcal{G}
, and
B\mathcal{H}
are isomorphic. We see the proof of this result in
Chapter

3
.

We end this section with a result about transitive Lie groupoids, which we will use in
Chapter

3
.

Lemma 2.3.39
.

Any transitive Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
is Morita equivalent to the Lie group
\mathcal{G}_{x}
for any
x\in\mathcal{G}_{0}
, that is,
the Lie groupoid
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
is Morita equivalent to the Lie groupoid
[\mathcal{G}_{x}\rightrightarrows*]
.

Proof.

Let
x
be an element in
\mathcal{G}_{0}
. Consider a morphism of Lie groupoids
\psi\colon[\mathcal{G}_{x}\rightrightarrows*]\rightarrow[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
with the following description:

•

the element
*
is mapped to the element
x
in
\mathcal{G}_{0}
,

•

an element
g
in
\mathcal{G}_{x}
is mapped to the element
g
in
\mathcal{G}_{1}
.

We see the above morphism as the following diagram,

Observe that the morphism set of the pull-back groupoid is

\displaystyle*\times_{\psi_{0},\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t\circ{\pr}_{2},\mathcal{G}_{0},\psi_{0}}*

\displaystyle=\{(*,g,*)|\psi_{0}(*)=s(g),(t\circ{\pr}_{2})(*,g)=\psi_{0}(*)\}

\displaystyle=\{(*,g,*)|s(g)=x,t(g)=x\}

\displaystyle=\{(*,g,x)|g\in s^{-1}(x)\bigcap t^{-1}(x)\}

\displaystyle=\{(*,g,*)|g\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\}=\mathcal{G}_{x}.

So, the pull-back groupoid of
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
along the map
*\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
is the Lie groupoid
[\mathcal{G}_{x}\rightrightarrows*]
. Thus, we conlude that
\psi\colon[\mathcal{G}_{x}\rightrightarrows*]\rightarrow[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
is a Morita morphism of Lie groupoids. So,
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
is Morita equivalent to the Lie groupoid
[\mathcal{G}_{x}\rightrightarrows*]
.
∎

2.4
Atiyah sequence and Chern-Weil theory for principal bundles over smooth manifold

This section recalls the differential geometry of principal bundles over smooth manifolds, their connections, curvature, and other results. We also recall the notion of the Atiyah sequence associated to a principal bundle and use it to introduce the notion of a connection on a principal bundle.

Throughout this section we will assume our smooth manifolds to be second countable and Hausdorff,
G
will denote a Lie group and
\mathfrak{g}
its Lie algebra. For
g\in G
, let
\text{Ad}(g):G\rightarrow G
be the adjoint map defined as
\text{Ad}(g)(h)=ghg^{-1}
for all
h\in G
. Let
{\rm ad}(g):\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
be the differential of
\text{Ad}(g):G\rightarrow G
at the identity.

Let
P
be a smooth manifold with an action of
G
. For
g\in G
, let
\delta_{g}:P\rightarrow P
be the right translation map, defined as
p\mapsto pg
for
p\in P
. For
p\in P
, let
\delta_{p}:G\rightarrow P
be the map defined as
g\mapsto pg
for
g\in G
. Given an element
A\in\mathfrak{g}
, let us denote by
A^{*}:P\rightarrow TP
, the vector field on
P
, defined as

A^{*}(p)=(\delta_{p})_{*,e}(A)
for all
p\in P
.
We call
A^{*}
to be the fundamental vector field on
P
associated to the element
A
of the Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}
.

Definition 2.4.1

(connection structure on a principal bundle)
.

Let
M
be a smooth manifold,
G
a Lie group and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle.
A
connection structure on
P(M,G)
is given by a
\mathfrak{g}
-valued differential
1
-form
\omega:P\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
, satisfying the following conditions:

1.

\omega(p)(A^{*}(p))=A
for all
p\in P
and
A\in\mathfrak{g}
,

2.

(\delta_{g}^{*}\omega)(p)(v)=({\rm ad}(g^{-1}))(\omega(p)(v))
for all
g\in G,p\in P
and
v\in T_{p}P
.

Example 2.4.2
.

Let
M
be a smooth manifold, and
G
a Lie group. Let
\theta:G\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}G
be the Maurer-Cartan form of
G
. Let
{\pr}_{1}:M\times G\rightarrow M
be the first projection map, considered as a principal
G
-bundle. Let
{\pr}_{2}:M\times G\rightarrow G
be the second projection map. The pull-back
{\pr}_{2}^{*}\theta:M\times G\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}(M\times G)
is a connection structure on the principal bundle
{\pr}_{1}:M\times G\rightarrow M
.

Remark 2.4.3
.

Using the partition of unity argument, we can conclude that a connection exists on any principal bundle
P(M,G)
. Later in this section, we see that giving a connection structure on
P(M,G)
is the same as providing a splitting of some short exact sequence of vector bundles over
M
. As any short exact sequence of vector bundles over a smooth manifold splits (again using the partition of unity argument), we can say that connection exists on any principal bundle
P(M,G)
.

The notion of connection (and curvature) on a principal bundle over a smooth manifold in terms of a differential form (and distribution) is classical and is discussed in many books. In
Chapter

4
, we define a connection on a principal bundle over a Lie groupoid using the Atiyah sequence.
The language of Atiyah sequence and its splitting to define a connection on principal bundle over a manifold is relatively less commonly found in standard textbooks. So, here we will discuss this topic in bit more details.
The only place where we could find it is the appendix of
[
43
]
.
We use
[
43
]
as a reference for this section. We first introduce the construction of quotient vector bundles.

2.4.1
Quotient vector bundles

Proposition 2.4.4

(
[
43
, Appendix A, Proposition
2.1
]
)
.

Let
\pi:P\rightarrow M
be a principal
G
-bundle, and
p^{E}\colon E\rightarrow P
a vector bundle. Suppose that
G
acts on
E
, from the right side such that the following two conditions are satisfied:

1.

for each
g\in G
, the right translation maps
\delta_{g}^{E}:E\rightarrow E,\delta_{g}^{P}:P\rightarrow P
induce an isomorphism of vector bundles
(\delta^{E}_{g},\delta^{P}_{g})\colon(E,p^{E},P)\rightarrow(E,p^{E},P)
,

2.

there exists an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in\Lambda}
of
P
with a trivialization
\{\psi_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\times V\rightarrow(p^{E})^{-1}(U_{\alpha})\}
of the vector bundle
p^{E}:E\rightarrow P
, satisfying the following conditions:

(a)

each
U_{\alpha}
is a
\pi
-saturated open set
1
1

1

that is
\pi^{-1}(\pi(U_{\alpha}))=U_{\alpha}
.
of the form
\pi^{-1}(V_{\alpha})
for some open
V_{\alpha}\subseteq M
, for each
\alpha\in\Lambda
,

(b)

the trivialization map
\psi_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\times V\rightarrow(p^{E})^{-1}(U_{\alpha})
is
G
-equivariant, in the sense that

\psi_{\alpha}(ug,v)=\psi(u,v)g
for all
u\in U_{\alpha},v\in V,g\in G
and
\alpha\in\Lambda
.

Then, the orbit set
E/G
has a unique vector bundle structure over
M
such that the quotient map
q^{E}\colon E\rightarrow E/G
is a surjective submersion, and
(q^{E},\pi)\colon(E,p^{E},P)\rightarrow(E/G,p^{E/G},M)
is a morphism of vector bundles. Further,

(2.4.2)

Example 2.4.6
.

be a smooth manifold,
G
a Lie group and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle. Consider the trivial bundle
p^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}\colon P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow P
, a vector bundle over the smooth manifold
P
. Consider the action of
G
on
P\times\mathfrak{g}
given by
((p,A),g)\mapsto(pg,{\rm ad}(g^{-1})(A))

G
on
P\times\mathfrak{g}
satisfies the conditions mentioned in the
Proposition

2.4.4
, giving the quotient vector bundle
(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
, which we call

(2.4.3)

2.4.2
Morphisms of quotient vector bundles

Let
M,M^{\prime}
be smooth manifolds,
G,G^{\prime}
are Lie groups and
P(M,G),P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G^{\prime})
are principal bundles. Consider vector bundles
(E,p^{E},P)
and
(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},P^{\prime})
over
P(M,G)
and
P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G^{\prime})
respectively satisfying the conditions mentioned in
Proposition

2.4.4
. This gives quotient vector bundles
(E/G,p^{E/G},M)
and
(E^{\prime}/G^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}/G^{\prime}},M^{\prime})
. The following result gives a criterion for a morphism of vector bundles
(E,p^{E},P)\rightarrow(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},P^{\prime})
to induce a morphism of vector bundles

(E/G,p^{E/G},M)\rightarrow(E^{\prime}/G,p^{E^{\prime}/G^{\prime}},M^{\prime})
.

Proposition 2.4.7

(
[
43
, Appendix
A
, Proposition
2.2(i)
]
)

P(M,G),P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G^{\prime})

P(M,G)
and
P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G^{\prime})
respectively, satisfying the conditions in the
Proposition

2.4.4
. Let
F(f,\phi)\colon P(M,G)\rightarrow P^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G^{\prime})

Example 2.4.8
.

The
Proposition

2.4.7
, allows us to construct a morphism of vector bundles from the adjoint bundle of
P(M,G)
to the Atiyah bundle of
P(M,G)
, which would be the first half of the Atiyah sequence associated to the principal bundle
P(M,G)
.

Consider the morphism of vector bundles
(j,1_{P})\colon(P\times\mathfrak{g},p^{P\times\mathfrak{g}},P)\rightarrow(TP,p^{TP},P)
given by
j(p,A)=A^{*}(p)
, where
A^{*}\colon P\rightarrow TP
is the fundamental vector field on
P
associated to the element
A\in\mathfrak{g}
. It turns out that, this morphism of vector bundles satisfies the condition in the
Proposition

2.4.7
giving the morphism of quotient vector bundles,

of quotient vector bundles is the first half of the Atiyah sequence of vector bundles over

.

2.4.3
Morphism from a quotient vector bundle

Let
G
be a Lie group, and
M
a smooth manifold. Consider a principal bundle
P(M,G)
and a vector bundle
(E,p^{E},P)
over
P(M,G)
. Suppose further that there is an action of
G
on
E
satisfying the conditions in
Proposition

2.4.4
. This gives the quotient vector bundle
(E/G,p^{E/G},M)
associated to the vector bundle
(E,p^{E},P)
. Let
(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},M^{\prime})
be another vector bundle. The following result gives a criterion for a morphism of vector bundles
(E,p^{E},P)\rightarrow(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},M^{\prime})
to induce a morphism of vector bundles

(E/G,p^{E/G},M)\rightarrow(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},M^{\prime})
.

Proposition 2.4.9

(
[
43
, Appendix
A
, Proposition
2.2(ii)
]
)
.

Let
P(M,G)
be a principal bundle, and
(E,p^{E},P)
a vector bundle over
P(M,G)
satisfying the conditions as in the
Proposition

2.4.4
. Let
(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},M^{\prime})
be a vector bundle, and
(\Phi,F)\colon(E,p^{E},P)\rightarrow(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},M^{\prime})
a morphism of vector bundles such that
\Phi(\xi g)=\Phi(\xi)
for all
\xi\in E,g\in G
and
F(ug)=F(u)
for all
u\in P,g\in G
.
Then, there exists a unique vector bundle morphism

(\Phi^{/G},F^{/G})\colon(E/G,p^{E/G},M)\rightarrow(E^{\prime},p^{E^{\prime}},M^{\prime}),

as in the following diagram,

(2.4.4)

As the above diagram is a pull-back diagram, it turns out that there is a bijective correspondence between the set of
G
-invariant sections of the vector bundle
(E,p^{E},P)
and the set of sections of the quotient vector bundle
(E/G,p^{E/G},M)
.

Let
X\colon M\rightarrow E/G
be a section of the vector bundle
p^{E/G}\colon E/G\rightarrow M
. As the above diagram is a pull-back diagram, by the uniqueness of pull-back, the following diagram

}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{76.84744pt}{-29.36313pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

(2.4.5)

gives a unique smooth map
\overline{X}\colon P\rightarrow E
such that
p^{E}\circ\overline{X}=1_{P}
and
q^{E}\circ\overline{X}=X\circ\pi
.
The property
p^{E}\circ\overline{X}=1_{P}
says that
\overline{X}\colon P\rightarrow E
is a section of the vector bundle
p^{E}\colon E\rightarrow P
. The property
q^{E}\circ\overline{X}=X\circ\pi
says that
q^{E}(\overline{X}(u))=X(\pi(u))
for all
u\in P
.
Moreover, the section
\overline{X}:P\rightarrow E
is
G
-equivariant. Thus, given a section
X\colon M\rightarrow E/G
of the vector bundle
p^{E/G}\colon E/G\rightarrow M
, we have constructed a
G
-equivariant section
\overline{X}\colon P\rightarrow E
of the vector bundle
p^{E}\colon E\rightarrow P
.

Conversely, let
X\colon P\rightarrow E
be a section of the vector bundle
p^{E}\colon E\rightarrow P
; that is
p^{E}\circ X=1_{P}
.
We impose the condition that
X\colon P\rightarrow E
is
G
-equivariant;
that is,
X(ug)=X(u)g
for all
u\in P
and
g\in G
. Define
\underline{X}\colon M\rightarrow E/G
as
\underline{X}(m)=(q^{E}\circ X)(p)
, for each
m\in M
, where
p\in P
is such that
\pi(p)=m
.
To see this is well defined, take
p_{1},p_{2}\in P
such that
\pi(p_{1})=\pi(p_{2})
.
Then, there exists
g\in G
such that
p_{2}=p_{1}g
.
Then,
q^{E}(X(p_{2}))=q^{E}(X(p_{1}g))=q^{E}(X(p_{1})g)=q^{E}(X(p_{1}))
.
Thus,
\underline{X}\colon M\rightarrow E/G

is well-defined. The condition
\underline{X}\circ\pi=q^{E}\circ X
implies that
p^{E/G}\circ\underline{X}=1_{M}
.
This can be seen as follows: as
\underline{X}\circ\pi=q^{E}\circ X
,
we have

p^{E/G}\circ\underline{X}\circ\pi=p^{E/G}\circ q^{E}\circ X=\pi\circ p^{E}\circ X=\pi;

that is,
p^{E/G}\circ\underline{X}\circ\pi=\pi
.
As
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
is surjective, the condition
p^{E/G}\circ\underline{X}\circ\pi=\pi
imply that
p^{E/G}\circ\underline{X}=1_{M}
; that is
\underline{X}\colon M\rightarrow E/G
is a section of the vector bundle
p^{E/G}\colon E/G\rightarrow M
.

We have
\underline{X}\circ\pi=q\circ X
. As
\pi
is a surjective submersion, the condition that the composition
\underline{X}\circ\pi
is smooth implies that
\underline{X}
is smooth. Thus, given a section
X\colon P\rightarrow E
of
p^{E}\colon E\rightarrow P
that is
G
-equivariant; in the sense that
X(pg)=X(p)g
, we get a section
\underline{X}\colon M\rightarrow E/G
of
p^{E/G}\colon E/G\rightarrow M
.

The conditions
q\circ\overline{X}=X\circ\pi
for all
X\in\Gamma(E/G)
and
\underline{X}\circ\pi=q\circ X
for each
G
-equivariant
X\in\Gamma(E)
says that the constructions
X\rightarrow\overline{X}
and
X\rightarrow\underline{X}
are inverses of each other. Thus, we have the following result:

Proposition 2.4.11
.

Let
G
be a Lie group and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle. Let
(E,p^{E},P)
be a vector bundle over
P(M,G)
as in
Proposition

2.4.4
. Denote by
\Gamma^{G}(E)
the set of sections of
E
which are
G
-equivariant. Then, there is an isomorphism of
C^{\infty}(M)
- modules
\Gamma^{G}(E)\rightarrow\Gamma(E/G)
.

2.4.5
Atiyah sequence of vector bundles

Consider the principal bundle
P(M,G)
. In
Example

2.4.8
and
Example

2.4.10
we have found morphisms of vector bundles

\displaystyle(j^{/G},1_{M})

\displaystyle\colon((P\times\mathfrak{g})/G,p^{(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G},M)\rightarrow((TP)/G,p^{(TP)/G},M),

\displaystyle(\pi_{*}^{/G},1_{M})

\displaystyle\colon((TP)/G,p^{(TP)/G},M)\rightarrow(TM,p^{TM},M).

These two morphisms of vector bundles combine to give a short exact sequence

0\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\xrightarrow{j^{/G}}(TP)/G\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}^{/G}}TM\rightarrow 0,

(2.4.6)

of vector bundles over the smooth manifold
M
. We call this short exact sequence to be the
Atiyah sequence associated to the principal bundle
P(M,G)
. It turns out that this short exact sequence of vector bundles over
M
induce a short exact sequence of (vector spaces) of sections,

0\rightarrow\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)\rightarrow\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)\rightarrow\Gamma(M,TM)\rightarrow 0.

Observe that the vector space
\Gamma(M,TM)
, of vector fields on
M
, has a Lie algebra structure. Using the Lie algebra structure of
\mathfrak{g}
, we introduce a Lie algebra structure on the vector space
\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)
. Similarly, the Lie algebra structure on the vector space
\Gamma(P,TP)
induces a Lie algebra structure on the vector space
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)
.

2.4.5.1
Lie algebra structure on
\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)

Let
X\colon M\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
be an element of
\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)
;
that is, a section of the vector bundle
p^{(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G}\colon(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
. By
Proposition

2.4.11
, this section
X:M\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
gives a
G
-equivariant section
\overline{X}:P\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
of the trivial bundle
p^{(P\times\mathfrak{g})}:P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow P
.
We can consider
\overline{X}:P\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
as a
G
-equivariant map
\overline{X}\colon P\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
.
Let
Y\colon M\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
be an element of
\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)
; a section of the vector bundle
p^{(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G}\colon(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
. This gives a
G
-equivariant map
\overline{Y}\colon P\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
.
For elements
X,Y
of
\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)
, define
[\overline{X},\overline{Y}]\colon P\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
as
p\mapsto[\overline{X}(p),\overline{Y}(p)]
for
p\in P
. This map
[\overline{X},\overline{Y}]\colon P\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
is in fact
G
-equivariant. The map
[\overline{X},\overline{Y}]:P\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
can be seen as a
G
-equivariant section
[\overline{X},\overline{Y}]\colon P\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
of the trivial bundle
p^{(P\times\mathfrak{g})}:P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow P
. By
Proposition

2.4.11
, this section
[\overline{X},\overline{Y}]\colon P\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
gives a section
[X,Y]\colon M\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
of the adjoint bundle
p^{(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G}:(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
. It is easy to see that the description
(X,Y)\mapsto[X,Y]
of the map

\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)\times\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)\rightarrow\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)
satisfies the condition for a binary operation to be a Lie bracket. With this Lie bracket structure, we consider
\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G)
as a Lie algebra.

2.4.5.2
Lie algebra structure on
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)

Let
X\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
be an element of
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)
; that is a section of the vector bundle
p^{(TP)/G}\colon(TP)/G\rightarrow M
. By
Proposition

2.4.11
, this section
X\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
gives a
G
-equivariant section
\overline{X}\colon P\rightarrow TP
. Let
Y\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
be an element of
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)
. This gives a
G
-equivariant section
\overline{Y}\colon P\rightarrow TP
. For elements
X,Y
of
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)
, consider the Lie bracket
[\overline{X},\overline{Y}]\colon P\rightarrow TP
. The Lie bracket
[\overline{X},\overline{Y}]\colon P\rightarrow TP
is a
G
-equivariant map, thus producing a section
[X,Y]\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
of the Atiyah bundle
(TP)/G\rightarrow M
. Moreover, the assignment
(X,Y)\mapsto[X,Y]
induces a Lie algebra structure on
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)
. With this Lie bracket structure, we consider
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)
as a Lie algebra.

Given a principal bundle
P(M,G)
, we have the associated Atiyah sequence

0\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\xrightarrow{j^{/G}}(TP)/G\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}^{/G}}TM\rightarrow 0.

This produces a short exact sequence of vector spaces

0\rightarrow\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g}))/G\xrightarrow{j^{/G}}\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)\xrightarrow{\pi_{*}^{/G}}\Gamma(M,TM)\rightarrow 0.

(2.4.7)

The Lie bracket structures on
\Gamma(M,(P\times\mathfrak{g}))/G
,
\Gamma(M,(TP)/G)
and
\Gamma(M,TM)
turn the Diagram
2.4.7
into a short exact sequence of Lie algebras.

2.4.6
Connection on
P(M,G)

We have covered the necessary background to introduce the notion of connection on a principal bundle as a splitting of the Atiyah sequence. The following definition appears for example in

[
3
, Section
2
, page
188
]
,
[
23
, Definition
1.21
]
, and

[
7
, Section
2
]

Definition 2.4.12

(connection on
P(M,G)
)
.

Let
P(M,G)
be a principal bundle. A
connection on
P(M,G)
is defined to be a splitting of the Atiyah sequence of vector bundles over
M
(Diagaram
2.4.6
).

Remark 2.4.13
.

Recall that any exact sequence of vector bundles admits a splitting. So, for every principal bundle, there exists a connection.

A splitting of a short exact sequence
0\rightarrow P\xrightarrow{f}Q\xrightarrow{g}R\rightarrow 0
constructs a retract of the morphism
f\colon P\rightarrow Q
; that is a morphism
\theta:Q\rightarrow P
such that
\theta\circ f=1_{P}
or, equivalently, a section of the morphism
g\colon Q\rightarrow R
; that is a morphism
\psi:R\rightarrow Q
such that
g\circ\psi=1_{R}
.

Definition 2.4.14

(infinitesimal connection)
.

Let
G
be a Lie group and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle. An
infinitesimal connection on
P(M,G)
is defined to be a section
\gamma\colon TM\rightarrow(TP)/G
of the morphism of vector bundles
\pi_{*}^{/G}\colon(TP)/G\rightarrow TM
.

Definition 2.4.15

(back-connection)
.

Let
G
be a Lie group and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle. A
back-connection on
P(M,G)
is defined to be a retract
\mathcal{D}\colon(TP)/G\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
of the morphism of vector bundles
j_{*}^{/G}\colon(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow(TP)/G
.

Let
P(M,G)
be a principal bundle, and
\mathcal{D}:(TP)/G\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
a back connection of
P(M,G)
. Consider the following diagram, obtained by combining the Diagrams
2.4.2
,
2.4.3
, and adding the maps
1_{P}:P\rightarrow P,1_{M}:M\rightarrow M,\mathcal{D}:(TP)/G\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
,

Rewriting the above diagram gives the following diagram,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TP}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P\times\mathfrak{g}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{D}\circ q^{TP}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{TP}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G}}

As the square is a pull-back diagram, there exists unique map
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}:TP\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
, such that

q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}\circ\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}=\mathcal{D}\circ q^{TP}
. This map
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}:TP\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
gives a
\mathfrak{g}
-valued differential
1
-form
\omega:P\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
, with the property that,

\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(v)=(p,\omega(p)(v))
for all
p\in P
, and
v\in T_{p}P
.

Lemma 2.4.16
.

The differential
1
-form
\omega:P\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
associated to the back connection
\mathcal{D}
satisfies the following conditions:

1.

\omega(p)(A^{*}(p))=A
for all
p\in P
and
A\in\mathfrak{g}
,

2.

\omega(pg)((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v))={\rm ad}(g^{-1})(\omega(p)(v))
for all
g\in G,p\in P,v\in T_{p}P
.

Proof.

We first observe that
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}:TP\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
is a retract of the map
j:P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow TP
. Observe that, the smooth maps
j:P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow TP
and
j^{/G}:(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow(TP)/G
are related as
q^{TP}\circ j=j^{/G}\circ q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}
. Thus, we have

\mathcal{D}\circ q^{TP}\circ j=\mathcal{D}\circ j^{/G}\circ q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}.

As
\mathcal{D}
is a retract of
j^{/G}
, we have
\mathcal{D}\circ j^{/G}=1
. Further,
q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}\circ\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}=\mathcal{D}\circ q^{TP}
. So,

q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}\circ\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\circ j=q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}.

Consider the following diagram,

\hbox to225.43pt{\vbox to116.41pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 110.6724pt\lower-50.78477pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
