As the square in above diagram is a pull-back diagram, there exists unique map
P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
that fill the above diagram. As the maps
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\circ j,1_{P\times\mathfrak{g}}
both fill the above diagram, we have
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\circ j=1_{P\times\mathfrak{g}}
. Thus,
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}:TP\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
is a retract of the map
j:P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow TP
.

Let
(p,A)\in P\times\mathfrak{g}
. We have
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(j(p,A))=(p,A)
; that is,
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(A^{*}(p))=(p,A)
. By the definition of
\omega
, we have

\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(A^{*}(p))=(p,\omega(p)(A^{*}(p)))
. Thus, the condition

(p,A)=\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(A^{*}(p))=(p,\omega(p)(A^{*}(p)))
imply that

A=\omega(p)(A^{*}(p))
.

Let
g\in G,p\in P,v\in T_{p}P
. Consider
(\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v)\in T_{pg}P
.
We have

\displaystyle q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v)))

\displaystyle=(q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}\circ\widetilde{\mathcal{D}})((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v))

\displaystyle=(\mathcal{D}\circ q^{TP})((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v))

\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}(q^{TP}((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v))

\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}(q^{TP}(v))

\displaystyle=q^{P\times\mathfrak{g}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(v)).

Thus, there exists unique
h\in G
such that

\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v))=h\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(v)
. Rewriting this in terms of
\omega
, we have

(pg,\omega(pg)((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v)))=(ph,{\rm ad}(h^{-1})(\omega(p)(v)))
. As the action is free, we have
h=g
. So,

\omega(pg)((\delta_{g})_{*,p}(v))={\rm ad}(g^{-1})(\omega(p)(v))
.
∎

Similarly, given a
\mathfrak{g}
-valued differential
1
-form
\omega:P\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
, satisfying the conditions in
Lemma

2.4.16
, one can associate a back-connection
\mathcal{D}
on
P(M,G)
. For
\omega:P\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
, define
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}:TP\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
as
v\mapsto(a,\omega(a)(v))
for all
v\in T_{a}P
and
a\in P
. The
G
-equivariance of
\omega
implies that this map
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}:TP\rightarrow P\times\mathfrak{g}
induce a map

\mathcal{D}:(TP)/G\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
. The condition
\omega(p)(A^{*}(p))=A
for all
p\in P
and
A\in\mathfrak{g}
implies that
\mathcal{D}:(TP)/G\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
is a retract of the map
j^{/G}:(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow(TP)/G
. Thus, we get a back connection
\mathcal{D}:(TP)/G\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
on the principal bundle
P(M,G)
.

Let
\gamma\colon TM\rightarrow(TP)/G
be an infinitesimal connection on
P(M,G)
. Consider the image
\gamma(TM)\subseteq(TP)/G
. Let
p\in P
. Consider the inverse image
(q^{TP}_{p})^{-1}(\gamma(T_{\pi(p)}M))\subseteq T_{p}P
. This defines a distribution
\mathcal{H}\subseteq TP
. Similarly, given a distribution
\mathcal{H}\subseteq TP
satisfying the conditions of definition of a connection as in
[
36
]
, we get an infinitesimal connection on
P(M,G)
.

2.4.7
Curvature form of the connection on the principal bundle
P(M,G)

Let
G
be a Lie group and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle. Let
\mathcal{D}\colon TM\rightarrow(TP)/G
be a connection of the principal bundle
P(M,G)
; that is, a section of the morphism
\pi_{*}^{/G}\colon(TP)/G\rightarrow TM
.

Let
X\colon M\rightarrow TM
be a vector field on the smooth manifold
M
; that is, a section of the vector bundle
TM\rightarrow M
. Then, the composition
\mathcal{D}\circ X\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
is a section of the quotient vector bundle
(TP)/G\rightarrow M
. By
Proposition

2.4.11
, this section
\mathcal{D}\circ X\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
of the quotient vector bundle
q^{(TP)/G}:(TP)/G\rightarrow M
gives a section
\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ X}\colon P\rightarrow TP
of the vector bundle
TP\rightarrow P
; that is,
\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ X}\colon P\rightarrow TP
is a vector field on
P
.
We denote the vector field
\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ X}
as
\Phi(X)
.
Thus, a connection
\mathcal{D}
gives a linear map
\Phi\colon\mathfrak{X}(M)\rightarrow\mathfrak{X}(P)
, assigning to each vector field
X\colon M\rightarrow TM
on
M
, a vector field
\Phi(X)\colon P\rightarrow TP
on
P
.
As the vector spaces
\mathfrak{X}(M)
and
\mathfrak{X}(P)
has the structure of a Lie algebra, one can ask if the map
\Phi
is a homomorphism of Lie algebras. The failure of the map
\Phi
to be a homomorphism of Lie algebras is measured as the curvature of the connection
\mathcal{D}
.

Let
X,Y:M\rightarrow TM
be vector fields on
M
.
Then,
\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]\colon P\rightarrow TP
is a vector field on
P
; that is a section of the vector bundle
TP\rightarrow P
. From
Proposition

2.4.11
, this section
\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]\colon P\rightarrow TP
of the vector bundle
TP\rightarrow P
gives a section
\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
of the quotient vector bundle
(TP)/G\rightarrow M
. Observe that

\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}=\underline{\Phi([X,Y])}-[\underline{\Phi(X)},\underline{\Phi(Y)}]=\underline{\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ[X,Y]}}-[\underline{\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ X}},\underline{\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ Y}}].

Observe from
Proposition

2.4.11
that the operations
X\mapsto\overline{X}
and
Y\mapsto\underline{Y}
are inverses to each other. Thus,

\underline{\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ[X,Y]}}-[\underline{\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ X}},\underline{\overline{\mathcal{D}\circ Y}}]=\mathcal{D}\circ[X,Y]-[\mathcal{D}\circ X,\mathcal{D}\circ Y]
. Consider the composition

\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}\colon M\rightarrow TM;

that is

\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ(\mathcal{D}\circ[X,Y]-[\mathcal{D}\circ X,\mathcal{D}\circ Y])\colon M\rightarrow TM

As
\pi_{*}^{/G}
induce a Lie algebra homomorphism on sections, we have

\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ[\mathcal{D}\circ X,\mathcal{D}\circ Y]=[\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\mathcal{D}\circ X,\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\mathcal{D}\circ Y].

So, for the section
\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
of the quotient vector bundle
(TP)/G\rightarrow M
we have

\displaystyle\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}

\displaystyle=\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ(\mathcal{D}\circ[X,Y]-[\mathcal{D}\circ X,\mathcal{D}\circ Y])

\displaystyle=\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ(\mathcal{D}\circ[X,Y])-\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ([\mathcal{D}\circ X,\mathcal{D}\circ Y])

\displaystyle=(\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\mathcal{D})\circ[X,Y]-[(\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\mathcal{D})\circ X,(\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\mathcal{D})\circ Y]

\displaystyle=[X,Y]-[X,Y]=0.

As
\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}\colon M\rightarrow(TP)/G
is a section of the vector bundle
(TP)/G\rightarrow M
such that
\pi_{*}^{/G}\circ\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}\colon M\rightarrow TM
is the zero section of the vector bundle
TM\rightarrow M
, there exists a section
\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)\colon M\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
of the vector bundle
(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
such that
j^{/G}\circ\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)=\underline{\Phi([X,Y])-[\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)]}
. Thus, given vector fields
X,Y\colon M\rightarrow TM
of the smooth manifold
M
, we have a section
\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)\colon M\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
of the adjoint bundle
(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
. Observe that, for each
m\in M
, the element
\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)(m)
belongs to the fiber of
m\in M
in the vector bundle
(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
.
As mentioned before, the fiber of
p\in P
in the vector bundle
P\times\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow P
is isomorphic to the fiber of
m=\pi(p)\in M
in the vector bundle
(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
; that is,
\mathfrak{g}
is the fiber of
m\in M
in the vector bundle
(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G\rightarrow M
.
So, we can see the section
\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)\colon M\rightarrow(P\times\mathfrak{g})/G
as a smooth map
\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)\colon M\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
.
Thus, for vector fields
X,Y\colon M\rightarrow TM
of
M
, we have a smooth map
\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)\colon M\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}
.
Thus, a connection
\mathcal{D}\colon TM\rightarrow(TP)/G
, gives a
\mathfrak{g}
-valued differential
2
-form on
M
, denoted by

\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}\colon M\rightarrow\Lambda^{2}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}M,

(2.4.8)

defined as
\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(m)(v_{1},v_{2})=\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)(m)
,
for all
m\in M
and
v_{1},v_{2}\in T_{m}M
,
where,
X,Y
are vector fields on
M
such that
X(m)=v_{1}
and
Y(m)=v_{2}
. This
\mathfrak{g}
-valued
2
-form on
M
is called
the curvature form associated to the connection
\mathcal{D}
of the principal bundle
P(M,G)
.

Proposition 2.4.17

(
[
43
, Proposition
4.17
]
)
.

Let
P(M,G)
be a principal bundle. Let
\mathcal{D}
be a connection on
P(M,G)
, and
\omega:P\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}:M\rightarrow\Lambda^{2}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}M
the differential forms associated to
\mathcal{D}
. Then, we have

\pi^{*}\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}=d\omega-[\omega,\omega].

Remark 2.4.18
.

Given a principal bundle
P(M,G)
, the
curvature form associated to connection
\mathcal{D}
is usually a declared to be the
2
-form on
P
, defined to be the pull-back
\pi^{*}\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{D}}:P\rightarrow\Lambda^{2}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
.

2.4.8
Chern-Weil morphism associated to a principal bundle

Let
G
be a Lie group and
P(M,G)
a principal bundle. In this section, we outline the construction of Chern-Weil morphism and recall the fact that the construction is independent of the choice of connection.

Let
\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
denote the set of all symmetric multi-linear mappings
f\colon\underbrace{\mathfrak{g}\times\cdots\times\mathfrak{g}}_{k~\text{times}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
such that

f({\rm ad}(a)t_{1},\cdots,{\rm ad}(a)t_{k})=f(t_{1},\cdots,t_{k})
for all
a\in G
and
t_{i}\in\mathfrak{g}
for
1\leq i\leq k
. This set
\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
is an
\mathbb{R}
-vector space for each
k\geq 1
. The direct sum

\text{sym}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}=\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G},

is then made into an
\mathbb{R}
-algebra by defining the multiplication of
f\in\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
and
g\in\text{sym}_{l}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
as

fg(t_{1},\cdots,t_{k+l})=\frac{1}{(k+l)!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k+l}}f(t_{\sigma(1)},\cdots,t_{\sigma(k)})g(t_{\sigma(k+1)},\cdots,t_{\sigma(k+l)}),

and extending it linearly to all of
\text{sym}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
. Thus, we have an
\mathbb{R}
-algebra
\text{sym}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
.

For the smooth manifold
M
, we have the
\mathbb{R}
-vector space
H^{k}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
, the
k
-th de Rham cohomology group of
M
for each
k\geq 0
. The direct sum

H_{{\rm dR}}^{*}(M,\mathbb{R})=\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}H^{k}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R}),

is turned into an
\mathbb{R}
-algebra, with the product being the wedge product of differential forms.

For each
f\in\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
, we define an element in
H^{2k}(M,\mathbb{R})
giving an
\mathbb{R}
-linear map of vector spaces
\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}\rightarrow H^{2k}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
, and extend it linearly to give an
\mathbb{R}
-algebra morphism
\text{sym}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}\rightarrow H^{*}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
. This map is called the Chern-Weil map associated to the principal bundle
P(M,G)
. The outline of the construction is as follows:

1.

Fix a connection
\omega\colon P\rightarrow\Lambda^{1}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
on
P(M,G)
. Let
\Omega\colon P\rightarrow\Lambda^{2}_{\mathfrak{g}}T^{*}P
be the associated curvature form for the connection
\omega
.

2.

Given an element
f\in\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
, we associate a differential
2k
-form
f(\Omega)
on
P
. We have

\begin{split}f(\Omega)(X_{1},X_{2},&\cdots,X_{2k-1},X_{2k})\\
&=\frac{1}{(2k)!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2k}}\text{sgn}(\sigma)f(\Omega(X_{\sigma(1)},X_{\sigma(2)}),\cdots,\Omega(X_{\sigma(2k-1)},X_{\sigma(2k)})),\end{split}

(2.4.9)

for vector fields
X_{i}
on
P
for
1\leq i\leq 2k
,
where, sum is taken over elements of
S_{2k}
; that is the set of permutations of the set
\{1,\cdots,2k\}
and
\text{sgn}(\sigma)
denotes the sign of the permutation
\sigma\in S_{2k}
.

3.

We generalize the construction in step
2
to associate a differential
q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k}
-form on
P
for each
f\in\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
and differential forms
\varphi_{1},\cdots,\varphi_{k}
on
P
of degree
q_{1},\cdots,q_{k}
respectively. We have

\begin{split}f(\varphi_{1},&\cdots,\varphi_{k})(X_{1},X_{2},\cdots,X_{q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k}-1},X_{q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k}})\\
&=\frac{1}{(q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k})!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2k}}\text{sgn}(\sigma)f(\varphi_{1}(X_{\sigma(1)},\cdots,X_{\sigma(q_{1})}),\\
&~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\cdots,\varphi_{k}(X_{\sigma(q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k-1})},\cdots,X_{\sigma(q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k})})),\end{split}

(2.4.10)

for vector fields
X_{i}
on
P
for
1\leq i\leq 2k
, where, sum is taken over elements of
S_{q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k}}
; that is the set of permutations of the set
\{1,\cdots,q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k}\}
and
\text{sgn}(\sigma)
denotes the sign of the permutation
\sigma\in S_{q_{1}+\cdots+q_{k}}
.

4.

Given
f\in\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}
, the
2k
-form
f(\Omega)
on
P
constructed in step
2
is seen to be projected to a unique
2k
-form
\widetilde{f(\Omega)}
on
M
; that is,
\pi^{*}\widetilde{f(\Omega)}=f(\Omega)
. It is also observed that, this
\widetilde{f(\Omega)}
is a closed form on
M
, giving an element in the
de Rham cohomology group
H^{2k}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
.

Thus, we have an
\mathbb{R}
-linear map
\text{sym}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}\rightarrow H^{2k}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
. As mentioned before, we extend this to get an
\mathbb{R}
-algebra morphism

W\colon\text{sym}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}\rightarrow H^{*}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
. This map is called the Chern-Weil homomorphism. It is a standard fact that, though we fix a connection
\omega
on
P(M,G)
when defining the map
W
, this map does not depend on the connection. In other words, for any two connections
\omega_{0}
and
\omega_{1}
on
P(M,G)
with curvatures
\Omega_{0}
and
\Omega_{1}
respectively, the
2k
-forms
\widetilde{f(\Omega_{0})}
and

\widetilde{f(\Omega_{1})}
represent same element in the de Rham cohomology group
H^{2k}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
; that is,
\widetilde{f(\Omega_{0})}-\widetilde{f(\Omega_{1})}

is an exact form on
M
. To prove this result, we recall the following standard result:

Lemma 2.4.19
.

Let
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
be a surjective submersion. Let
\omega
be a
k
-form on
M
and
\tau
a
k
-form on
P
such that
\pi^{*}\omega=\tau
. If
\tau
is exact, and
\tilde{\tau}=\pi^{*}\tilde{\omega}
for some
k-1
form
\tilde{\omega}
on
M
, then,
\omega
is exact.

Observe, by above result, that, to prove exactness of
\widetilde{f(\Omega_{0})}-\widetilde{f(\Omega_{1})}
, it suffices to prove that
f(\Omega_{0})-f(\Omega_{1})=d\Phi
for a
2k-1
form
\Phi
on
P
, and that
\Phi
projects to a
2k-1
form on
M
. The outline of this construction is as follows:

1.

Set
\alpha=\omega_{1}-\omega_{0}
and
\omega_{t}=\omega_{0}+t\alpha
for
0\leq t\leq 1
. Observe that these
\omega_{t}
are connection forms on the principal bundle
P(M,G)
. Let
\Omega_{t}
be the corresponding curvature forms.

2.

We need to get a
2k-1
form on
P
. If we are given a differential
1
-form on
P
and
k-1
differential
2
-forms on
P
, we know (
Equation

2.4.10
) how to construct a
2k-1
form. Considering the
1
-form
\alpha
on
P
and the
2
-form
\Omega_{t}
for
k-1
times, we get differential
2k-1
form,
f(\alpha,\Omega_{t},\cdots,\Omega_{t})
on
P
.

3.

We only needed one differential
2k-1
form on
P
, but, we have a family of differential
2k-1
forms on
P
, indexed by elements of
[0,1]
. Consider the integral

\Phi=k\int_{0}^{1}f(\alpha,\Omega_{t},\cdots,\Omega_{t})dt.

(2.4.11)

This
\Phi
is a differential
2k-1
form on
P
.

4.

Observe that this
\Phi
projects to a
2k-1
form on
M
and that

d\Phi=f(\Omega_{1})-f(\Omega_{0})=f(\Omega_{1},\cdots,\Omega_{1})-f(\Omega_{0},\cdots,\Omega_{0}).

5.

Thus, as observed before, the difference
\widetilde{f(\Omega_{1})}-\widetilde{f(\Omega_{0})}
is also an exact form on
M
. Thus,
\widetilde{f(\Omega_{1})}
and
\widetilde{f(\Omega_{0})}
gives same element in the
2k
-th de Rham cohomology group
H^{2k}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
.

Thus, the Chern-Weil morphism
\text{sym}(\mathfrak{g})^{G}\rightarrow H^{*}_{{\rm dR}}(M,\mathbb{R})
associated to the principal bundle
P(M,G)

does not depend on the choice of connection on
P(M,G)
.

Chapter 3
On two notions of a gerbe over a stack

In the
Section

2.3
, we have introduced the notions of Lie groupoids, differentiable stacks and their correspondence.
In the
Section

2.3.2
, we have assigned a differentiable stack
B\mathcal{G}
, for a Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
.
In
Lemma

2.3.24
, we saw that, for each differentiable stack
\mathcal{D}
, we can associate a Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
with the property that
\mathcal{D}\cong B\mathcal{G}
. We have mentioned in
Lemma

2.3.30
that, any two Lie groupoids obtained from any two atlases of a differentiable stacks are Morita equivalent. Then, we observed in
Remark

2.3.38
that, for any two Lie groupoids that are Morita equivalent, the associated stacks
B\mathcal{G}
and
B\mathcal{H}
are isomorphic. Thus, there is a one-one correspondence between the collection of Morita equivalent Lie groupoids and the collection of differentiable stacks.

The main aim of this chapter is to extend the above correspondence to a correspondence between a particular type of morphism of Lie groupoids and a particular type of morphism of differentiable stacks. More precisely, we study morphism of Lie groupoids that are Lie groupoid extensions, and morphism of differentiable stacks that are epimorphisms along with the condition that the associated diagonal morphism is an epimoprhism of stacks. In literature, these two seemingly different notions (Lie groupoid extension, morphism of stacks with extra conditions) goes by the name of a gerbe over a stack.
The notion of a gerbe over a stack as a (Morita equivalence class of a) Lie groupoid extension is studied by Laurent-Gengoux, Stienon, and Xu in
[
39
]
. The notion of a gerbe over a stack as a morphism of differentiable stacks is studied by Behrend and Xu in
[
6
]
, Ginot in
[
30
]
, and Heinloth in
[
33
]
, to name a few.

This chapter, based on our paper
[
21
]
, is split into three sections. In the first section, we will recall the two notions of a gerbe over a stack. In the second section, assuming an extra condition on a morphism of stacks that is a gerbe over a stack, we associate a Lie groupoid extension.
We also prove that the Lie groupoid extension produced in this way is unique up to a Morita equivalence. In the last section, we prove that the morphism of stacks associated to a Lie groupoid extension is a gerbe over a stack.

3.1
Two notions of a gerbe over a stack

In this section, we recall the existing notions of a gerbe over a stack from references
[
39
,
6
]
.

Definition 3.1.1
.

Let
[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
be a Lie groupoid. A
Lie groupoid extension of
[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
is given by a Lie groupoid
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
, and a morphsim of Lie groupoids

(F,1_{M}):[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
, such that
F:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}
is a surjective submersion.

We denote a Lie groupoid extension by
F\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M
.

In
[
39
]
the authors assume
F:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}
to be a smooth fibration, but we restrict ourselves to the case of a surjective submersion. Note that every (smooth) fibration is a surjective submersion.

The notions of a Morita morphism of Lie groupoids (
Definition

2.3.27
) and Morita equivalent Lie groupoids (
Definition

2.3.29
) extends respectively to the notions of a Morita morphism of Lie groupoid extensions and Morita equivalent Lie groupoid extensions.

Definition 3.1.2

(Morphism of Lie groupoids extensions)
.

Let
F:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M
and
F^{\prime}:\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
be Lie groupoid extensions. A
morphism of Lie groupoid extensions from
\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M
to
\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
is given by a triple

(\psi_{\mathcal{G}}:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime},\psi_{\mathcal{H}}:\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime},f:M\rightarrow M^{\prime}),

of smooth maps, such that, the following conditions are satisfied:

1.

F^{\prime}\circ\psi_{\mathcal{G}}=\psi_{\mathcal{H}}\circ F
,

2.

(\psi_{\mathcal{G}},f):[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{1}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}]
is a morphism of Lie groupoids,

3.

(\psi_{\mathcal{H}},f):[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{1}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}]
is a morphism of Lie groupoids.

We see a morphism of Lie groupoid extensions as the following diagram,

(3.1.1)

We sometimes denote a morphism of Lie groupoid extensions as a pair
((\psi_{\mathcal{G}},f),(\psi_{\mathcal{H}},f))
of morphisms of Lie groupoids instead of a triple
(\psi_{\mathcal{G}},\psi_{\mathcal{H}},f)
of smooth maps.

Definition 3.1.3

(Morita morphism of Lie groupoid extensions)
.

Let
F:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M
and
F^{\prime}:\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
be Lie groupoid extensions. A morphism
((\psi_{\mathcal{G}},f),(\psi_{\mathcal{H}},f))
of Lie groupoid extensions from
\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M
to
\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
is said to be
a Morita morphism of Lie groupoid extensions
, if
(\psi_{\mathcal{G}},f)
, and
(\psi_{\mathcal{H}},f)
are Morita morphisms of Lie groupoids.

Definition 3.1.4

(Morita equivalent Lie groupoid extensions)
.

Let
\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
and

\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M
be a pair of Lie groupoid extensions. We say that
\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
and

\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M
are
Morita equivalent Lie groupoid extensions
, if there exists a third Lie groupoid extension
\phi^{\prime\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow Y^{\prime\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime\prime}
and a pair of Morita morphisms of Lie groupoid extensions

(\phi^{\prime\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow Y^{\prime\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime\prime})\rightarrow(\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M)

and

(\phi^{\prime\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow Y^{\prime\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime\prime})\rightarrow(\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}).

Definition 3.1.5

(Gerbe over a stack as a Lie groupoid extension
[
39
]
)
.

A
gerbe over a stack
is the Morita equivalence class of a Lie groupoid extension.

This is all about the notion of a gerbe over a stack as a Morita equivalence class of a Lie groupoid extension. Now, we introduce the notion of a gerbe over a satck as as morphism of differentiable stacks satisfying certain conditions.

Definition 3.1.6

(A Gerbe over a stack
[
6
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a differentiable stack. A morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is said to be
a gerbe over the stack
\mathcal{C}
, if the morphism
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
and the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
associated to
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
are epimorphisms of stacks.

Using the
2
-Yoneda Lemma (
Lemma

2.2.28
) one can give a following characterization of a gerbe over a stack.

Suppose that
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism of stacks. Given a manifold
U
and a morphism of stacks
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, there exists a cover
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and a morphism of stacks
L_{\alpha}\colon\underline{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
with the following
2
-commutative diagram,

and

are categories fibered in groupoids, we can use the
2
-Yoneda lemma. As
U
is an object of
Man
, the morphism
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
corresponds
to an object
a
of
\mathcal{C}(U)
.
Similarly for
U_{\alpha}
, the morphism
L_{\alpha}\colon\underline{U}_{\alpha}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
corresponds
to an object
x_{\alpha}
of
\mathcal{D}(U_{\alpha})
. The
2
-commutative Diagram
3.1.2
, corresponds to an isomorphism
F(x_{\alpha})\rightarrow a|_{U_{\alpha}}
in
\mathcal{C}(U_{\alpha})
for each
\alpha
.

Thus, if a morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism, then given a manifold
U
and an object
a
of
\mathcal{C}(U)
, there exists an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and objects
x_{\alpha}
of
\mathcal{D}(U_{\alpha})
with an isomorphism
F(x_{\alpha})\rightarrow a|_{U_{\alpha}}
in
\mathcal{C}(U_{\alpha})
for each
\alpha
. It turns out that the converse is true as well.

Suppose that
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is a morphism of stacks with the following property: for a manifold
U
and an object
a
of
\mathcal{C}(U)
, there exists an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and objects
x_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{D}(U_{\alpha})
such that
F(x_{\alpha})
is isomorphic to
a|_{U_{\alpha}}
for each
\alpha
. Then
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism of stacks.

In other words, we have
p|_{U_{\alpha}}\circ F(a_{\alpha})=F(b_{\alpha})\circ F(\text{Id})=F(b_{\alpha})
. As
a_{\alpha}
is an isomorphism, we have

p|_{U_{\alpha}}=F(b_{\alpha})\circ F(a_{\alpha}^{-1})=F(b_{\alpha}\circ a_{\alpha}^{-1})
; that is,
p|_{U_{\alpha}}\colon F(a|_{U_{\alpha}})\rightarrow F(b|_{U_{\alpha}})
is equal to
F(\tau_{\alpha})
for some isomorphism
\tau_{\alpha}\colon a|_{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow b|_{U_{\alpha}}
.

Thus, if the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism, then given a manifold
U
and an arrow
p\colon F(a)\rightarrow F(b)
in
\mathcal{C}(U)
, there exists an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and a family of isomorphisms
\{\tau_{\alpha}\colon a|_{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow b|_{U_{\alpha}}\}
such that
F(\tau_{\alpha})=p|_{U_{\alpha}}
.
Again the converse holds.
We summarize our last couple of observations in the following lemma.

Lemma 3.1.7
.

A morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is a gerbe over a stack if and only if the following two conditions hold:

1.

Given a manifold
U
and an object
a
of
\mathcal{C}(U)
, there exists an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and objects
x_{\alpha}
of
\mathcal{D}(U_{\alpha})
with an isomorphism
F(x_{\alpha})\rightarrow a|_{U_{\alpha}}
in
\mathcal{C}(U_{\alpha})
for each
\alpha
.

2.

Given a manifold
U
and an arrow
p\colon F(a)\rightarrow F(b)
in
\mathcal{C}(U)
, there exists an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and isomorphisms
\tau_{\alpha}\colon a|_{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow b|_{U_{\alpha}}
in
\mathcal{D}(U_{\alpha})
such that
F(\tau_{\alpha})=p|_{U_{\alpha}}
in
\mathcal{C}(U_{\alpha})
for each
\alpha
.

Example 3.1.8
.

Let
X
be a smooth manifold. Let
G
be a Lie group acting on the smooth manifold
X
. Consider a central extension of Lie groups
1\rightarrow S^{1}\rightarrow\hat{G}\xrightarrow{\pi}G\rightarrow 1
. Let
[X/G]

and
[X/\hat{G}]
respectively be the quotient stacks associated to the actions of
\hat{G}
and
G
on
X
. The morphism of Lie groups
\pi:\hat{G}\rightarrow G
defines a morphism of Lie groupoids
(X\times\hat{G}\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times G\rightrightarrows X)
, given by
x\mapsto x
and
(x,\hat{g})\mapsto(x,\pi(\hat{g}))
. Then, as we will see in
Section

3.3
, this morphism of Lie groupoids
(X\times\hat{G}\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times G\rightrightarrows X)
associates a morphism of stacks
[X/\hat{G}]\xrightarrow{\pi}[X/G]
. In fact, this morphism of stacks
[X/\hat{G}]\xrightarrow{\pi}[X/G]
is a gerbe over the quotient stack
[X/G]
.

Example 3.1.9
.

Let
M,N
be manifolds. Let
f:M\rightarrow N
be a diffeomorphism. Then, the associated morphism of stacks
F:\underline{M}\rightarrow\underline{N}
is a gerbe over the stack
\underline{N}
. More over, a morphism of stacks
G:\underline{M}\rightarrow\underline{N}
is a gerbe over the stack
\underline{N}
implies that the associated map of manifolds
g:M\rightarrow N
is a diffeomorphism.

Remark 3.1.10
.

Let
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over the stack
\mathcal{C}
. When the stack
\mathcal{C}
is representable by a manifold; that is
\mathcal{C}\cong\underline{M}
for a manifold
M
, we recover the notion of
a gerbe over a manifold
M
. It is immediate from
Lemma

3.1.7
that, a gerbe over a manifold
M
, associates a groupoid
\mathcal{G}(U)
with each open set
U\subseteq M
, such that the following conditions are satisfied:

•

given
x\in M
there is an open subset
U\subseteq M
containing
x
such that
\mathcal{G}(U)
is non empty,

•

given
a,b\in\mathcal{G}(U)
and
x\in U\subseteq M
, there exists an open subset
V
of
U
containing
x
such that
a|_{V}
is isomorphic to
b|_{V}
.

These two properties respectively, are called “locally non empty” and “locally connected”.
For further details on this topic, we
refer to the Section
3
of
[
47
]

Example 3.1.11
.

Let
M
be a manifold and
\mathcal{O}(M)
be the category of open sets of the manifold
M
. Let
G
be a Lie group. For an open set
U\subseteq M
, let
{\rm Tor}(G)|_{U}
denote the groupoid of principal
G
bundles over the manifold
U
. Then, the assignment
U\mapsto{\rm Tor}(G)|_{U}
for the open set
U\subseteq M
gives a gerbe over the manifold
M
.

3.2
A Lie groupoid extension associated to a Gerbe over a stack

Let
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
and
\pi_{\mathcal{C}}\colon\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\text{Man}
be differentiable stacks, and
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
a gerbe over a stack in the sense of
Definition

3.1.6
. Throughout this section, by a gerbe over a stack we mean an epimrorphism of stacks
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
whose associated diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism. Assume further that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion. In this section, we associate a Lie groupoid extension for this morphism of stacks
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
.
The outline of the construction is as follows:

1.

We use the fact that
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism of stacks to prove that there exists an atlas
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
for
\mathcal{C}
and a morphism of stacks

satisfying the following

),

By

commutative diagram above,

and

can be identified up to a
2
-isomorphism.

2.

The fact that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism of stacks implies that the morphism of stacks
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
obtained in step
1
is an epimorphism of stacks (
Lemma

3.2.2
).

3.

Under the assumption that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion, we prove that, the morphism of stacks
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
mentioned in step
2
is an atlas for the stack
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
(
Lemma

3.2.4
).

4.

For the choices made in step
(2)
and step
(3)
for atlases
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
we respectively obtain Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}_{p}=(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)

and
\mathcal{G}_{q}=(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X)
.
We then prove that, the morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
gives a Lie groupoid extension
\mathcal{G}_{p}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{q}
(
Lemma

3.2.6
).

5.

Finally we prove that the above construction does not depend on the choice of
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
(
Lemma

3.2.7
).

(3.2.7)

We further note from Diagram
Equation

3.2.6
that,
r\circ{\rm pr}_{2}\circ\Phi={\rm pr}_{2}\circ\Delta_{F}\circ\gamma
and

p\circ{\rm pr}_{1}\circ\Phi={\rm pr}_{1}\circ\Delta_{F}\circ\gamma
.
As
{\rm pr}_{1}\circ\Delta={\rm pr}_{2}\circ\Delta
, we see that

{\rm pr}_{1}\circ\Delta\circ\gamma={\rm pr}_{2}\circ\Delta\circ\gamma
.
Thus,
r\circ{\rm pr}_{2}\circ\Phi=p\circ{\rm pr}_{1}\circ\Phi
. So, the Diagram
Equation

3.2.7
is a
2
-commutative diagram. Thus, given a morphism of stacks
r\colon\underline{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
, there exists a surjective submersion
\Gamma={\rm pr}_{2}\circ\Phi\colon\underline{W}\rightarrow\underline{M}
and a morphism of stacks
\Psi={\rm pr}_{1}\circ\Phi\colon\underline{W}\rightarrow\underline{X}
with following
2
-commutative diagram,

(3.2.8)

Thus, we conclude that the morphism
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}

Lemma 3.2.2
.

The morphism of stacks
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
mentioned in Diagram
Equation

3.2.1
is an epimorphism of stacks.

3.2.3
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over a stack. We further assume that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion. Let
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
be as in
Lemma

3.2.2
. In general
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is not an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
. We have proved that
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism of stacks. We use the following result to conclude that
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is in fact an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
.
The following proposition is a variant of Proposition
2.16
in
[
6
]
.

Proposition 3.2.3
.

A morphism of stacks
r\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
if

1.

the morphism
r\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism of stacks,

2.

the fibered product
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}
is representable by a manifold and that the projection maps

{\rm pr}_{1}\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightarrow X
and

{\rm pr}_{2}\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightarrow X
are submersions.

By above Proposition, to prove
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
, it only remains to prove that
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}
is representable by a manifold and that the projection maps
{\rm pr}_{1}\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightarrow X
and

{\rm pr}_{2}\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightarrow X
are submersions. We prove them below.

For
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and for
F\circ p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, we have following pull
back diagrams,

(3.2.11)

As the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion, the
2
-fiber product
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}}(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X})
is representable by a manifold and the projection map
{\rm pr}_{2}\colon\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}}(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X})\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
is a surjective submersion at the level of manifolds. Thus, we see that
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}
is representable by manifold and
\Psi\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
is a surjective submersion at the level of manifolds.

Both being compositions of surjective submersions, we see that
{\rm pr}_{1}^{\mathcal{D}}={\rm pr}_{1}^{\mathcal{C}}\circ\Psi
and

{\rm pr}_{2}^{\mathcal{D}}={\rm pr}_{2}^{\mathcal{C}}\circ\Psi
are surjective submersions at the level of manifolds as well. Thus,
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
. So, we have shown the following:

Lemma 3.2.4
.

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over a stack. Further assume that, the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion. Then, the morphism of stacks
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
mentioned in Diagram
3.2.1
is an atlas for the stack
\pi_{\mathcal{D}}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
. In particular, there exists an atlas
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
for
\mathcal{D}
and an atlas
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
for
\mathcal{C}
with a
2
-commutative diagram as in Diagram
3.2.1
.

3.2.4
A gerbe over a stack gives a Lie groupoid extension

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over a stack. We further assume that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion.
By
Lemma

3.2.4
, there exists an atlas
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
for
\mathcal{D}
and an atlas
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
with a
2
-commutative diagram as in Diagram
3.2.1
. For atlases
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
for
\mathcal{C}
, we have respectively associated the Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}_{p}=(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)
and
\mathcal{G}_{q}=(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows Y)
. The morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
induces a morphism of stacks
\Psi\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
as in Diagram Diagram
3.2.9
.
Explicitly,
\Psi\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
is given at the level of objects by

(y,z,\alpha\colon p(y)\rightarrow p(z))\mapsto(y,z,F(\alpha)\colon F(p(y))\rightarrow F(p(z))).

At the level of morphisms, an arrow

(u,v)\colon\big(y,z,\alpha\colon p(y)\rightarrow p(z))\rightarrow\big(y^{\prime},z^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}\colon p(y^{\prime})\rightarrow p(z^{\prime})\big)

in
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}
is mapped to the arrow

(u,v)\colon\big(y,z,F(\alpha)\colon F(p(y))\rightarrow F(p(z)))\rightarrow\big(y^{\prime},z^{\prime},F(\alpha^{\prime})\colon F(p(y^{\prime}))\rightarrow F(p(z^{\prime}))\big)

in
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
.
This morphism of stacks
\Psi\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
is compatible with projection morphisms
{\rm pr}_{1},{\rm pr}_{2}\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}
and
{\rm pr}_{1},{\rm pr}_{2}\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}
in the sense that following diagrams are commutative diagram of morphisms of stacks,

(3.2.13)

We have the following result.

Proposition 3.2.5
.

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over a stack. Assume further that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion. Then the morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
gives a morphism of Lie groupoids

\mathcal{G}_{p}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{q}\colon(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X),

where
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
are as in
Lemma

3.2.4
.

Observe that the morphism of stacks
\Psi\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
is a surjective submersion at the level of manifolds (discussion after Diagram
3.2.11
); that is, the map
\Theta\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightarrow X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X
is a surjective submersion. Thus,
(\Theta,\text{Id})\colon(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X)
(Diagram
3.2.13
) is a Lie groupoid extension.

Lemma 3.2.6
.

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over a stack. Assume that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion. Then the morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
gives a Lie groupoid extension

\mathcal{G}_{p}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{q}\colon(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X)

where
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
are as in
Lemma

3.2.4
.

3.2.5
Uniqueness of a Lie groupoid extension associated to a gerbe over a stack

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over a stack. We further assume that
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion. For atlases
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
mentioned in
Lemma

3.2.4
, we have assigned a Lie groupoid extension

(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X)

in
Lemma

3.2.6
. We prove in this subsection that, up to a Morita equivalence, this Lie groupoid extension does not depend on the choice of atlases.

Let
q_{Y}\colon\underline{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be another atlas for
\mathcal{C}
and
p_{Y}\colon\underline{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
be the corresponding atlas for
\mathcal{D}
as in
Lemma

3.2.4
. These atlases
p_{Y}\colon\underline{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{D},q_{Y}\colon\underline{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
gives a Lie groupoid extension

(Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)\rightarrow(Y\times_{\mathcal{C}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)

as in
Lemma

3.2.6
.

We prove that

(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X)
and
(Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)\rightarrow(Y\times_{\mathcal{C}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)
are Morita equivalent Lie groupoid extensions.
It means that there exists a Lie groupoid extension
(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0})\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0})
and a pair of Morita morphisms of Lie groupoid extensions

\displaystyle\big((\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0})\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0})\big)

\displaystyle\rightarrow\big((X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)\rightarrow(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X)\big),

\displaystyle\big((\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0})\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0})\big)

\displaystyle\rightarrow\big((Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)\rightarrow(Y\times_{\mathcal{C}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)\big).

Diagrammatically that means we have to find a Lie groupoid extension and a pair of Morita morphisms of Lie groupoid extensions,

As
p_{X}\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas, the morphism of stacks
{\rm pr}_{2}\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y}\rightarrow\underline{Y}
induces a surjective submersion,

g\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow Y
at the level of manifolds.
Similarly

{\rm pr}_{1}\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y}\rightarrow\underline{X}
induces a surjective submersion
f\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow X
at the level of manifolds.

We now construct a Lie groupoid extension
of the form
(**\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)\rightarrow(***\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)
.
In order to describe an overall outline of the construction, for the time being we denote the respective morphism sets by
**
and
***
.

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}},

(3.2.22)

gives a Morita morphism of Lie groupoids
(f^{*}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)\rightarrow(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows N)
.

Let
(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)
be the pull-back of the Lie groupoid
(X\times_{\mathcal{D}}X\rightrightarrows X)
along
f\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow X
and
(\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)
be the pull-back of the Lie groupoid
(Y\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)
along
g\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow Y
.
However, as we will shortly see, we do not have to distinguish between these two pull-backs as they are isomorphic.
We have following diagrams representing the pull-back groupoids,

(3.2.23)

Similarly, we write
(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)
for pull-back of the Lie groupoid
(X\times_{\mathcal{C}}X\rightrightarrows X)
along
f\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow X
and
(\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y)
for pull-back of the Lie groupoid
(Y\times_{\mathcal{C}}Y\rightrightarrows Y)
along
g\colon X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow Y
. As before, the Lie groupoids

\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
and
\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
will be isomorphic. We have following diagrams representing the pull-back groupoids,

(3.2.24)

Now we give an isomorphism between
\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
and
\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
. The construction of isomorphism between
\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
and
\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
is very much same. We define map
\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}
by giving a morphism of stacks
\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}}
, where

\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}}=(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y})\times_{f,X,s}(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X})\times_{f,X,t}(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y}),

and

\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}}=(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y})\times_{g,X,s}(\underline{Y}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y})\times_{g,X,t}(\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y}\big).

A typical element in the object set of
\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}}
is of the form

\bigg(\big(m,n,\alpha\colon p(m)\rightarrow q(n)\big),\big(a,b,p(a)\rightarrow p(b)\big),\big(m^{\prime},n^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}\colon p(m^{\prime})\rightarrow q(n^{\prime})\big)\bigg)

such that
m=s\big(a,b,p(a)\rightarrow p(b)\big)=a
,
n=t(a,b,p(a)\rightarrow p(b))=b
and
p(a)\rightarrow p(b)
is just
p(m)\rightarrow p(m^{\prime})
. So, this demands a typical element to be of the form

\bigg(\big(m,n,\alpha\colon p(m)\rightarrow q(n)\big),\big(m,m^{\prime},p(m)\rightarrow p(m^{\prime})\big),\big(m^{\prime},n^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}\colon p(m^{\prime})\rightarrow q(n^{\prime})\big)\bigg).

The corresponding image in
\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}}^{\prime}
is

\bigg(\big(m,n,\alpha\colon p(m)\rightarrow q(n)\big),\big(n,n^{\prime},q(n)\rightarrow q(n^{\prime})\big),\big(m^{\prime},n^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}\colon p(m^{\prime})\rightarrow q(n^{\prime})\big)\bigg)

This gives a map of stacks
\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}}
at the level of objects. The map at the level of morphisms can be defined similarly. This gives an isomorphism of stacks
\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}}
, which in turn induces an isomorphism of Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
and
\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y
. Hence, the pull-backs are isomorphic.

Lemma 3.2.7
.

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
be a gerbe over a stack.
Assume that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable surjective submersion.
Then, upto a Morita equivalence, the Lie groupoid extension in
Lemma

3.2.6
does not depend on the choice of
q\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
.

Thus, using
Lemma

2.3.24
,
Lemma

3.2.1
,
Lemma

3.2.2
,
Lemma

3.2.4
,
Lemma

3.2.6
and
Lemma

3.2.7
we have the following result.

Theorem 3.2.8
.

Let
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}

p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}

\mathcal{D}

\mathcal{C}

Lemma

3.2.4

and

\Phi\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
associated to
\phi\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}

and

are as mentioned in

. Further, if there exists another gerbe over the stack
F^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
isomorphic to the gerbe
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, then the Lie groupoid extensions associated to
F^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
and
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
are Morita equivalent.

Remark 3.2.9
.

Observe that we have not made full use of the condition
\Delta_{F}
being a surjective submersion. We have only used the following. The morphism of stacks
p\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
obtained in
Lemma

3.2.4
is such that,
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}
is representable by a manifold and the morphism of stacks

\Psi\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{X}
is a surjective submersion at the level of manifolds.

3.3
A gerbe over a stack associated to a Lie groupoid extension

This section is divided into four parts. In the first part, we will associate a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle for a morphism of Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
. In the second, we associate a morphism of stacks
BP:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
for a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle. In the next, we recall the notion of composition of bibundles and use it to prove that for Morita equivalent Lie groupoids, the associated differentiable stacks are isomorphic. In the last part, we prove that the morphism of stacks associated to a Lie groupoid extension is a gerbe over a stack.

Before we proceed to these constructions, we recall the construction of a fiber bundle from a principal bundle
Q(M,G)
and a manifold
F
with an action of
G
from the left side. This is a classical construction. More details about this can be found in
[
36
, Section
1.5
]
.

Let
M
be a manifold,
G,H
are Lie groups,
\pi\colon Q\rightarrow M
a principal
G
-bundle,
\mu:G\times H\rightarrow H
an action of the Lie group
G
on the manifold
H
. Consider the action of
G
on
Q\times H
, given by
(q,h)\cdot g=(qg,g^{-1}h)
. This action satisfies the conditions mentioned in
Proposition

2.4.4
, giving the principal
H
-bundle
(Q\times H)/G\rightarrow M
, as in the following diagram,

(3.3.2)

This
[H\rightrightarrows*]
-bundle over
M
is precisely the data of a principal
H
-bundle

(Q\times H)/G\rightarrow M
over
M
. Using the
Proposition

2.4.7
, for each morphism of principal bundles
Q(M,G)\rightarrow Q^{\prime}(M^{\prime},G)
, we have the
morphism of principal bundles
(Q\times H)(M,G)\rightarrow(Q^{\prime}\times H)(M^{\prime},G)
.
Thus, we have a functor
BG\rightarrow BH
.

The above construction assigns a morphism of stacks
BG\rightarrow BH
, for Lie groups
G,H
, with an action of
G
on
H
.
In particular, given a morphism of Lie groups
G\rightarrow H
, we have the associated morphism of stacks
BG\rightarrow BH
. As Lie groups are special cases of Lie groupoids, we may aim for a similar construction in the case of Lie groupoids; that is, for a morphism of Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
to induce a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. Before assigning a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
, for a morphism of Lie groupoids
\phi:\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
, as promised in
Remark

2.3.36
, we associate a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
\left<\phi\right>\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
(
[
41
, Remark
3.24,3.27
]
).

3.3.1
A morphism of Lie groupoids
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
gives a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle

\phi\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}

2.3.16

(
Section

2.3.1
),

(3.3.3)

The map
\mu\colon(\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1})\times_{s\circ{\rm pr}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
,
((u,h),\tilde{h})\mapsto(u,h\circ\tilde{h})
gives a right action of
\mathcal{H}
on
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
(
Section

2.3.1
).

The map
\tilde{\mu}\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},{\rm pr}_{1}}(\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1})\rightarrow(\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1})
,

(g,(u,h))\mapsto(t(g),\phi(g)\circ h)
gives a left action of
\mathcal{G}
on
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
.

Thus, the manifold
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
along with maps
{\rm pr}_{1}\colon\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},s\circ{\rm pr}_{2}\colon\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
produce a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle.
This
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle is described by the following diagram,

(3.3.4)

Thus, given a morphism of Lie groupoids
\phi\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
, the manifold
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
along with the maps
{\rm pr}_{1}\colon\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},s\circ{\rm pr}_{2}\colon\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
is a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle.
We denote the manifold
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
by
\phi^{*}\mathcal{H}_{1}
and the
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle by
\left<\phi\right>\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
.

As a Morita morphism of Lie groupoids is a special case of a morphism of Lie groupoids, it is natural to ask what properties does a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle

\left<\phi\right>\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
associated to a Morita morphism of Lie groupoids
\phi\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
would have. It turns out that the action of
\mathcal{G}
on
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
is such that the map
s\circ{\rm pr}_{2}
is a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle. More precisely, we have the following result.

Lemma 3.3.1
.

[
41
, Lemma
3.34
]

A morphism of Lie groupoids
f\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
is a Morita morphism of Lie groupoids if and only if the corresponding
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
\left<f\right>\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
is a
\mathcal{G}
-principal bibundle (
Remark

2.3.33
).

3.3.2
A
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle gives a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}

In this section, we associate a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
for a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle. As a morphism of Lie groupoids is a special case of a bibundle (
Section

3.3.1
), this construction would in particular associate a morphism of stacks for a morphism of Lie groupoids.

(3.3.7)

At the level of objects, the morphism of stacks
BP\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is defined as

BP(\pi\colon Q\rightarrow M)=(\widetilde{\pi}\circ\widetilde{{\rm pr}_{1}}\colon(Q\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}P)/\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow M).

(3.3.8)

At the level of morphisms, it is defined similarly as in the case of
\mathcal{G}=(G\rightrightarrows*)
and
\mathcal{H}=(H\rightrightarrows*)
.
Thus, given a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
P\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
we have associated a morphism of stacks
BP\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
.

Remark 3.3.2
.

For a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle
P:\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
we have associated a morphism of stacks
BP:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. We can ask if the converse is true; that is if we can associate a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle for an arbitrary morphism of stacks. The answer is yes, as we show below.

Let
F:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
be a morphism of stacks. To obtain a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle, we need a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle with
\mathcal{G}_{0}
as the base space. We have the principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle
t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
with
\mathcal{G}_{0}
as the base space. As
F
is a morphism of stacks, we have the functor
F:B\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{G}_{0})\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{G}_{0})
. The image
P=F(t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0})
gives an object of
B\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{G}_{0})
; that is, a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle with base space as
\mathcal{G}_{0}
. It turns out that this is a

\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle, and that there is a natural isomophism of functors
F\Rightarrow BP:B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. Thus, giving a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is same as giving a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle. More details can be found in
[
41
, Remark
4.18
]
.

Combining the construction of associating a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle for a morphism of Lie groupoids
\phi:\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
and associating a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
for a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle, we have the construction of a morphism of stacks
BP\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
for a morphism of Lie groupoids
f\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
.

Now we are in a position to prove that, for a Lie groupoid extension

[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
, the associated morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is a gerbe over the stack
B\mathcal{H}
. To prove that the diagonal morphism
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism of stacks (
Section

3.3.4.2
), we use a trick. Instead of proving
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism, we prove that there exists a Lie groupoid
\mathcal{K}
such that
B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}\cong B\mathcal{K}
, and that
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{K}
is an epimorphism. As
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{K}
is related to
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
, the observation that
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{K}
is an epimorphism of stacks then imply that
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism of stacks. In this, we use the result that if two Lie groupoids are Morita equivalent, then the associated differentiable stacks are isomorphic. To prove this, we need the terminology of the composition of bibundles, which we will describe below.

3.3.3
composition of bibundles

Observe that the Diagram
3.3.7
associates a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle for each principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle
Q(M,\mathcal{G})
and a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle. As
BP(Q(M,\mathcal{G}))
is a
[M\rightrightarrows M]-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle, we can see the construction in Diagram
3.3.7
as a construction that associates a
[M\rightrightarrows M]-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle for each
[M\rightrightarrows M]-\mathcal{G}
-bibundle and a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle. This construction can be generalized to the case of assigning a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{K}
-bibundle for each
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle and a
\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{K}
-bibundle.

Let
P\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
be a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle and

Q\colon\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
a
\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{K}
bibundle. We have the
following diagrams for bibundles,

(3.3.10)

Given
a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle and a
\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle, we know (
Equation

3.3.8
) how to associate a principal
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
-bundle. For the principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle
a_{\mathcal{G}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
, we associate the principal
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
-bundle
BQ(a_{\mathcal{G}})\colon(P\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}Q)/\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
.

Action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
induces an action of
\mathcal{G}
on
(P\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}Q)/\mathcal{H}_{1}
, producing the following
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle,

(3.3.11)

Definition 3.3.3
.

Let
P\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle and
Q\colon\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
be a

\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle. We define
the composition of
Q
with
P
to be the
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle (in the Diagram
3.3.11
),

Q\circ P=(P\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}Q)/\mathcal{H}_{1}.

(3.3.12)

Using the terminology of composition of bibundles, we now prove that, if
\mathcal{G}
and
\mathcal{H}
are Morita equivalent Lie groupoids, then the stacks
B\mathcal{G}
and
B\mathcal{H}
are isomorphic.

Proposition 3.3.4
.

Let
\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
be Morita equivalent Lie groupoids, then, the stacks
B\mathcal{H}
and
B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
are isomorphic.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{H}
and
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
be Morita equivalent Lie groupoids; that is, there exists a Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}
and a pair of Morita morphisms of Lie groupoids
f\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
and
g\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
. With this data, we produce an isomorphism of stacks
B\mathcal{H}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
.

As mentioned in
Remark

3.3.2
, giving a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{H}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
is same as giving a
\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle.
The morphism of Lie groupoids
f\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
gives the following
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle,

(3.3.15)

Composing the
\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{G}
bibundle (Diagram
3.3.14
)
\left<f\right>\colon\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}
with the
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle (Diagram
3.3.15
)
\left<g\right>\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
,
we get the
\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle
\left<g\right>\circ\left<f\right>\colon\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
(
Equation

(3.3.16)

is also a Morita morphism of Lie groupoids, interchanging
f
and
g
we obtain a
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle as follows,

(3.3.17)

The
\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
bibundle
\left<g\right>\circ\left<f\right>\colon\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
gives a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{H}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
and the
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
\left<f\right>\circ\left<g\right>\colon\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
gives a morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. It is easy to see that the maps
B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
and
B\mathcal{H}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
are inverses to each other, giving an isomorphism of stacks
B\mathcal{H}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
. Thus, the stacks
B\mathcal{H}
and
B\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
are isomorphic.
∎

3.3.4
A Lie groupoid extension gives a gerbe over a stack

Let
\phi\colon(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0})\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0})
be a Lie groupoid extension.
For this morphism of Lie groupoids, we have a morphism of stacks
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
, which at the level of objects have the following description,

F(\pi\colon Q\rightarrow M)=(\widetilde{\pi}\circ\widetilde{{\rm pr}_{1}}\colon(Q\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1})/\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow M).

(3.3.18)

Now we will prove that
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is a gerbe over a stack; that is, the morphism
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
and the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
are epimorphisms of stacks.

(3.3.19)

Let
q:\underline{U}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
be a morphism of stacks. We see this as a morphism of stacks
B(U\rightrightarrows U)\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. Then, the
Remark

3.3.2
says that, there is a unique
[U\rightrightarrows U]-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle representing the morphism
q:\underline{U}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. As we have mentioned before, an
[U\rightrightarrows U]-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle
is same as a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle over the manifold
U
.

Let
\pi\colon P\rightarrow U
be the
\mathcal{H}
-bundle associated to the morphism of stacks
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. For similar reasons as in the case of a principal Lie group bundle, there exists an open cover
\{U_{i}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
, such that, the restriction is pull-back of the trivial
\mathcal{H}
-bundle
t:\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
. As the trivial bundle is with base
\mathcal{H}_{0}
, we also have a collection of maps
r_{i}:U_{i}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
, such that the restriction
\pi^{-1}(U_{i})\rightarrow U_{i}
is pull-back of the bundle

(3.3.21)

This principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle
l_{i}\colon W_{i}\rightarrow U_{i}
gives a morphism of stacks
\underline{U_{i}}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}
, which we denote by
l_{i}
. So, we have the morphism of stacks
l_{i}\colon\underline{U_{i}}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}
for each
i
. This gives a pair of compositions of morphisms of stacks
q\circ\Phi\colon\underline{U}_{i}\rightarrow\underline{U}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
and
F\circ l_{i}\colon\underline{U}_{i}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
.
We prove that these two compositions give the
2
-commutative Diagram
3.3.19
, which would then imply that
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is an epimorphism of stacks.

(3.3.24)

Thus, we have
F(\pi\colon Q\rightarrow U)=((Q\times_{M}\mathcal{H}_{1})/\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow U)
.
As
Q=U\times_{M}\mathcal{G}_{1}
, we have

\displaystyle(Q\times_{M}\mathcal{H}_{1})/\mathcal{G}_{1}=(U\times_{M}\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{M}\mathcal{H}_{1})/\mathcal{G}_{1}=U\times_{M}(\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{M}\mathcal{H}_{1})/\mathcal{G}_{1}.

Note that
U\times_{M}(\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{M}\mathcal{H}_{1})/\mathcal{G}_{1}
is precisely the pull-back of
(\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{M}\mathcal{H}_{1})/\mathcal{G}_{1}
along
r\colon U\rightarrow M
. Thus,
F(\pi\colon Q\rightarrow U)
is the pull-back of
F(t\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow M)
along
r\colon U\rightarrow M
.
∎

As the Diagrams
3.3.20
and
3.3.21
are pull-back diagrams, observe that

F(l_{i}:W_{i}\rightarrow U_{i})=(\pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U_{i})}\colon\pi^{-1}(U_{i})\rightarrow U_{i}),

and

(\pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U_{i})}\colon\pi^{-1}(U_{i})\rightarrow U_{i})=q(U_{i}\rightarrow U)=(q\circ\Phi)(\text{Id}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U_{i}).

Here,
(W_{i}\rightarrow U_{i})=l_{i}(\text{Id}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U_{i})
.
So,
(F\circ l_{i})(\text{Id}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U_{i})
is equal to
(q\circ\Phi)(\text{Id}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U_{i})
. So, there is an isomorphism
(F\circ l_{i})(\text{Id}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U_{i})\rightarrow(q\circ\Phi)(\text{Id}\colon U_{i}\rightarrow U_{i})
. For similar reasons we see that there is an isomorphism

(F\circ l_{i})(f\colon N\rightarrow U_{i})\rightarrow(q\circ\Phi)(f\colon N\rightarrow U_{i})
for each
f\colon N\rightarrow U
in
\underline{U_{i}}
. Thus, we have the following
2
-commutative diagram,

Proposition 3.3.6
.

Given a Lie groupoid extension
f\colon(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)
, the corresponding morphism of stacks
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is an epimorphism of stacks.

3.3.4.2
Proof that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism.

As
\phi\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
is a Lie groupoid extension, the
2
-fiber product
\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
is a Lie groupoid. As stackification and Yoneda embedding preserves the
2
-fiber product (
[
18
,
\text{I}.2.4
]
,
[
63
,
Tag 04Y1
]
), we see that

B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}\cong B(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}).

Further, the diagonal morphism of stacks
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is the morphism of stacks associated to the diagonal morphism of Lie groupoids
\Delta_{\phi}\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
, given by
\Delta_{\phi}(a)=(a,\text{Id}\colon a\rightarrow a,a)
and
\Delta_{\phi}(g)=(g,g)
for
a\in\mathcal{G}_{0}
and
g\in\mathcal{G}_{1}
.

As the above morphism of Lie groupoids is not identity on base space, we can not use
Proposition

3.3.6
to conclude that
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism of stacks.

Remark 3.3.7
.

As
\phi\colon(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0})\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0})
is a Lie groupoid extension, the map
\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
is an identity map. Thus, we have

(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G})_{0}=\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{Id,\mathcal{H}_{0},s}\mathcal{H}_{1}\times_{t\circ{\rm pr}_{2},\mathcal{K}_{0},Id}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\mathcal{H}_{1}.

Lemma 3.3.8
.

The Lie groupoid
\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
is a transitive Lie groupoid .

Proof.

To prove
\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
is a transitive Lie groupoid, we prove that, for
h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H}_{1}=(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G})_{0}
(
Remark

3.3.7
) there exists

(g_{1},h,g_{2})\in(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G})_{1}
such that

s(g_{1},h,g_{2})=h\circ\phi(g_{1})=h_{1}
and
t(g_{1},h,g_{2})=\phi(g_{2})\circ h=h_{2}
.

As
\phi\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}
is surjective, we can choose
g_{1}\in\mathcal{G}_{1}
to be such that
\phi(g_{1})=1_{s(h_{1})}
. Choose such a
g_{1}\in\mathcal{G}_{1}
.
Choose
h=h_{1}
and
g_{2}\in\mathcal{G}_{2}
such that

\phi(g_{2})=h_{2}\circ h_{1}^{-1}
.
So, given
h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H}_{1}=(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G})_{0}
, there exists
(g_{1},h,g_{2})\in(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G})_{1}
such that
s(g_{1},h,g_{2})=h\circ\phi(g_{1})=h_{1}
and
t(g_{1},h,g_{2})=\phi(g_{2})\circ h=h_{2}
. Thus,
\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
is a transitive Lie groupoid.
∎

Combining
Lemma

3.3.8
and
Lemma

2.3.39
we see that
\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
is Morita equivalent to a Lie groupoid of the form
(K\rightrightarrows*)
. Thus, by
Proposition

3.3.4
,
the stacks
B(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G})
and
B(K\rightrightarrows*)
are isomorphic. So, the morphism of stacks
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is isomorphic to the map
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B(K\rightrightarrows*)
.

Using an argument similar to the proof of
Proposition

3.3.6
, we conclude that for any morphism of Lie groupoids
(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)\rightarrow(K\rightrightarrows*)
, the corresponding morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{K}
is an epimorphism of stacks. Thus,
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism of stacks. Therefore we obtain the following:

Proposition 3.3.9
.

Given a Lie groupoid extension
\phi\colon(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)
the diagonal morphism of stacks
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism of stacks.

Finally we conclude the following.

Theorem 3.3.10
.

1.

Given a Lie groupoid extension
\phi\colon(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)
, the corresponding morphism of stacks
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is a gerbe over the stack
B\mathcal{H}
.

2.

Let
\phi\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M
and
\phi^{\prime\prime}\colon\mathcal{G}^{\prime\prime}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^{\prime\prime}_{1}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime\prime}
be Morita equivalent Lie groupoid extensions. Let
\Phi\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
and
\Phi^{\prime\prime}\colon B\mathcal{G}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}^{\prime\prime}
be the respective morphism of stacks corresponding to
\phi
and
\phi^{\prime\prime}
. Then,
\Phi
and
\Phi^{\prime\prime}
are isomorphic in the sense that, the following diagram is
2
-commutative,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\mathcal{G}^{\prime\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\mathcal{H}^{\prime\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\mathcal{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\mathcal{H}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi}

and
