. We get the following diagram of morphism of vector bundles

0\rightarrow{\rm ad}(\mathcal{D})\rightarrow{\rm At}(\mathcal{D})\rightarrow T\mathcal{C}\rightarrow 0

(5.3.1)

over the stack
\mathcal{C}
.

Definition 5.3.4
.

Let
G
be a Lie group,
\mathcal{C}
a Deligne-Mumford stack, and
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
a principal
G
-bundle. The short exact sequence of vector bundles over
\mathcal{C}
, mentioned in Equation
5.3.1
, is called the
Atiyah sequence for the principal bundle
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
.

In our paper
[
8
]
, we have proved the following results:

Proposition 5.3.5

(
[
8
, Proposition
5.11
]
)
.

A principal
G
-bundle
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
over a Deligne-Mumford stack
\mathcal{C}
admits a connection if and only if its associated Atiyah sequence has splitting.

Theorem 5.3.6

(
[
8
, Theorem]
)
.

Giving a connection on a principal
G
-bundle
\mathcal{D}
over a Deligne-Mumford stack
\mathcal{C}
with etale atlas
x:X_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is equivalent to giving a connection on the associated principal
G
-bundle over the Lie groupoid
[X_{1}\rightrightarrows X_{0}]
.

Chapter 6
Extensions of topological groupoids

In
Chapter

2
, we have mentioned about Lie groupoids, differentiable stacks, and correspondence between them. In
Chapter

3
, we have given correspondence between a particular kind of morphism of Lie groupoids and a particular kind of differentiable stacks; that is, between Lie groupoid extensions and gerbes over differentiable stacks. In this Chapter, based on our paper
[
22
]
, we introduce the notion of topological groupoid extensions and give a correspondence between topological groupoid extensions and gerbes over topological stacks. Part of this chapter is analogous to
Chapter

3
. But, we have given enough details to make it self content.

6.1
Topological groupoids and topological stacks

In this section, we will recall standard definitions and results about topological groupoids and topological stacks. A major part of this section is based on
[
18
,
46
,
54
]
.

Definition 6.1.1

(topological groupoid)
.

A
topological groupoid
is a groupoid
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
whose object set
\mathcal{G}_{0}
, morphism set
\mathcal{G}_{1}
are topological spaces, and the structure maps
s,t,m,e,i
are continuous maps.

Example 6.1.2
.

Given a topological space
M
, the groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows M]
(mentioned in
Example

2.1.4
is a topological groupoid.

Example 6.1.3
.

For a topological group
G
, the groupoid
[G\rightrightarrows*]
(mentioned in
Example

2.1.5
) is a topological grouopoid.

Example 6.1.4
.

For an action of a topological group
G
on a topological space
M
, the action groupoid
[M\times G\rightrightarrows M]
is a topological groupoid.

Definition 6.1.5
.

Let
\mathcal{G},\mathcal{H}
be topological groupoids. A
morphism of topological groupoids from
\mathcal{G}
to
\mathcal{H}
is a functor
(F_{1},F_{0}):[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
, such that, the maps
F_{1}:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{1}
and
F_{0}:\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
are continuous maps.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a (locally-small) category, and
U
an object of
\mathcal{C}
. Consider the functor of points (associated to the object
U
)
h_{U}:\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Set}
. Seeing a set as a discrete category (
Example

2.1.4
), we can see
h_{U}
as a pseudo-functor
\mathcal{C}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
. As mentioned before, we are interested in Grothendieck topologies, on categories, that are subcanonical; that is,
h_{U}:\mathcal{C}^{\rm op}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
is a stack for each object
U
of
\mathcal{C}
.

Consider the Grothendieck topology
\mathcal{J}
on
{\rm Top}
described as follows. A covering of an object
U
of
Top
is given by a jointly surjective family
\{\sigma_{\alpha}\colon U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
, where each
\sigma_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U
is such that
\sigma_{\alpha}(U_{\alpha})
is an open subset of
U
and,
\sigma_{\alpha}
is a homeomorphism onto its image. Here, by jointly surjective family, we mean
\bigcup_{\alpha}\sigma_{\alpha}(U_{\alpha})=U
. We call this topology to be
the open-cover topology on
Top
. Unless mentioned otherwise, we will always assume
\rm{Top}
to be equipped with the open-cover topology.

In this chapter, we will be working in the category
Top
of topological spaces, with Grothendieck topology
\mathcal{J}
on
Top
being the open cover topology. The stacks we are interested are over the site
(\text{Top},\mathcal{J})
.

For each object
M
of
Top
we have a stack
h_{M}:\text{Top}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
with the description at the level of objects being
h_{M}(N)=\text{Hom}_{\text{Top}}(N,M)
for objects
N
in
Top
. Using the notion of morphisms of topological groupoids, we can associate a pseudo-functor
\text{Top}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
for a topological groupoid
\mathcal{G}
.

Let
\mathcal{G}
be a topological groupoid. Similar to the description of
h_{M}
for a topological space
M
, we describe a pseudo-functor
h_{\mathcal{G}}:\text{Top}\rightarrow\text{Cat}
. For an object
N
of
Top
, declare
h_{\mathcal{G}}(N)
as

h_{\mathcal{G}}(N)=\text{Hom}_{\text{TopGpd}}((N\rightrightarrows N),\mathcal{G}),

for an object
N
of
Top
. Here,
\text{Hom}_{\text{TopGpd}}((N\rightrightarrows N),\mathcal{G})
is the category whose objects are Lie groupoid morphisms and morphisms are natural transformations. This gives a pseudo-functor
h_{\mathcal{G}}:\text{Top}\rightarrow\text{Gpd}
. The stackification of this pseudo functor, denoted by
B\mathcal{G}
, is called the stack associated to the topological groupoid
\mathcal{G}
. More details about this can be found
[
18
,
I.2.4
]
. We do not follow this method of assigning a stack for a topological groupoid. We follow the method of using principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles for a topological groupoid
\mathcal{G}
. For that purpose, we first introduce the notion of action of a topological groupoid on a topological space.

Definition 6.1.6

(action of topological groupoid
[
43
, Definition
4.1
]
)
.

Let
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
be a topological groupoid, and
\pi:P\rightarrow M
a continuous map. Let
s^{*}P
denote the subspace

\{(\gamma,p)\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times P|s(\gamma)=\pi(p)\}
. An
action of
\mathcal{G}
on
(P,\pi,M)
is given by a continuous map
\mu:s^{*}P\rightarrow P
, with
(\gamma,p)\mapsto\gamma p
, such that

1.

\pi(\gamma p)=t(\gamma)
for all
(\gamma,p)\in s^{*}P
,

2.

\gamma(\gamma^{\prime}p)=(\gamma\circ\gamma^{\prime})p
for all
(\gamma,\gamma^{\prime})\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t,\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}
and
(\gamma^{\prime},p)\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{M}P
,

3.

1_{\pi(p)}p=p
for all
p\in P
.

Alternatively, we also refer to the above definition as “action of
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
on a topological space
P
” being given by a pair of maps
(\pi:P\rightarrow M,\mu:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}P\rightarrow P)
. We call the above action to be a left action of the topological groupoid on the topological space.

Similarly, a right action of a topological groupoid
\mathcal{G}
on a topological space is given by a pair of continuous maps

(\pi:P\rightarrow M,\mu:P\times_{\pi,\mathcal{G}_{0},t}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow P),

(6.1.1)

satisfying the following conditions:

1.

\pi(p\gamma)=s(\gamma)
for all
(p,\gamma)\in P\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{G}_{1}
,

2.

(p\gamma)\gamma^{\prime}=p(\gamma\circ\gamma^{\prime})
for all
(p,\gamma)\in P\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{G}_{1}
and
(\gamma,\gamma^{\prime})\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{G}_{1}
,

3.

p1_{\pi(p)}=p
for all
p\in P
.

Example 6.1.7
.

Let
[M\rightrightarrows M]
be the topological groupoid associated to a topological space
M
. An action of
[M\rightrightarrows M]
on a topological space
N
consists precisely of a continuous map
f:M\rightarrow N
.

Example 6.1.8
.

Let
[G\rightrightarrows*]
be the topological groupoid associated to a Lie group
G
. An action of
[G\rightrightarrows*]
on a topological space
M
is given by an action
\mu:M\times G\rightarrow M
of the topological group
G
on the topological space
M
.

Example 6.1.9
.

Let
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
be a topological groupoid. Consider the composition map

m:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t,\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1}.

The pair
(t:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},m:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t,\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1})
gives a left action of
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
on
\mathcal{G}_{1}
. The pair
(s:\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},m:\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{t,\mathcal{G}_{0},s}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{1})
gives a right action of
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
on
\mathcal{G}_{1}
.

Now, for a topological groupoid
\mathcal{G}
, we introduce the notion of a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over a topological space
M
. For that, we need to recall the notion of a map admitting local sections.

Definition 6.1.10
.

Let
f:X\rightarrow Y
be a continuous map. We say that
f:X\rightarrow Y
is a
map of local sections
or that
it admits local sections
, if there is an open cover
{U_{\alpha}}
of
Y
and sections
\sigma_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\rightarrow X
of
f:X\rightarrow Y
for each
\alpha
.

Definition 6.1.11

(
[
18
, Definition
I.2.13
]
)
.

Let
[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
a topological groupoid and
M
a topological space.
A
principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over
M
consists of a topological space
P
, with a continuous map
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
admitting local sections and a right action
(a_{\mathcal{G}},\mu)
of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
such that

1.

\pi(p\gamma)=\pi(p)
for all
(p,\gamma)\in P\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{G}_{1}
,

2.

the map
P\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow P\times_{M}P
,
(p,\gamma)\mapsto(p,p\cdot\gamma)
is a homeomorphism.

Definition 6.1.12
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
be a topological groupoid and
(P,\pi,M),(P^{\prime},\pi^{\prime},M^{\prime})
principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles. A
morphism
from
P(\pi,M)
to
P^{\prime}(\pi^{\prime},M^{\prime})
is given by a pair of continuous maps

(F\colon P\rightarrow P^{\prime},f\colon M\rightarrow M^{\prime})
, satisfying the following compatibility conditions

1.

a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}\circ F=a_{\mathcal{G}}
, and

F(p\cdot\gamma)=F(p)\cdot\gamma
for all

(p,\gamma)\in P\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}\mathcal{G}_{1}
,

2.

\pi^{\prime}\circ F=f\circ\pi
.

Example 6.1.13
.

Let
\mathcal{H}=[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
be a topological groupoid. The target map
t\colon\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
can be considered a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle, with action of
\mathcal{H}
given by the pair, composition of arrows and the source map
s\colon\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
.

6.1.1
stack associated to a topological groupoid

In the same way as we pull-back a topological structure on a topological space along a continuous map, we have the notion of pull-back of a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over a topological space
M
along a continuous map
f:M\rightarrow M^{\prime}
.

Let
\pi:P\rightarrow M
be a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle, and
f\colon M^{\prime}\to M
a continuous map. Consider the set
f^{*}P=\{(p,m^{\prime})\in P\times M^{\prime}:f(m^{\prime})=\pi(p)\}
. The action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
induce an action of
\mathcal{G}
as
((p,n),\gamma))\mapsto(\mu(p,\gamma),n)
. The projection map
\pr_{2}:f^{*}P\rightarrow M^{\prime}
is then considered as a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle. We call
\pr_{2}:f^{*}P\rightarrow M^{\prime}
to be the pull-back of
(P,\pi,M)
along the map
f:M\rightarrow M^{\prime}
.

We use the above notion of pull-back of principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle along a continuous map to introduce the notion of a pseudo-functor associated to a topological groupoid.

Let
\mathcal{G}
be a topological groupoid. Let
M
be an object of
Top
. Consider the category of principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles over
M
,
B\mathcal{G}(M)
.

For the same reason as in the class of principal
G
-bundle for a Lie group
G
, any morphism of principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundles of the form
(F,1_{M})
is an isomorphism. So,
B\mathcal{G}(M)
is a groupoid for each object
M
of
Top
. Thus, we get a pseudo-functor
B\mathcal{G}\colon\text{Top}^{\rm op}{\rightarrow\text{Gpd}}\subset\text{Cat}
, with the following description:

•

an object
M
in
\rm{Top}
to the category of
\mathcal{G}
-bundles over the topological space
M
,

•

a continuous map
f\colon M^{\prime}\to M
is sent to a functor
B\mathcal{G}(f)\colon B\mathcal{G}(M)\to B\mathcal{G}(M^{\prime})
defined by the pull-back of principal bundles

For a morphism
(F\colon P_{1}\to P_{2},{\rm Id}_{M})
in
B\mathcal{G}(M)
, the morphism
(f^{*}P_{1}\to f^{*}P_{2},{\rm Id}_{M^{\prime}})
in
B\mathcal{G}(M^{\prime})
is the unique morphism defined by the universal property of the pull-back diagram with respect to the maps
f\colon M^{\prime}\to M
and
P_{2}\to M
.

Example 6.1.14
.

Let
\mathcal{G}
be a topological groupoid. The pseudo-functor
B\mathcal{G}:\text{Top}^{\op}\rightarrow\text{Gpd}
is a stack over the site
(\text{Top},\mathcal{J})
.

As in the smooth setup, we will be interested in stacks that are isomorphic to
B\mathcal{G}
for some topological groupoid
\mathcal{G}
.
In the smooth case, we declare a stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Man}
to be a differentiable stack, if there is a morphism of stacks
\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
with an extra condition. In the continuous case, we define topological stacks to be stacks that come from topological groupoids.

Definition 6.1.15

(topological stack

[
18
]
)
.

Let
(\text{Top},\mathcal{J})
be the site of topological spaces with open cover topology. A stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Top}
is called a
topological stack
if there exists a topological groupoid
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
and an isomorphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\cong\mathcal{D}
.

Remark 6.1.16
.

In
[
54
, Definition
7.1
]
the topological stack defined above has been called a pretopological stack. Whereas the topological stack in the same paper has been defined [Definition
13.8
.] as a pretopological stack with some additional conditions.

Example 6.1.17
.

Let
X,Y
be topological space, and
f\colon X\rightarrow Y
be a continuous map. Let
\underline{X}
and
\underline{Y}
be stacks associated to
X
and
Y
respectively. Then, the map
f\colon X\rightarrow Y
induces a morphism of stacks

F\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\underline{Y}
defined by compositions (both at the level of objects and at the level of morphisms)

Likewise, for the smooth set up, we want to characterize topological stacks in terms of morphisms of stacks from a topological space. First of all, let us recall the notions of representable morphism and epimorphism of stacks from
Chapter

2
.

Let
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
be a subcanonical site. A stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
over the site
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
is said to be a
representable stack
if there exists an object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
and an isomorphism of stacks
\mathcal{D}\cong\underline{U}
.

A morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
a
representable morphism
, if for each object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
and a morphism of stacks
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, the
2
-fiber product stack
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\underline{U}

is representable by an object of
\mathcal{S}
.
A morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is said to be
an epimorphism of stacks
, if for each object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
and a morphism of stacks
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, there exists a covering
\{\sigma_{\alpha}\colon U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and a family of morphisms
\{q_{\alpha}\colon\underline{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\}
such that the following diagram is
2
-commutative

Definition 6.1.18
.

Let
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\text{Top}
be a stack. Let
X
be a topological space. A morphism of stacks
f\colon\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is said to be
an atlas for the stack
\mathcal{D}
if, for every topological space
Y
and a morphism of stacks
\underline{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
, the
2
-fibered product
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y}
is representable by a topological space
X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y

and the map of topological spaces
X\times_{\mathcal{D}}Y\rightarrow Y
associated to the morphism of stacks
{\rm pr}_{1}\colon\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{Y}\rightarrow\underline{Y}
is a map of local sections.

An epimorphism of stacks can be described in terms of local sections, which we discuss below.

Remark 6.1.19
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{C}
be stacks over a subcanonical site
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{J})
.
Then it is easy to see that a morphism of stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism of stacks, if and only if for each object
U
of
\mathcal{S}
and an object
b
of
\mathcal{C}(U)
, there exists a cover
\{U_{\alpha}\rightarrow U\}
of
U
and objects
a_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{D}(U_{\alpha})
such that
F(a_{\alpha})\cong b|_{U_{\alpha}}
in
\mathcal{C}(U_{\alpha})
for each
\alpha
.

As we will see in the next result, an epimorphism of topological stacks can be described in terms of maps that admit local sections.

A morphism of topological stacks

there exists a topological space

, a map of local sections

Proposition 6.1.21

(
[
18
]
)
.

A stack
\mathcal{D}
over
Top
with the open cover topology is a topological stack (
Definition

6.1.15
) if and only if it has an atlas, that is, a representable epimorphism of stacks
\underline{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
for an object
X
of
Top
.

We end this section by making a note of the following properties of a topological stack.

Lemma 6.1.22
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a topological stack. Then, for every topological space
X
, any morphism of stacks
X\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is representable.

Proof.

Let
X
be a topological space,
\mathcal{X}
a topological stack, and
p:X\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
a morphism of topological stacks. As
\mathcal{X}
be a topological stack, the diagonal morphism
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}
is a representable morphism (
[
54
, Proposition
7.2
]
).

Let
Y
be a topological space and
g:Y\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
a morphism of stacks. We show that
X\times_{\mathcal{X}}Y
is a representable stack.

Consider the morphism of stacks
(p,g):X\times Y\rightarrow\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}
. As
the diagonal morphism
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}
is representable, the
2
-fiber product
\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}}(X\times Y)
is representable (by a topological space). Moreover, by
[
46
, Corollary
69
]
,
\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}}(X\times Y)\cong X\times_{\mathcal{X}}Y
, and hence,

X\times_{\mathcal{X}}Y
is representable. Thus,
p:X\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is a representable morphism of topological stacks.
∎

As a consequence, we have the following result that produces an atlas from a map of local sections. We have a similar result in the case of smooth setup (
Remark

2.3.23
). We have omitted the proof in the smooth setup. Here we give proof for the continuous case.

Lemma 6.1.23
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be a topological stack and
X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
. Then, for any map of local sections
Y\rightarrow X
, the composition
Y\rightarrow X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
.

Proof.

As
\mathcal{D}
is a topological stack, any morphism of stacks
\underline{P}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is a representable morphism. In particular,
Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is a representable morphism of stacks.

Let
M
be a topological space and
M\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
a morphism of topological stacks. As
X\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas, the
2
-fiber product
\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{M}
is representable by a topological space and
{\rm pr}_{2}:\underline{X}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{M}\rightarrow\underline{M}
is a map of local sections, as in the

Thus, for any topological space
M
and a morphism of topological stacks
\underline{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
, the
2
-fiber product
\underline{Y}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{M}
is representable by a topological space and the projection map
\underline{Y}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\underline{M}\rightarrow\underline{M}
is a map of local sections. Hence,
Y\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for
\mathcal{D}
.
∎

6.2
Morphism of topological groupoids and topological stacks

Definition 6.2.1

(
[
46
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]
and
\mathcal{H}=[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
be a pair of topological groupoids. A
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
consists of

•

a topological space
P
,

•

a left action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P
given by the pair
(a_{\mathcal{G}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0},\mu_{\mathcal{G}}\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},a_{\mathcal{G}}}P\rightarrow P)
,

•

a right action of
\mathcal{H}
on
P
given by the pair
(a_{\mathcal{H}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0},\mu_{\mathcal{H}}\colon P\times_{a_{\mathcal{H}},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow P)
,

satisfying the following conditions:

1.

the map
a_{\mathcal{G}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
is a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle,

2.

the map
a_{\mathcal{H}}\colon P\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
is
\mathcal{G}
-invariant, ; that is
a_{\mathcal{H}}(\gamma\cdot p)=a_{\mathcal{H}}(p)
for all
(\gamma,p)\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{\mathcal{G}_{0}}P
,

3.

the action of
\mathcal{G}
on
P

is compatible with the action of
\mathcal{H}
on
P
, that is

\gamma\cdot(p\cdot\delta)=(\gamma\cdot p)\cdot\delta
for each
(\gamma,p,\delta)\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0},a_{\mathcal{G}}}P\times_{a_{\mathcal{H}},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}
.

We denote a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle by
P\colon\mathcal{G}\to{\mathcal{H}}
.

Example 6.2.2
.

Let
[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
be a topological groupoid and
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle. The map
\pi:P\rightarrow M
gives an action of the topological groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows M]
on the topological space
P
. Thus,
P
is considered as a
[M\rightrightarrows M]-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle. We call
P
to be the
[M\rightrightarrows M]-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle associated to the principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
.

Example 6.2.3
.

Let
(\phi_{1},\phi_{0})\colon[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
be a morphism of topological groupoids. As the target map
t\colon\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
is a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle, its pull-back
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}\mathcal{H}_{1}
is given by the pull back of
t\colon\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
along
\phi_{0}\colon\mathcal{G}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
. Then the map
\text{pr}_{1}\colon\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}
and the map

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{1}\times_{s,\mathcal{G}_{0}}(\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1})\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1},

\displaystyle(\gamma,(a,\delta))\mapsto(t(\gamma),\phi_{1}(\gamma)\circ\delta)

define a left action of
\mathcal{G}
on
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}
. Whereas
s\circ\text{pr}_{2}\colon\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{0}
and the map

\displaystyle(\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1})\times_{\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1},

\displaystyle((a,\delta),\delta^{\prime})\mapsto(a,\delta\circ\delta^{\prime})

define a right action of
\mathcal{H}
on
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}
. Then we have a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}
. We call it the
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle associated to the morphism of topological groupoids
(\phi_{1},\phi_{0})\colon[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
and, denote it by
\mathcal{G}_{0}\times_{\phi_{0},\mathcal{H}_{0},t}\mathcal{H}_{1}\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
.

6.2.1
morphism of topological stack
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
associated to a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle

Consider a
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle
Q\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
. Let
M
be a topological space, and
\pi\colon P\rightarrow M
be a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle. As mentioned in
Example

6.2.2
, we see
(P,\pi,M)
as a
[M\rightrightarrows M]-\mathcal{G}
-bibundle. The composition
P\colon[M\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow\mathcal{G}
and
Q\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
then gives a
[M\rightrightarrows M]-\mathcal{H}
bibundle
P\circ Q\colon[M\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
, which is nothing but a principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle over a topological space
M
. This produces a morphism of stacks
BQ\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
. The morphism of stacks
BQ\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
will be called the morphism of stacks associated to the
\mathcal{G}-\mathcal{H}
-bibundle
Q\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
.

6.2.2
a morphism of topological stacks associated to a morphism of topological groupoids

Let
(\phi_{1},\phi_{0})\colon[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{G}_{0}]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}_{0}]
be a morphism of topological groupoids. Combining
Example

6.2.3
with construction in
Section

6.2.1
, we have a morphism of topological stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
associated to
(\phi_{1},\phi_{0})\colon\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
. This morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
will be called the morphism of topological stacks associated to the morphism of topological groupoids
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
.

In this paper, we will particularly be interested in a special type of morphism of stacks, known as a gerbe over topological stack.

Definition 6.2.4

(a gerbe over a topological stack
[
54
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a topological stack. A morphism of topological stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is said to be
a gerbe over the topological stack
\mathcal{C}
, if

•

the morphism
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is an epimorphism of topological stacks,

•

the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism of topological stacks.

With this, we conclude our review of standard material.

6.3
Topological groupoid extension and the associated morphism of stacks

In the paper
[
39
]
, the authors claimed without many details that there is a possible relation between gerbes over differentiable stacks and Lie groupoid extensions. In
[
21
]
we have given an explicit construction for the correspondence between differentiable gerbes and Lie groupoid extension, with some additional conditions imposed on the differentiable gerbe. But, in the topological set-up, the notion of a groupoid extension has not been explored. So, in this paper, we introduce the notion of topological groupoid extensions and study the correspondence with gerbes over topological stacks.

Definition 6.3.1

(topological groupoid extension)
.

Let
[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
be a topological groupoid. A
topological groupoid extension of
[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
is a morphism of topological groupoids

(F,1_{M})\colon[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]

such that
F\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}
admits local sections. We often denote such a topological groupoid extension by
F\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M
.

Now, we introduce the notion of Morita morphism of Lie groupoid extensions and Morita equivalent topological groupoid extensions imitating the notion of Lie groupoids setup.

Let
[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
be a topological groupoid and
J:P_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
be a map of local sections. Let
P_{1}
denote the fiber product

P_{0}\times_{J,\Gamma_{0},s}\Gamma_{1}\times_{t,\Gamma_{0},J}P_{0}
. Then
[P_{1}\rightrightarrows P_{0}]
has a topological groupoid structure with source and target maps being the projection maps
{\rm pr}_{1},{\rm pr}_{3}\colon P_{1}\rightarrow P_{0}
respectively. We call
[P_{1}\rightrightarrows P_{0}]
to be the
pull-back groupoid
of
[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
along
J\,\colon\,P_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
.

A morphism of topological groupoids
[\Delta_{1}\rightrightarrows\Delta_{0}]\rightarrow[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
is said to be a
Morita morphism of topological groupoids
if
\Delta_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
is a map of local sections and
[\Delta_{1}\rightrightarrows\Delta_{0}]
is isomorphic to the pullback groupoid of
[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
along the morphism
\Delta_{0}\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}
.

Definition 6.3.2
.

Let
[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
and
[\Delta_{1}\rightrightarrows\Delta_{0}]
be a pair of topological groupoids. We say that
[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
and
[\Delta_{1}\rightrightarrows\Delta_{0}]
are
Morita equivalent
if there exists a third topological groupoid
[P_{1}\rightrightarrows P_{0}]
with a pair of Morita morphisms

[P_{1}\rightrightarrows P_{0}]\rightarrow[\Delta_{1}\rightrightarrows\Delta_{0}]
and
[P_{1}\rightrightarrows P_{0}]\rightarrow[\Gamma_{1}\rightrightarrows\Gamma_{0}]
.

Definition 6.3.3

(Morita morphism of topological groupoid extensions)
.

Let
\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
and

\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M
be a pair of topological groupoid extensions.
A
Morita morphism of topological groupoid extensions
from
\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
to

\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M
is given by a pair of Morita morphisms of topological groupoids,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
and
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

(6.3.1)

such that the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

(6.3.2)

is commutative.

Definition 6.3.4

(Morita equivalent topological groupoid extensions)
.

Let
\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
and

\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M
be a pair of topological groupoid extensions. We say that
\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}
and

\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M
are
Morita equivalent topological groupoid extensions
, if there exists a third topological groupoid extension
\phi^{\prime\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow Y^{\prime\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime\prime}
and a pair of Morita morphisms of topological groupoid extensions

(\phi^{\prime\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow Y^{\prime\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime\prime})\rightarrow(\phi\colon X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightrightarrows M)

and

(\phi^{\prime\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow Y^{\prime\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime\prime})\rightarrow(\phi^{\prime}\colon X_{1}^{\prime}\rightarrow Y_{1}^{\prime}\rightrightarrows M^{\prime}).

Let
(F,1_{M})\colon[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
be a topological groupoid extension. This morphism of topological groupoids gives a morphism of stacks
F:B\mathcal{G}\to B\mathcal{H}
.
We will see in the following result that this morphism
B\mathcal{G}\to B\mathcal{H}
is a gerbe over a topological stack.

Theorem 6.3.5
.

Let
F\colon[\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]\rightarrow[\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M]
be a topological groupoid extension. Then, the associated morphism of topological stacks
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is a gerbe over the topological stack
B\mathcal{H}
.

Proof.

Step1:
We first prove that
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
is an epimorphism of topological stacks.

Let
U
be an object of
Top
and
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
be a morphism of topological stacks. Let
\pi:Q\rightarrow U
be the principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle associated to the morphism of stacks
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
.

Since
\pi:Q\rightarrow U
admits local sections, there exists an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\to U\}_{\alpha\in\Lambda}
of
U
and a family of maps
\{\sigma_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\to M\}
, such that
\pi|_{\pi^{-1}U_{\alpha}}\colon\pi^{-1}(U_{\alpha})\rightarrow U_{\alpha}
is pull-back of the trivial principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle
t\colon\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightarrow M
.

Next, we pull-back the principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle
t\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow M
along the morphism
\sigma_{\alpha}\colon U_{\alpha}\rightarrow M
to obtain a principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle over the topological space
U_{\alpha}
, for each
\alpha
. In turn we obtain a morphism of topological stacks
q_{\alpha}\colon\underline{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}
. So, given a morphism of stacks
q\colon\underline{U}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
, we have an open cover
\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in\Lambda}
and morphism of stacks
q_{\alpha}\colon\underline{U_{\alpha}}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}
forming the
2
-commutative diagram

(6.3.3)

The
2
-commutativity of the diagram follows from the observation that the morphism of stacks
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
maps the pull-back of the principal
\mathcal{G}
-bundle along a map
\eta\colon U\rightarrow M
to the pull-back of the principal
\mathcal{H}
-bundle along a map
\eta\colon U\rightarrow M
(
[
21
, Lemma
5.5
.]
).

We now prove that the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism of stacks. Observe that, the
2
-fiber product
\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
is a topological groupoid. As the stackification and Yoneda embedding are preserved under
2
-fiber product, we see that
B(\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G})\cong B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
. It turns out that the
2
-fibered product
\mathcal{G}\times_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{G}
is a transitive topological groupoid and so is Morita equivalent to a topological groupoid
(K\rightrightarrows*)
for some topological group
K
(
[
21
, Lemma
5.8
, Lemma
5.9
]
). So, the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{H}
is equivalent to morphism of stacks
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B(K\rightrightarrows*)
. By similar justification as in the case of
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
, we can see that
B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B(K\rightrightarrows*)
is an epimorphism of stacks. Thus, the diagonal morphism
\Delta_{F}\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B\mathcal{G}\times_{B\mathcal{H}}B\mathcal{G}
is an epimorphism of stacks. In conclusion, the morphism of topological stacks associated to a topological groupoid extension
\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
is a gerbe over the topological stack
B\mathcal{H}
.
∎

.

The condition that
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism implies that the morphism
p\colon\underline{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an epimorphism of stacks. On the other hand the morphism
p:\underline{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is an atlas for the stack
\mathcal{D}
follows from the fact that
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable map of local sections. The atlases
p:\underline{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
and
q:\underline{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
respectively produce the topological groupoids
(V\times_{\mathcal{D}}V\rightrightarrows V)
and
(V\times_{\mathcal{C}}V\rightrightarrows V)
representing the stacks
\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{C}
respectively. The morphism of stacks
F:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
will then induce a morphism of topological groupoids
(f,1_{V})\colon(V\times_{\mathcal{D}}V\rightrightarrows V)\rightarrow(V\times_{\mathcal{C}}V\rightrightarrows V)
. The condition that
\Delta_{F}\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{D}
is a representable morphism of local sections further impose the condition that
f\colon V\times_{\mathcal{D}}V\rightarrow V\times_{\mathcal{C}}V
is a map of local sections. Thus, we get a topological groupoid extension associated to a gerbe over a topological stack
\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
satisfying the extra condition that
\Delta_{F}
is a representable morphism of local sections. The Morita invariance follows from the corresponding argument in
[
21
]
.
∎

6.4
Serre, Hurewicz fibrations and gerbes

In this section, we will recall the notions of Serre and Hurewicz stacks introduced in
[
58
]
and study certain properties of a gerbe over such stacks.

Definition 6.4.1

(
[
58
]
)
.

A topological stack
\mathcal{D}
is said to be a
Hurewicz stack
(respectively,
Serre stack
) if it admits a presentation
\mathbb{X}=[R\rightrightarrows X]
by a topological groupoid in which the source (hence also the target) map
s\colon R\rightarrow X
is locally a Hurewicz fibration (respectively, Serre fibration).

Let
(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)
be a topological groupoid with the source map
s\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow M
being a locally a Hurewicz fibration (respectively, Serre fibration). Then
B\mathcal{G}
is a Hurewicz stack (respectively, Serre stack).

Definition 6.4.2

(
[
58
]
)
.

A morphism of topological stacks
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is said to be a Hurewicz (respectively, Serre) morphism if for every object
U
of
Top
and a morphism of topological stacks
U\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, the fiber product
\mathcal{D}\times_{\mathcal{C}}U
is a Hurewicz (respectively, Serre) stack.

We say that a gerbe
F\colon\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is a
Hurewicz gerbe
(respectively, a
Serre gerbe
), if the underlying morphism of stacks is Hurewicz (respectively, Serre).

A straightforward consequence of the results
Theorem

6.3.5
and
[
58
, Lemma 2.4.]
is the following proposition.

Proposition 6.4.3
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)
be a topological groupoid with the source map
s\colon\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightarrow M
a locally a Hurewicz fibration (respectively, Serre fibration) and
F\colon(\mathcal{G}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)\rightarrow(\mathcal{H}_{1}\rightrightarrows M)
a topological groupoid extension. Then the gerbe
F\colon B\mathcal{G}\rightarrow B{\mathcal{H}}
constructed in
Theorem

6.3.5
is a Hurewicz gerbe (respectively, Serre gerbe).

We give an alternate proof of
[
58
, Lemma 2.4.]
.

Lemma 6.4.4
.

[
58
]

Let
f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
be a morphism of topological stacks. If
\mathcal{X}
is a Serre or Hurewicz stack, then
f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
is a Serre or Hurewicz morphism of stacks.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a Serre stack, that is, there exists a topological space
X
and an atlas
X\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
such that the source and target maps of the associated topological groupoid
[X\times_{\mathcal{X}}X\rightrightarrows X]
are (locally) Serre fibrations of topological spaces.

Let
Y
be a topological space and
g:Y\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
a morphism of topological stacks. We show that the fiber product
\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
is representable by a topological groupoid
[M\rightrightarrows N]
whose source and target maps are (locally) Serre fibrations of topological spaces.

Let
R
denote the fiber product
X\times_{\mathcal{X}}X
, and
R\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
be the composition
R\rightarrow\mathfrak{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
. Let
X\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
denote the composition
X\rightarrow\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
. Consider the following pull-back diagrams,

As
\mathcal{Y}
is a topological stack, the map
R\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
is representable (
Lemma

6.1.22
), thus, the fiber product
R\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
is representable by topological space. For the same reason,
X\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
is representable, thus, the fiber product
X\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
is representable by topological space.

By pulling back
s:R\rightarrow X
along the map
X\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y\rightarrow X
we obtain a map
R\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y\rightarrow X\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
. As
s:R\rightarrow X
is a Serre fibration, the pull-back
R\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y\rightarrow X\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
is a (locally) Serre fibration. Similarly,
t:R\rightarrow X
(a (locally) Serre fibration of spaces) is pulled back to give a morphism
R\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y\rightarrow X\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
(which would be a (locally) Serre fibration of spaces). Similarly, the other structure maps on
[R\rightrightarrows X]
is pulled back to produce a topological groupoid
[R\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y]
. It turns out that
\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
is representable by
[R\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y\rightrightarrows X\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y]
. Thus,
\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{Y}}Y
is a Serre stack. The same proof goes verbatim if we consider
\mathcal{X}
to be a Hurewicz stack instead of Serre stack.
∎

An immediate outcome of the above lemma is the following.

Corollary 6.4.5
.

Any morphism of stacks
B[X\rightrightarrows X]\rightarrow B\mathcal{H}
induced by a morphism of topological groupoids
[X\rightrightarrows X]\rightarrow\mathcal{H}
is a Serre morphism as well as a Hurewicz morphism.
